en: The Dhāraṇī Sūtra of the Sovereign Who Protects the Realm of the Nation, Scroll One.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Śramaṇa Prajña of Kapiśa together with Munisri.
Part One: The Prologue. Chapter One: The Prologue.
Thus have I heard.
At one time the Bhagavān was staying at the city of Gayā,
not far from the city, beneath the Bodhi tree.
He was accompanied by a great assembly of seven thousand bhikṣus,
all of whom were great arhats whose outflows were exhausted and who were free from further afflictions.
Having done what was to be done and accomplished what was to be accomplished,
his mind was well-liberated and his wisdom was well-liberated;
like a great dragon, he had attained the knowledge of recollecting past lives.
Having already cast off the heavy burden and attained their own benefit,
they have exhausted the fetters of the three realms of existence and shall not undergo further rebirth;
regarding all phenomena, they have attained true knowledge.
They have deeply penetrated the nature of phenomena and reached the further shore;
they are skillful in the Dharma and born from the transformation of the Dharma;
their minds are free from attachment toward both what is favorable and what is adverse.
His speech was harmonious and pleasant, and he inquired after others' welfare with forethought.
His holy life was pure, his right mindfulness was bright and clean,
and he had already attained perfection in the path to liberation.
Only Ānanda remained on the stage of training (śaikṣa-bhūmi).
There were also eighty-four thousand bodhisattva-mahāsattvas,
all of whom were destined to attain awakening in their final birth.
Spontaneously and deeply penetrating to the very source of all-knowledge, the Buddhas of the ten directions constantly appear before them.
They attain the dharani-door of non-attachment.
They dwell in the various samādhi-gates of Śūraṅgama,
having attained great mastery in the playful exercise of supernormal powers and the various gates of liberation.
Having already transcended all obstacles of affliction,
they universally cover all worlds throughout the ten directions with great compassion,
traveling everywhere through the boundless oceans of lands within the Dharma-realm.
Entering the nature of space by means of the mark of non-abiding,
they constantly and diligently benefit all sentient beings,
having attained skillfulness regarding the realm of the Buddhas.
The mind, intellect, and wisdom are vast and immeasurable,
like space; they are profoundly deep and boundless, like the great ocean.
Abiding immovably like Mount Sumeru;
unstained by attachment like a lotus flower;
pure within and without like a mani jewel.
His radiance was blazing like molten pure gold.
He possessed such an immeasurable and boundless accumulation of merits as these.
His names were the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Samantabhadra and the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Samantanetra.
The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Samantadarśin, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Samantaprabha,
the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Samantajvāla,
and the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Jayamati.
The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas Vṛddhimati, Anantamati, Vaipulyamati, Vipulamati, Akṣayamati, and Dharaṇīdharamati.
The Bodhisattva Sustaining the Intentions of All Beings, the Bodhisattva Attaining Supreme Intent,
the Bodhisattva Skillfully Discerning Intent, the Bodhisattva Sovereign King of Dhāraṇīs,
the Bodhisattva Holding the Precious Torch, and the Bodhisattva Jewel-Seal Hand.
Bodhisattva Ratnacūḍa, Bodhisattva Ratnaśikhin,
Bodhisattva Ratnakūṭa, Bodhisattva Ratnasaṃbhava,
Bodhisattva Ratnaśṛṅga, and Bodhisattva Ratnadhvaja.
Vajragarbha Bodhisattva, Śrīgarbha Bodhisattva, Vimalagarbha Bodhisattva, Viśuddhigarbha Bodhisattva,
Tathāgatagarbha Bodhisattva, and Jñānagarbha Bodhisattva.
The Bodhisattva Sūryagarbha, the Bodhisattva Samantagarbha,
the Bodhisattva Padmagarbha, the Bodhisattva Vimukticandra,
the Bodhisattva Samantacandra, and the Bodhisattva Mahāsthāmaprāpta.
The Bodhisattva Universal Vision, the Bodhisattva Lotus-Eye,
the Bodhisattva Vast Adorned Eye, the Bodhisattva Universal Dignified Conduct,
the Bodhisattva Universal Uprightness, and the Bodhisattva Universal Practice-Mind.
The Bodhisattva Wisdom-Mind, the Bodhisattva Dharma-Mind,
the Bodhisattva Vajra-Mind, the Bodhisattva Lion’s Play,
the Bodhisattva Sovereign King of Great Clouds, and the Bodhisattva Lion’s Fierce Roar.
The Bodhisattva Vast and Profound Wondrous Sound, the Bodhisattva Unstained Attachment,
the Bodhisattva Free from All Defilements, the Bodhisattva Moonlight Flame,
the Bodhisattva Sunlight Flame, and the Bodhisattva Wisdom Light Flame.
The Bodhisattva Jñānaśrī, the Bodhisattva Candanaśrī, the Bodhisattva Padmaśrī, the Bodhisattva Bhadraśrī,
the Bodhisattva Ratnaśrī, and the youthful Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī.
Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva, Maitreya Bodhisattva, and others were their leaders;
all of them were destined to attain bodhi within this Bhadrakalpa.
Together with eighty-four thousand such bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, [he sat].
Furthermore, there were immeasurable gods of the Four Great Kings,
with the Four Great Heavenly Kings as their leaders;
there were also immeasurable sons of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven.
Śakra Devānām Indra was their leader.
Furthermore, there were immeasurable Suyāma devaputras,
with the King of the Suyāmas as their leader.
Furthermore, there were immeasurable devaputras of Tuṣita,
with the King of Tuṣita as their leader;
and there were also immeasurable devaputras of Nirmāṇarati.
The King of the Heaven of Delight in Emanations was the chief,
and there were also immeasurable sons of the gods from the Heaven of Mastery over Others' Emanations,
with the King of the Heaven of Mastery over Others' Emanations as their chief.
Furthermore, there were the Sunlight Deva King, the Full-Moon Deva King, and the Merchant-Chief Deva King,
each accompanied by an immeasurable retinue of devas;
there was also the Great Brahma Heavenly King.
Together with an immeasurable host of Brahmā deities,
there were also the various gods of the Śuddhāvāsa heavens and the celestial king Maheśvara,
each accompanied by an immeasurable retinue.
In this way, immeasurable devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, and mahoragas were each accompanied by their own immeasurable hundreds of thousands of retinues.
Furthermore, there were immeasurable bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, and upāsikās,
each accompanied by their retinues;
such was this boundless assembly of all beings.
Each arrived at the place where the Buddha was, prostrated at his feet,
withdrew to sit on one side, and respectfully surrounded him.
At that time, the Tathāgata sat upon the vajrāsana amidst the assembly.
His majestic virtue is so towering that it surpasses all,
like Mount Sumeru rising above the great ocean;
his radiant marks shine brilliantly, eclipsing everything else.
He is like the bright sun rising high in the void;
to those who behold him, he is as refreshing as the full moon in autumn;
his body and mind are as tranquil as the Great Brahma King.
He is revered by all like Śakra, Lord of the Devas;
he possesses the seven jewels of the noble ones like a wheel-turning monarch;
and he resolutely proclaims the emptiness of phenomena and selflessness with the roar of a lion.
The radiance shines through all worlds,
like a great fire kindled in the darkness of night;
emitting various kinds of light, it universally illuminates all worlds throughout the ten directions.
Like a celestial maṇi jewel and a mass of various precious gems, he is free from discrimination;
like a great elephant king, he subdues the enmity of Māra and crushes all heterodox views;
like a pure pool, his mind remains unstained by turbidity whether confronted with favorable or adverse circumstances.
He dwells among the multitude without fear, like a lion.
His wisdom is profound and vast, immeasurable and boundless;
it is impossible to reach its bottom, and it gives rise to a treasury of all merits and virtues, like the great ocean.
Like a great dragon, he universally rains down the rain of Dharma, moistening and saturating all beings so that they may grow and reach maturity;
he is endowed with such immeasurable merits as these.
At that time, the entire assembly joined their palms in single-minded devotion.
Beholding the Tathāgata, they conceived the thought that such an encounter is difficult to find.
At that moment, as the Tathāgata’s great compassion and compassionate eyes surveyed all beings and his body-light shone everywhere, the King of Bodhi Trees—
For seven yojanas on each of its four sides,
both upon the earth and in the sky, the assembly of the eight classes of beings— gods, nāgas,
and others— completely filled the surrounding area.
There is not even a space the size of a mote of dust or the tip of a hair where no assembly of noble ones is present.
The Vajra Seat upon which the Tathāgata resides is one yojana in height,
and its length and breadth are each exactly half a yojana.
Upon it were spread countless hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of exquisite celestial garments;
various jeweled canopies were suspended, with nets and bells hanging down, and banners and streamers made of various precious silks were displayed.
Arranged in rows and established all around, they hung suspended on all four sides of the seat.
The ground was composed entirely of vajra,
as level as the palm of a hand, pure, lustrous, fragrant, and soft.
When he stepped upon it, his foot sank in; when he lifted it, it returned to its original state.
All sentient beings who saw this rejoiced without ever growing weary.
At that time, the various devas, in order to make offerings to the Buddha, rained down exquisite celestial flowers.
That is to say: the campaka flower, the atimuktaka flower, the pāriyātaka flower, the māndārava flower, the mahāmāndārava flower, the mañjūṣaka flower, and the mahāmañjūṣaka flower.
With these various kinds of celestial flowers,
they scattered them over the Buddha and the great assembly, completely covering the ground.
A gentle breeze stirred them, emitting a sublime fragrance that wafted forth and cleansed all impurities.
Suddenly, from that ground, there emerged countless hundreds of precious lotus flowers,
as large as chariot wheels, with petals of pure gold and stalks of *vaiḍūrya* lapis lazuli, numbering each by hundreds of thousands of millions.
Its pedestal is made of indranīla mani-jewels,
and its filaments are made of asmagarbha jewels;
they emit various exquisite fragrances that surpass those of all the devas.
These flowers are soft, radiant, pure, and smooth;
sentient beings who behold them can never tire of them.
Should anyone touch them, they are able to eliminate their feverish afflictions, and both body and mind become cool and refreshed.
All these were manifested as auspicious omens for the purpose of making offerings to the Tathāgata.
At that time, at the four corners of the Vajrāsana,
neither too near nor too far, [these signs appeared].
There were jeweled trees, each sprouting from the earth;
these trees were each composed of the seven treasures,
their trunks rising to a height of two and a half yojanas.
Its branches and leaves spread out to cover one yojana.
At that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Mañjuśrī Dharmaputra gazed upon the Tathāgata,
who was seated upon the Vajra-throne amidst the great assembly.
His majestic virtue was preeminent and his radiance was brilliantly manifest;
it eclipsed the great assembly, surpassing a hundred thousand suns,
and outshone all other splendors within the entire congregation.
Beholding him without weariness, he gave rise to a pure mind.
He immediately rose from his seat, knelt with his right knee on the ground, joined his palms,
and praised the Buddha with these sublime verses:
The majestic presence of the Tathāgata is immeasurable, transcending humans, devas, and all the sages;
like the full moon in a clear sky, it eclipses the brilliance of all the stars.
Abiding within the great ocean of compassion, the Buddha radiates hundreds of thousands of rays of light that shine forth brilliantly.
Just as Mount Sumeru rises from the great ocean, Where the devas dwell and radiate light,
So should you abide in the meditative concentration of liberation, Radiating sovereign light that illumines all.
Like the Great Brahmā Lord of the Trichiliocosm, Your tranquil radiance transcends all Brahmā heavens.
Adorning the mind with merit and wisdom, his precious marks adorn the body and its light shines everywhere like the radiance of Śakra; surpassing all the gods of the Trāyastriṃśa heaven,
he is self-adorned with the intent of great compassion, establishing sentient beings upon the noble path.

Just as the Four Heavenly Kings protect the world, The Buddha-Sun constantly radiates the light of Dharma, Consoling, encouraging, and transforming all sentient beings, Universally illuminating them to extinguish false views;
Like the radiance of a thousand suns shining forth, It outshines the brilliance of mani jewels and fire.
The Buddha’s face is perfectly round and its features are sublime; Those who behold it find joy and their minds become pure.
Like the full, clear moon at midnight, Sentient beings delight in seeing it and attain refreshing coolness.
The Great Sage constantly radiates the light of wisdom, Extinguishing all the darkness of ignorance.
Like a great mass of fire upon a high mountain at night, whose radiance shines forth and leaves nothing distant unilluminated;
so the Buddha has taught that all phenomena are empty and selfless.
All non-Buddhists are terrified by this, like the roar of a lion from within a mountain cave, which causes the hundred beasts who hear it to lose their vital luster.
The Buddha’s body is like a mountain of molten purple gold; His radiance outshines the great assembly, Just as the brilliance of a mani jewel Surpasses and eclipses the light of all other jewels.
Through the gates of merit, wisdom, and skillful means, He is diligent and adept in all things.
Surveying the world, I see none who are his equal; how much less could anyone surpass the World-Honored One?
I behold the Great Hero, who takes pity on the world; he is an ocean of wisdom, his radiance shining forth.
I prostrate myself at the Buddha’s feet, leaping for joy, unable to contain my own delight.
I praise the Tathāgata, the lamp of the world, who is able to produce supreme wisdom and merit;
by this accumulation of merit, may all sentient beings quickly realize great bodhi.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta—
Having spoken these verses in praise of the Buddha,
he joined his palms in reverence, gazed up at the Tathāgata without averting his eyes for a moment, and focused his mind single-mindedly on the state in which the Tathāgata abides.
The subtle and wondrous nature of phenomena is extremely profound and difficult to enter;
it is not a characteristic that can be seen, being hard to perceive and hard to understand.
It is not within the realm of ordinary fools or non-Buddhist practitioners.
It is subtle, wondrous, tranquil, and inconceivable.
It can give rise to the peerless wisdom of all Buddhas, which is inconceivable.
It flows forth the diverse teachings of the Dharma-realm, which is inconceivable.
Only the Tathāgata has thoroughly and completely understood this,
abiding in the realm of space where there is no abiding,
having directly realized the limit of reality— the intrinsic purity of the nature of all phenomena.
They attain the unimpeded liberation of all Buddhas,
abiding eternally and unchangingly in peace, bliss,
and tranquility; their bodies pervade all buddha-fields.
It manifests universally before all sentient beings,
entering the equal source and foundation of the three periods of time;
it is not a realm that can be measured by the mind or consciousness.
Even if one were to contemplate and proclaim this for immeasurable eons, it could never be exhausted.
Mañjuśrī, having thus scrutinized and minutely observed the profound nature of phenomena, remained silent.

Chapter Two: Dhāraṇī Section, Part One of the *Sūtra on the Protector of the State*. At that time, the World-Honored One, abiding in the dharma-nature that is equal throughout the three periods of time, entered into samādhi.
He is named "Universally Accordant with the Mental Conduct of Sentient Beings.
By the power of samādhi, within that assembly,
he is able to discipline all the great multitude as required.
Each perceives the Buddha in various different ways.
That is to say, some sentient beings perceive the Tathāgata’s body endowed with the primary and secondary marks;
others perceive the body of a śrāvaka.
Some sentient beings see the body of a bodhisattva;
some sentient beings see the body of Brahmā;
and some sentient beings see the body of Maheśvara.
There may be sentient beings who see the body of the god Nārāyaṇa,
and so on, up to the various distinctions among the eight classes of gods, nāgas, humans,
non-humans, and others; yet those without faith see nothing at all.
It is like those born blind who do not see the sun or the moon;
those who are able to see perceive his various physical postures according to their own respective natures.
According to their respective vocal types, they hear various sounds;
according to what they delight in, they hear various teachings;
and according to their respective capacities, they give rise to various understandings.
Although the Tathāgata’s body appears according to the various cognitions and views of sentient beings, it is of a single flavor and non-dual;
that is to say, the single flavor of liberation.
It is like space, which is free from all coarse and subtle discriminations as well as non-discrimination;
it is also like the great earth, which can support everything mundane and supramundane.
The eight classes of gods and dragons dwell supported by it,
growing, developing, and maturing without weariness;
furthermore, just as the element of fire can burn the fuel of sentient beings' afflictions without ever becoming weary.
Furthermore, it is like the element of wind, which can waft away all the dust and grime of afflictions without ever becoming weary;
and it is also like the element of water, which can nourish and cause all the roots of goodness of all sentient beings to grow.
Having removed the heat of afflictions, they attained the bliss of coolness and were free from weariness.
At that time, the World-Honored One suddenly emitted a great radiance from the skin, bones, and pores within the *uṣṇīṣa* on the crown of his head.
That light was brilliant white;
furthermore, with immeasurable hundreds of thousands of rays as its retinue, it illuminated the world universally,
reaching downward to the Avīci Hell and upward to the Akaniṣṭha Heaven.
Everything that exists was entirely white.
Within it, all sentient beings saw all mountains, forests, rivers, oceans,
and all things animate and inanimate as being uniformly bright white, like the color of milk.
It was also like the Snowy Mountains;
furthermore, from his mouth he emitted a great radiance the color of sapphire,
with immeasurable hundreds of thousands of rays of light as its retinue.
It illuminated the eastern direction,
extending from the east of the Vajrāsana as far as worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges River;
all that was therein— mountains, rivers, stone walls, grasses, trees, and forests— was likewise revealed.
Sentient beings and insentient objects alike are all the color of Indra-blue.
Within that realm, all sentient beings perceive everything as being the color of Indra-blue.
Furthermore, from his right shoulder, he emits a great radiance like the color of molten gold.
Furthermore, with immeasurable hundreds of thousands of light rays as its retinue,
it illuminates the southern direction,
extending from the south of the Vajrāsana as far as the worlds of the Ganges-sand in the south.
Everything therein was of molten golden color;
those sentient beings also saw everything as being of molten golden color.
Furthermore, from their backs, they emitted a great radiance of red crystal color.
Furthermore, with immeasurable hundreds of thousands of rays of light as its retinue,
it illuminates the western direction,
extending from west of the Vajrāsana to the worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges throughout the entire western quarter.
Everything therein was the color of red crystal,
and the sentient beings within it also saw everything as being the color of crystal.
Furthermore, from his left shoulder, he emitted light of five colors.
That is to say, blue, yellow, red, white, and green; these,
with immeasurable hundreds of thousands of light rays as their retinue,
illuminate the northern direction.
From the north of the Vajrāsana to the limit of the worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges in the northern direction,
everything therein was entirely five colors;
the sentient beings within that region also saw everything as being endowed with these five colors.
In this manner, all the worlds thus illuminated extend from each individual world downward as far as the Avīci Hell and upward as far as the Akaniṣṭha Heaven, illuminating all those worlds.
Having performed the Buddha-work, the light retracted and returned to its source;
that white light then descended from above,
came to where the Buddha was, and circled the Tathāgata to the right.
Having circled three times, it entered through the crown of the Buddha’s head.
A light of deep blue color then emerged from the east,
approached the Buddha, circled him three times to the right, and entered through his mouth.
The golden light returned from the south and came to where the Buddha was;
it circled him three times to the right and entered his right shoulder.
The light of red crystal color returned from the west.
It came to where the Buddha was, circled him three times to the right, and entered his back;
the five-colored light then returned from the north,
came to where the Buddha was, circled him three times to the right, and entered his left shoulder.
Although this radiance spreads forth to illuminate and then withdraws,
the body of the Tathāgata neither increases nor decreases.
It is like the moonlight that shines everywhere throughout space without increasing or decreasing.
It is also like water, oil, or melted butter;
when cast into a heap of sand, there is neither increase nor decrease.

Furthermore, it is like the floating clouds that rise from the Snowy Mountains and pervade the void, which in an instant are withdrawn back to the Snowy Mountains without leaving so much as a trace of fiber.
Yet the substance of that Snowy Mountain neither increases nor decreases.
At that time, the World-Honored One again entered samādhi; this samādhi has no name.
It is beyond words, beyond speech, and inconceivable;
it is the realm of all Buddhas, the wisdom of omniscience.
Having entered into samādhi, [he beheld it].
At that time, this great earth shook in six ways:

namely, rising in the east and sinking in the west; rising in the west and sinking in the east; rising in the south and sinking in the north; rising in the north and sinking in the south; rising in the center and sinking at the edges; and rising at the edges and sinking in the center.
At that time, there was a bodhisattva mahāsattva in the assembly named Sarvadharmaviśeṣavikrāmin.
Empowered by the Buddha’s spiritual authority, he immediately rose from his seat.
Adjusting his physical deportment, he bared his right shoulder,
prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, knelt with palms joined, and addressed the Buddha,
saying: "World-Honored One, by what cause and by what condition [did this occur]?"
A great radiance was emitted and the earth shook in six ways.
At that time, the Buddha addressed the Bodhisattva Sovereign King of All Dharmas, saying:
"Excellent, excellent, son of good family!"
You have now skillfully raised this question;
I shall explain it to you in detail.
Noble son, there are four causes and conditions for the emission of this light and the great trembling of the earth.
What are the four? First,
all Buddhas of the three periods of time have, by entering this supreme samādhi,
attained anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
I, too, likewise cultivated all the perfections throughout three incalculable eons;
yet, despite six years of ascetic practice, I did not realize bodhi.
It was by entering this samādhi that I attained unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening.
For these reasons, this auspicious omen has appeared.
Second, because this samādhi is beyond verbal expression,
its essential nature is quiescent and cannot be proclaimed.
He manifested this auspicious sign because he intends to preach for the sake of sentient beings through the power of skillful means.
Third, in the past, beneath this very Bodhi tree...
Having attained this samādhi, one achieves perfect enlightenment.
Out of gratitude for this kindness, I now teach this samādhi at this place;
all Buddhas of the three periods of time do likewise.
In all these places, this samādhi was preached;
therefore, he manifested this auspicious sign.
Fourth, he desired to act for the sake of worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges throughout the ten directions.
Countless bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who had come from afar,
as well as King Ajātaśatru, the ruler of the kingdom of Magadha,
along with bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, and upāsikās.
To the devas, nāgas, yakṣas,
and all beings in this assembly as well as throughout the entire dharma realm,
he preached this samādhi.
For these reasons, this auspicious omen has appeared.
When the great assembly heard this teaching, they leaped for joy with exultation;
their bodies and minds became cool and refreshed.
Overwhelmed by grief and longing, he could not contain himself.
It was as if someone had been struck in the heart by a poisoned arrow;
having no other thought, he thought only of a skilled physician.
"Extract the poisonous arrow and grant us peace and happiness.
The assembly of Bodhisattvas is likewise;
they long only for the Tathāgata to preach this samādhi of inconceivable dharmas.
They pull sentient beings out from the great night of birth and death;
they shatter the darkness of ignorance where there is no knowledge or vision,
destroy all afflictions, open the eye of the True Dharma, and attain the light of wisdom.
At that time, although those in the assembly conceived this thought,
they did not dare to inquire because of the Buddha’s majestic power.
Then, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Sovereign King of All Dharmas...
Receiving the Buddha’s spiritual power,
he prostrated himself with his five limbs touching the ground to worship the Buddha’s feet;
then, kneeling with palms joined, he addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Bhagavān, as for that inconceivable samādhi of the realm of all Buddhas—
the wisdom of omniscience— by what dharma does it have its cause,
and by what dharma does it have its root?"
"How is it cultivated? How is it brought to completion?
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Sovereign King of All Dharmas, saying:
"Excellent, excellent, son of good family!"
"You have now skillfully inquired about this meaning.
It will bring great benefit and great peace and happiness to all sentient beings in future ages.
Listen attentively, listen attentively, and reflect upon it well; I shall explain it for you."
Good son, this profound samādhi takes the bodhicitta as its cause and great compassion as its root.
One practices skillful means with unsurpassed bodhi as the ultimate goal.
Good son, what herein is called bodhi?
Good son, if you wish to know bodhi, you must understand your own mind.
If one realizes one's own mind, one immediately realizes bodhi.
Why? Because the true nature of both mind and bodhi, when thoroughly investigated, is ultimately unfindable.
Because it is identical to empty space,
the characteristic of bodhi is itself the characteristic of empty space.
Therefore, bodhi has no characteristic that is realized, nor any characteristic that realizes.
Furthermore, there is no characteristic of the union between subject and object.
Why? Because bodhi is ultimately devoid of all characteristics.
Son of good family, this is because all dharmas are identical to the characteristic of empty space.
Therefore, bodhi is ultimately without marks.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Sovereign King of All Dharmas again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Blessed One, if this bodhi is identical to space,
what is there to be sought in the essence of omniscience?
How can one realize and manifest the presence of bodhi?"
"From where should the knowledge of all modes of knowledge (sarvajñajñāna) arise?
The Buddha addressed the Bodhisattva Sovereign King of All Dharmas, saying:
"Good son, the essence of the knowledge of all modes of knowledge should be sought within the mind."
The knowledge of all modes and awakening arise from the mind. Why is this?
Because the true nature of the mind is fundamentally pure.
Good son, this nature of the mind does not abide within,
nor does it abide without, nor does it abide in between.
Good son, all Tathāgatas have taught this characteristic of the mind.
It is neither blue nor yellow, neither red nor white;
it is neither crimson nor purple, nor is it golden in color.
It is neither long nor short, neither round nor square.
It is neither light nor darkness, neither male nor female;
it is neither non-male-and-non-female, nor is it both male and female.
Good son, this mind is not of the nature of the desire realm, not of the nature of the form realm, and not of the nature of the formless realm.
Neither deva, nor nāga, nor yakṣa, nor gandharva;
neither asura, nor garuḍa, nor kiṃnara, nor mahoraga.
Whether humans, non-humans, or any other similar beings—
good son, this mind does not abide in the eye,
nor does it abide in the ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind.
It cannot be seen even within the three periods of time.
Why is this? Because this mind has the same characteristic as empty space. For this reason:
It is far removed from all coarse and subtle conceptual discriminations. Why is this?
Because the nature of this space is itself the nature of the mind.
As the nature of the mind is the nature of bodhi,
so the nature of bodhi is the nature of dhāraṇī.
O son of good family.
Therefore, this mind is the nature of the *ākāśa-bodhi-dhāraṇī*;
it is non-dual and without division,
without distinction and without interruption.
All of these have great loving-kindness and great compassion as their root and are embraced by the perfection of skillful means. Therefore,
son of good family, you should know this.
I now, amidst this great assembly of bodhisattvas,
proclaim such a Dharma for the sake of purifying the vast bodhicitta.
In order to cause all beings to realize their own minds,
he is therefore the Sovereign King of All Dharmas.
If there are good sons or good daughters, [who...]
Those who wish to know the true nature of bodhi should understand their own minds;
for the nature of the mind is itself the nature of bodhi.
How can one thoroughly understand the nature of the mind?
It means that this nature of the mind, with respect to all marks— whether form or appearance,
or furthermore the aggregates of form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness— [is understood as being empty].
Furthermore, whether it be the objects of form, sound, smell,
taste, or touch— whether they are appropriated or non-appropriated,
whether they belong to the twelve bases (āyatana) or the eighteen elements (dhātu).
When such dharmas as these have been observed and sought after in this manner,
they are ultimately unfindable. Noble son, if bodhisattvas understand them thus,
they will achieve the first gateway of the light of the utterly pure dharma.
Having dwelled in this gateway,
one spontaneously attains this inconceivable samādhi of the profound realm of all Buddhas, which is the wisdom of omniscience.
Once the bodhisattva has attained this samādhi,
He becomes equal and peerless with all Buddhas;
he attains the *dhāraṇī-samādhi* of the languages of all sentient beings,
and further attains the *dhāraṇī-gate* that accords with the minds of all sentient beings.
They are always able to benefit sentient beings without interruption;
they are fully perfected within the unconditioned realm (*asaṃskṛtadhātu*) and remain far removed from all false views, such as the sixty-two [views] including those of nihilism and eternalism.
Right view is perfectly clear and luminous.
Good son, if bodhisattvas abide in this samādhi,
all Buddha-dharmas are accomplished spontaneously without the need for effort.
Good son, I have now spoken briefly.
If there are those who can abide in this samādhi,
they will all fully perfect immeasurable, boundless, and innumerable merits.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Sovereign King of All Dharmas again addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One,
as the Buddha has taught, the nature of space is itself the nature of the mind."
Just as the nature of the mind is the nature of bodhi,
so too is the nature of bodhi the nature of dhāraṇī. Thus, the nature of space,
the nature of the mind, the nature of bodhi, and the nature of dhāraṇī [are one].
That which is non-dual and undifferentiated—
such a meaning is exceedingly profound;
it is difficult to penetrate and difficult to enter.
It is inconceivable and transcends the realm of the mind;
it is not something that can be known by the inferior understanding of ordinary, ignorant people.
Within this assembly, there are two kinds of persons.
First, those who have fulfilled the stage of a bodhisattva will obtain benefit;
second, those who have not yet attained the accomplishment of a bodhisattva’s merits.
This would be of no benefit to the King Ajātaśatru, ruler of the kingdom of Magadha,
nor to the immeasurable multitude of beings, including bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, and upāsikās.
These foolish commoners are like those born blind who do not see the light of a lamp;
they are like the deaf who do not hear soft speech;
they are like saline wasteland where lotus flowers do not grow.
World-Honored One, it is as if there were a king, a minister, or a householder who, during a time of famine,
partakes of various delicious foods and the exquisite delicacies of the gods;
ascending to a high tower, he addresses immeasurable starving sentient beings, speaking these words:
Although I have partaken of such various superior flavors and have spoken these words, they have been of no benefit whatsoever to those who are hungry;
yet now, what the Buddha has taught here in this assembly [is of great benefit].
Those who have not yet attained accomplishment are likewise entirely without benefit.
At that time, the Buddha addressed the Bodhisattva Sovereign King of All Dharmas, saying:
"Excellent, excellent, son of good family!"
You are well able to inquire about such profound dharmas,
which bring great benefit and happiness to all sentient beings.
Listen attentively, listen attentively, and reflect upon them well.
I shall, for your sake and for this assembly,
employ various skillful means to instruct and guide you,
so that you may attain the inconceivable wisdom of omniscience— the profound samādhi that is the domain of all Buddhas.
Good son, if any sons of the Buddha desire to achieve *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*,
or if they wish to skillfully know their own minds, [they should practice this].
If there are those who wish to pull sentient beings out from the mire of birth and death with the hands of great compassion,
they should first give rise to the mind of great compassion and universally take refuge in the Triple Gem for the sake of all sentient beings.
Having received the Bodhisattva precepts and resolved upon the Bodhicitta,
one should repent with utmost sincerity, speaking these words:
"I only pray that all Buddhas of the ten directions..."
And may the great Bodhisattvas who dwell on the stages and have attained vajra-wisdom bear witness to me and remember me. We,
such-and-such persons, having resolved upon bodhicitta, have not yet entered the sublime path.
I now take refuge in the Triple Gem of the ten directions with my very body and life.
I pray that all Buddhas and great Bodhisattvas will give rise to hearts of compassion and pity, and graciously accept me.
We, [Name] and others, since beginningless time and throughout our wandering in saṃsāra,
have dwelt within the wheel of birth and death in the triple world, sinking into the evil destinies,
entering the cage of suffering, and falling headlong into various evils.
The rākṣasa of ignorance possesses great power;
the enemies of the various afflictions oppress [beings] throughout the long night.
They have no master, no protector, no refuge, and no support.
They have no destination and no teacher;
dwelling upon the treacherous path of wrong views,
they head toward birth and death while turning their backs on nirvana.
They enter the three evil realms and cannot emerge from them on their own;
they fall into vast, deep, and perilous pits,
pursuing evil companions and following corrupt teachings.
They remain far removed from all spiritual friends and do not perceive at all what is detrimental or what is beneficial.
What is wholesome and what is unwholesome? They remain bound by and attached to unwholesome dharmas, refusing to relinquish them,
and turning their backs on all the noble ones of the three vehicles.
Throughout the long night, they are constantly ensnared by the various delusions, karmas, and afflictions of birth, old age, sickness, death, sorrow, lamentation, suffering, and despair;
oppressed by anxiety and terror, they perpetually lose their original mind and its inherent tranquility.
They are far removed from the various gateways of samādhi and dhāraṇī;
they are likewise far removed from the profound abodes of the various stages, the various patiences, and the perfection of wisdom,
as well as from loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, equanimity, and the various bodhisattva precepts.
The four unhindered knowledges, the six supernormal powers,
the ten powers, the four fearlessnesses, the quality of non-forgetfulness, and non-abiding nirvāṇa—
all these latent tendencies are fully present within my own body.
All merits are absent from my body; it is empty and void.
Such dharmas as the seven factors of enlightenment and the eightfold noble path—hundreds of thousands of millions of such types—are all utterly remote from me.
Constantly afflicted by countless sufferings, afflictions, obstacles, and hindrances,
we pray that all Buddhas and great Bodhisattvas will give rise to great compassion,
pity us, and protect us with their mindful care.
May you be our lord, our savior, our refuge, our reliance, and our destination.
We pray that you cause us to swiftly attain the path of great bodhi and its immeasurable retinue of bodhi-qualities.
The Tathāgata’s ten powers, four fearlessnesses, four unhindered understandings,
eighteen unique qualities, four means of integration,
samādhis, liberations, dhāraṇīs, six supernormal knowledges, the perfections, merit, and wisdom.
May we all attain fulfillment in all such oceans of merit.
Furthermore, may all the Buddhas and great Bodhisattvas of the ten directions [behold us].
May you bear witness to me; may you take pity on me and accept my offerings.
May these offering articles be gathered and perfected, and may they pervade all worlds throughout the ten directions along with my own body.
Furthermore, they encompass the ten directions, which are without a sovereign,
and manifest vast adornments and immeasurable offerings to present before all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas as worship.
These are the various celestial palaces made of diverse exquisite jewels, each adorned with wonderful gems,
and arranged in rows with railings of many precious substances.
Jewel trees and jewel mountains served as its surrounding adornments;
there were jewel thrones, jewel canopies, jewel banners, and jewel pennants;
as well as jewel vessels, jewel gems, jewel bells, and jewel nets.
The Jewel Light, Jewel Flame, and Jewel Merit [continents],
each consisting of immeasurable and incalculable jewel islands,
were filled with heaps of maṇi jewels.
Various exquisite jewel-lamp trees were interspersed and adorned with diverse precious gems,
while a net of jewels emitting golden flames spread over them as a canopy.
Furthermore, there were countless exquisite jewel lotuses,
with pedestals made of Jāmbūnada gold and petals of pure gold,
their buds fully blossoming in radiant splendor.
They raise clouds of celestial jewels and rain down rains of celestial jewels;
they cause celestial jewel-trees to descend and scatter celestial jewel-flowers;
they emit the radiance of myriad jewels and open the treasuries of myriad jewels.
Furthermore, there were countless Jambūnada gold celestial palaces adorned with various jewels;
their exquisite jeweled corridors had walls made of diamond.
It was surrounded on all sides by railings made of various jewels,
and featured diverse celestial gardens and groves where flowering forests and fragrant herbs spread in profusion.
There were countless dragon palaces and asura palaces,
each containing various kinds of forest trees, halls, incense, flowers, and precious vessels;
such things were immeasurable and boundless.
Never having personally used any of the various precious offerings,
he dedicated them all toward making offerings to the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas of the ten directions.
Furthermore, he gathered all kinds of wondrous medicines from every world throughout the ten directions.
Furthermore, the celestial sweet dew and the various precious delicacies of the heavens—
complete with perfect color, fragrance, and flavor—
are also gathered; moreover, all worlds throughout the ten directions are encompassed.
There are various trees of exquisite fragrance:
*karpūra* trees, *candana* trees, seasonal fragrance trees, and large-leafed fragrance trees;
these trees have flowers blooming continuously throughout the four seasons, their fragrances being most wonderful and sublime.
If anyone smells them, they become profoundly tranquil, serene,
and ethereal. Such immeasurable varieties of fragrant trees possess such intense and pervasive aromas that they can captivate the human heart.
Furthermore, there are various kinds of wish-fulfilling trees and the like that lack a presiding owner;
whatever one desires according to the mind's aspiration is fully satisfied.
Within the great ocean, there are various kinds of *maṇi* gems and wish-fulfilling jewels.
Furthermore, there are various kinds of Mount Meru,
Mahāmeru, Kalāsa, Gandhamādana, Malaya, and Vindhya mountains.
Mount Māndhara and Mount Mahāmāndhara; Mount Meru and Mount Mahāmeru;
Mount Vajra, and so forth—such are the mountain peaks.
Adorned with various jewels were the various jeweled pavilions;
there were various jeweled rock caves and various jeweled canopies and awnings;
there were various jeweled halls and various jeweled stairways.
It has windows and casements made of various jewels, adorned with various precious substances;
it possesses beams, pillars, and treasuries of various jewels,
and walls of various jewels such as vaidūrya.
Furthermore, there are various wondrous celestial palaces of diverse forms and colors,
which are without any presiding lords;
there are also various exquisite celestial flowers, such as the *kusu-ma* and others.
Those who behold it never tire of it; it is cool, refreshing, and delightful.
Furthermore, there are various kinds of exquisite sounds that bring peace and happiness to the bodies and minds of those who hear them.
Free from all feverish afflictions, one attains cool serenity;
greed and anger are severed and subdued, while the poison of delusion is dispersed and extinguished;
evil karma is destroyed and eliminated without remainder.

That is to say, there were the voices of Śakra, Lord of Devas, and the voices of Brahmā, Lords of Devas, as well as the various voices of the devas; the sounds of songs chanted by great celestial nymphs;
and the subtle, exquisite sounds produced by the various musical instruments of the devas without being struck.
The sounds of flutes, pipes, harps, lutes, zithers, and conch shells;
the sounds of the drums of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven and the mṛdaṅga drums;
and furthermore, the various songs of the celestial birds.
And as for the mountain forests, springs, and flowing streams,
there are the sounds of birds, namely: white cranes, peacocks, wild ducks, geese,
mandarin ducks, *kukkuta* birds, and *jīvajīvaka* birds.
There were the warbling sounds of various excellent birds such as the kalaviṅka,
as well as the exquisite voices of deer kings and other creatures,
and furthermore, the various sounds of clouds.
The sounds of earth, water, fire, and wind;
the sounds of the great ocean’s waves and surges— such sounds as these,
if heard by anyone, can all be understood and appreciated without weariness.
The faculty of hearing is tranquil and its sound is deep and far-reaching;
it is true and clear, capable of generating roots of goodness,
and fully endowed with phonemes, phrases, and sentences.
It accords with meaning, accords with the profound principle of the Dharma, and perfectly conforms to the requirements of the occasion.
It is the sound of the equality of the three vehicles;
it is the sound that expounds the three types of supernormal knowledge (*vidyā*).
The sound of the adornment of the dāna-pāramitā;
the sound of the purity of the śīla-pāramitā;
the sound capable of generating the kṣānti-pāramitā.
The sound of diligently practicing the perfection of vigor;
the sound of accomplishing the perfection of meditative concentration;
the sound of the vast perfection of wisdom.
The voice of great loving-kindness is in harmony with the mind;
the voice of great compassion is in harmony with awakening;
the voice of great sympathetic joy is in harmony with light and shadow.
The sound of great equanimity equal to empty space;
the sound of giving birth to the three vehicles; the sound of the uninterrupted continuity of the Three Jewels;
the sound of discerning the three categories of beings; and the sound of the purity of the three emptinesses.
It is the sound of observing the Four Noble Truths, the sound of observing wisdom,
the sound that the wise do not disparage, the sound praised by the noble ones, and the sound whose measure is equal to space.
Such pure sounds as these are emitted.
They dedicate these offerings to all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas.
Furthermore, there are various kinds of flowering trees that emit wondrous fragrances,
and various kinds of garland trees from which hang many garlands and ribbons.
Various banner-trees were erected high and prominent;
various pennant-trees joined their shadows and linked their brilliance.
Holding all such exquisite objects as these, they stood there.
With a mind free from self-attachment, one dedicates this offering to all Buddhas and great Bodhisattvas.
Furthermore, with the eyes of all Buddhas beholding it,
there are vast clouds of great offerings throughout the infinite worlds of the ten directions.
They were used as offerings,
namely: clouds of various flowers, clouds of various fragrances,
clouds of garlands, clouds of canopies, clouds of ointment-fragrance, and clouds of powdered incense.
Clouds of jewel canopies, clouds of jewel thrones, clouds of jewel banners,
clouds of exquisite jewel robes, and clouds of various precious requisites.
Clouds of the supreme flavors of the heavens, clouds of clusters of maṇi jewels,
and such various clouds of offerings of immeasurable colors and kinds of precious substances—
these are dedicated as offerings to all Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, and others.
Furthermore, one should further aspire that a small chiliocosm becomes a single lamp-vessel,
filled with fragrant oil equal in volume to a hundred Mount Sumerus,
with a wick made of precious flames that is lit.
Emitting great radiance, they make offerings to all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas.
Such offerings are inexhaustible.
Furthermore, one should then entreat all Tathāgatas.
Go to the Bodhi tree to subdue the hosts of Māras,
attain equal and perfect enlightenment, and turn the wondrous wheel of Dharma;
remain for great kalpas and do not pass into parinirvāṇa.
Furthermore, one should dedicate these various roots of goodness to sentient beings, making this vow:
"May all sentient beings swiftly realize anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
When dedicating in this manner:
One does not perceive the mind that performs the dedication;
one does not grasp at the object toward which it is directed;
and one does not cling to the roots of goodness being dedicated—thus, the three spheres are pure.

Furthermore, I rejoice in all the merits of all Tathāgatas, all Bodhisattvas, and all sentient beings, as well as those of all such categories; moreover, I make this aspiration: by means of these roots of goodness...
"May all our obstacles and extremely heavy evil karmas be completely extinguished.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke this Dharani of Dedication:
Oṃ samāra samāra vimana sara mahākāra va hūṃ. The Buddha said: "The various kinds of offering implements described above..."
By means of this power of dedication through the dhāraṇī,
one attains the fulfillment of true offerings before all Buddhas,
and all Buddhas will fully embrace and sustain one.
If any son of good family or daughter of good family is able,
at this great wheel of dedication dharani gateway,
whether at the proper time or the improper time, by day or by night, [to practice it...]
Recite this silently once while observing and visualizing it.
With these previously prepared offerings, reverently make offerings to all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas.
By the power of this, even the most grievous karmic offenses, such as the five crimes of immediate retribution, will all be extinguished.
How much more so for minor offenses, which will not fail to be eliminated.
All afflictions shall become as slight as previously described,
and one will be fully endowed with the ten powers, the fearlessnesses, and all other such meritorious qualities.
If a person contemplates this dhāraṇī even once for a moment,
they will immediately attain birth in the palace of Śakra for one hundred lifetimes,
and further attain birth in the palace of Brahmā for one hundred lifetimes.
In dreams at night, one shall see Buddhas and Bodhisattvas expounding the sublime Dharma, and shall have no evil dreams.
One shall achieve mastery in all dhāraṇīs and be protected and sustained by the Vajrapāṇi Bodhisattva.
Rebirth in the Pure Lands of all Buddhas according to one’s vows.
*The Dhāraṇī Sūtra of the Sovereign Who Protects the Realm*, Scroll One.
*The Dhāraṇī Sūtra of the Sovereign Who Protects the Realm*, Scroll Two.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Prajñā of Kaśmīra together with Munisri.
Chapter Two on Dhāraṇīs, Part Two.
At that time, the World-Honored One turned his gaze toward the great assembly like an elephant king.
He further addressed the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Sovereign King of All Dharmas, saying:
"Good son, within this assembly there are two kinds of persons:
first, those who have attained accomplishment; second, those who have not yet attained accomplishment."
I now, for the sake of those who have not yet attained realization,
employ skillful means in accordance with conventional truth,
using analogies and words to expound the Dharma of the One Vehicle.
Just as there is a dharma in the world called Garuḍa;
if one wishes to cultivate this dharma, one should first draw an image of the Garuḍa and observe it with meticulous attention until the practice of contemplation becomes fully matured.
However, remove the hand seals from the painted image and visualize yourself as a garuḍa,
performing the five great visualizations.
First, one contemplates the earth as having the color white.
Second, one contemplates water as having the color green.
Third, one contemplates fire as having the color yellowish-red.
Fourth, one contemplates wind as a black-colored visualization.
Fifth, one contemplates space as a blue-colored visualization.
Once these visualizations are accomplished, all poisons become non-poisons.
That is to say, whether it be poison from sentient beings or poison from non-sentient things,
he may cause them to be exchanged, or take them, or discard them,
exercising complete mastery and autonomy. Son of good family, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva is also like this.
If one wishes to enter meditative contemplation,
one should first silently recite this previously mentioned dharani-gate of dedication;
thereafter, one should enter the samādhi of the Tathāgata Vairocana.
That is to say, one contemplates this body as being composed of vajra, firm and indestructible.
One should then assume the vajra-paryanka posture,
pressing the right foot upon the left thigh.
With body upright and sitting straight, move the tongue slightly;
with lips and teeth joined, produce the "Vajra Speech.
Vajra Speech means that there is no vocal sound, but one silently recites it within the mind.
With firm and stable wisdom, one should contemplate one's own mind as a lunar disc.
One should fix it upon the tip of the nose so that it does not wander or scatter.
It is pure and perfect, its color like frozen snow, cow’s milk, or crystal.
This lunar disc is the bodhicitta.
This bodhicitta is fundamentally devoid of color or form;
it is described as being like a lunar disc for the sake of sentient beings who have not yet attained realization.
One should form a vajra-fist with the right hand and grasp the index finger of the left hand at the heart;
this is called the Supreme Seal that Grants Unsurpassed Bodhi.
This is the seal of the Original Teacher, Vairocana Tathāgata.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke this dhāraṇī:
Oṃ hūṃ jaḥ huḥ phaṭ. How should one contemplate this dhāraṇī?
One should place the syllable Oṃ within the lunar disc visualized previously and position it upon the crown of the head;
contemplate this syllable Oṃ as being white in color like snow or a conch shell.
Once this visualization is accomplished,
one sees oneself seated within a moon disc,
thereby attaining the realization of Vairocana.
By means of such immeasurable and boundless wisdom, as numerous as the atoms of dust, this body is perfected.
This is what is called "possessing all-knowledge" (sarvajñatā),
and it is also called "possessing vajra-wisdom."
This is the yogic wisdom of the practitioner of meditation; it is also the *prajñāpāramitā*,
and it is likewise called the fruit of all bodhisattvas.
This fruit can attain three kinds of reality. What are the three?
First, one attains the samādhi of the inconceivable omniscient wisdom (*sarvajñajñāna*), which is the realm of all Buddhas, as previously described.
Second, one obtains the aforementioned true secret mantra;
third, one obtains the aforementioned true secret mudrā.
Once the preceding visualization has been accomplished:
Then, one should imagine white light emerging from the crown of the head,
with hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of rays as its retinue,
extending downward as far as the Avīci Hell.
Upward as far as the Akaniṣṭha Heaven,
all sentient beings therein have been blinded by the darkness of ignorance throughout beginningless birth and death, lacking the eye of wisdom.
By means of this lamp of the prajñāpāramitā, one opens the Buddha-eye for them.
It is like a deep mountain valley in a place of profound darkness,
which cannot be illuminated by the light of the sun or the moon.
Just as a single lamp removes all long-standing darkness,
for such is the nature of phenomena (*dharma*),
so too is it with the white light emitted from the samādhi of the Tathāgata Vairocana.
Furthermore, son of good family,
once the practitioner has arisen from this samādhi,
they next enter the Immovable Samādhi (Acalasamādhi).
Facing west, one should likewise assume the vajra-paryaṅka posture with the body held upright and sit correctly; then,
with the left hand, one should take hold of the garment being worn.
The two prongs cross over and encircle his wrists;
grasping them with his fists, the two prongs emerge above,
while his right hand presses upon the ground.
This is called the Seal that Subdues;
all Māras, heterodox teachers, afflictions,
karmas, and the like cannot move it.
This is the mudrā of Akṣobhya Tathāgata.
Next, one should also silently recite the mantra of Vairocana Tathāgata as previously described;
one should place the syllable HŪṂ within a moon disc at the crown of the head.
Visualize this syllable HŪṂ as being blue.
Once the visualization is complete,
next visualize that the entire body becomes blue.
This body immediately becomes the Tathāgata Akṣobhya.
Once this visualization is accomplished, blue light radiates from the crown of the head,
accompanied by a retinue of countless hundreds of thousands of billions of rays of light.
Within each and every ray of light,
there appear immeasurable blue Vajrasattva Bodhisattvas,
each forming this mudrā.
The light shines upon worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges in the eastern direction.
Among them, all sentient beings who encounter this light will have all their malicious intentions for deception, plunder, and killing extinguished.
Having completely relinquished all [distractions], he remains tranquil and unmoving.
Son of good family, once the practitioner has arisen from this samādhi,
he again sits facing north on the southern side.
One should also assume the aforementioned vajra-paryaṅka posture, sitting upright with the body straight;
the left hand holds the two corners of the robe as before,
while the right hand has its palm facing upward in the mudrā called Pūrṇamanoratha (Fulfilling the Vow).
This is the mudrā of the Tathāgata Ratnasaṃbhava.
Next, recite again the mantra of the Tathāgata Vairocana and perform the visualization of the syllable JAḤ.
One should place this syllable within a moon disc at the crown of the head, visualizing it as having the color of molten gold;
once this has been accomplished, one should gradually visualize the entire body becoming the color of molten gold.
This body immediately becomes the Tathāgata Ratnasaṃbhava.
Once this visualization is accomplished, golden light is emitted from the crown of the head,
with countless hundreds of thousands of billions of rays as its retinue.
Within each and every ray of light, there appeared immeasurable golden Vajra Bodhisattvas,
each forming this mudrā.
From the hands of each and every Bodhisattva, wish-fulfilling jewels rained down.
The light shines upon worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges in the southern direction.
Among them, all sentient beings who encounter this light have all their aspirations and requests fulfilled.
Again, facing east in the western direction,
he likewise sat upright with his body straight in the vajra-paryaṅka posture as described above;
his left hand, with the palm facing upward, rested upon his navel.
With the right hand, palm facing upward, placed upon the left hand,
the thumbs are brought together so that their tips touch.
This mudrā is called the mudrā of the foremost and most excellent samādhi.
To extinguish all deluded thoughts and mental agitation, and to cause the mind to become one-pointed,
this is the seal (mudrā) of the Tathāgata Amitābha.
Furthermore, recite the aforementioned mantra of the Tathāgata Vairocana and perform the visualization of the protective level-toned syllables.
One should place this syllable within a moon disc upon the crown of the head,
visualizing it as the color of a red lotus;
having completed this visualization, one should gradually contemplate the entire body as being the color of a red lotus.
This body immediately becomes the Tathāgata Amitābha.
Once this visualization is accomplished, light in the color of a red lotus is emitted from the crown of the head,
with countless hundreds of thousands of billions of rays of light serving as its retinue.
Within each ray of light, there appeared immeasurable Bodhisattvas with the color of red lotuses;
each entered a profound samādhi while forming this mudrā,
and the light illuminated worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges in the western direction.
Among those beings, all who encountered this light entered into samādhi.
Furthermore, he sat facing south on the northern side,
likewise assuming the aforementioned vajra-paryaṅka posture, sitting upright and straight.
With the left hand as before, grasp the two corners of the robe;
with the right hand, extend the palm and straighten the five fingers,
holding it at the shoulder and facing outward— this is called "Bestowing Fearlessness" (abhaya-mudrā).
This mudrā can bestow peace, happiness, and fearlessness upon all sentient beings;
no evil person can harm or afflict them.
It is the mudrā of the Tathāgata Amoghasiddhi.
Next, recite the mantra of the Tathāgata Vairocana once more;
perform the visualization of the syllable *SAḤ*, and place this syllable within the moon disc upon the crown of your head.
Possessing the five colors,
once the visualization is perfected, one gradually contemplates that the entire body becomes the five colors,
thereby becoming the Tathāgata Amoghasiddhi.
Once this contemplation is accomplished, five-colored light is emitted from the crown of the head,
with countless hundreds of thousands of billions of rays as its retinue.
Within each ray, there appear immeasurable bodhisattvas of five-colored radiance.
Each forms this mudrā, bestowing fearlessness upon all.
Light illuminates worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges in the northern direction;
all sentient beings within them who encounter this light attain fearlessness.
The Buddha again addressed the Bodhisattva Sovereign King of All Dharmas, saying:
"The Dharma of self-realization as described above can only be known through personal realization;
it cannot be expressed in words and is free from all marks of views."
For the sake of sentient beings who have not yet attained accomplishment,
he manifests signs within signlessness and proclaims through conventional speech that which is beyond words.
It is like a city of Gandharvas in the sky;
it is not a reality that can be realized as real.
At that time, the Buddha again addressed the Bodhisattva Sovereign King of All Dharmas.
Then the great assembly spoke:
"O sons of the Buddha, throughout all worlds in the ten directions,
there are immeasurable, incalculable hundreds of thousands of myriads of kotis of sentient beings of diverse kinds."
There may be sentient beings whose faculties are incomplete,
or those who have committed the five deeds of immediate retribution,
such as butchers, executioners, and caṇḍālas.
Within all these inconceivable samādhis, everyone has the capacity to cultivate and enter them,
with the exception of five types of persons. What are these five?
First is lack of faith; second is the view of nihilism; third is the view of eternalism; fourth is false view; and fifth is doubt.
These five types of sentient beings are unable to enter [the path].
Why is this? Because this profound samādhi takes great compassion as its root,
whereas these five people lack compassion.
Good son, if there should be anyone who can practice this samādhi even for a brief moment,
their body and mind will become light and tranquil.
One is then able to give rise to five kinds of samādhi. What are these five?
First, the kṣaṇa-samādhi; second, the paramāṇu-samādhi.
Third is the samādhi of gradual manifestation; fourth is the samādhi of rising and falling; fifth is the samādhi of stable abiding.
What is called the "momentary samādhi" (kṣaṇa-samādhi)?
It refers to contemplating the lunar disc moment by moment.
Because it is maintained for only a brief moment and then lost again,
it is called the "momentary samādhi" (*kṣaṇika-samādhi*).
What is called the "dust-like samādhi" (*rajas-samādhi*)?
This refers to a partial correspondence with samādhi;
for example, it is like a person who does not recognize the taste of honey,
yet obtains a mere speck of it upon the root of their tongue.
Delighting in peace and happiness, one completely forgets thoughts of hunger, thirst, or illness;
one merely focuses the mind with even greater intensity on the hope of obtaining more.
This samādhi-mind is also like this.
Having completely forgotten all afflictions and the thirst of hunger through partial correspondence,
the mind attains peace and happiness and seeks further advancement.
What is called the Samādhi of Gradual Manifestation?
That is to say, through the gradual increase and intensification of the love, joy, and bliss obtained from even a small amount,
the hairs of the body all stand on end and one weeps with streaming tears,
like seeing a single white thread amidst black objects.
In this way as well, by contemplating the lunar disk,
one attains a slight degree of stability amidst the darkness of ignorance and the afflictions;
one perceives a subtle manifestation of the concentrated mind.
What is called the "rising-and-falling samādhi"?
It refers to a state where contemplative practice is not yet pure, such that [the mind] alternately arises and ceases.
Just as a scale rises and falls, when contemplation is perfected, delusion ceases; when contemplation is lost, delusion arises.
What is called "abiding in samādhi"?
By means of the preceding four dhyānas, the mind attains stability and is able to fully protect all wholesome dharmas.
One’s new wholesome qualities increase and the body and mind attain peace and happiness,
like one who has traveled far through sandy deserts during the height of summer and,
after long enduring heat and thirst, suddenly finds the pure, cool, and delicious water of the Snowy Mountains.
All feverish thirst, grief, and suffering are eliminated;
likewise, upon attaining this samādhi,
karma, afflictions, and all distress are entirely dispelled.
This is the sprouting of the seed of unsurpassed bodhi.
Good son, as for those beings mentioned above who lack physical faculties,
those who have committed the five acts of immediate retribution, and other evil sentient beings—

If even those who have merely entered this stage possess such potential for cultivation, how much more so for all the bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, and upāsikās? Noble son, now that these countless beings in this great assembly have heard this Dharma, they shall surely enter [the path].
They all attained non-retrogression in *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
Their supernatural powers, the ten powers, and the four fearlessnesses increased with every thought-moment,
and countless samādhis all manifested before them.
These are the samādhi of wearying detachment from all phenomena, the samādhi of transcending all phenomena,
the samādhi of the equality of all phenomena, and the samādhi of departing from the dense forest of all views.
The samādhi of being far removed from the darkness of ignorance; the samādhi of all phenomena being devoid of marks;
the samādhi of liberation from all attachments; and the samādhi of being free from all indolence.
The Samādhi of Radiance from the Profound Dharma;
the Samādhi like Mount Sumeru;
the Samādhi of Perpetual Non-destruction; and the Samādhi of Crushing the Army of Māra.
The Samādhi of Non-attachment to the Three Realms, the Samādhi of the Radiance Born from Samādhi,
the Samādhi of Constantly Beholding the Tathāgata—
these and others such as these serve as the foremost.
Innumerable samādhis all manifested before them.
Furthermore, there were immeasurable varieties of sentient beings who attained countless dharanī-doors.
These are the so-called dhāraṇī-gateways of contemplating the nature of all phenomena, the dhāraṇī-gateway of generating the aspiration for enlightenment,
the dhāraṇī-gateway of producing the sprout of enlightenment, and the dhāraṇī-gateway of realizing the vajra-nature.
They attained the dhāraṇī-door of the equality of all Buddhas, the dhāraṇī-door of the intrinsic purity of the nature of all phenomena,
the dhāraṇī-door of the inclusion within the intrinsic nature of all phenomena, and the dhāraṇī-door of the non-apprehensibility of the intrinsic nature of all phenomena.
The dharani-door of the birth of wisdom regarding all phenomena; the dharani-door of the complete accomplishment of all phenomena; the dharani-door of sovereign transformation of all phenomena;

the dharani-door of the universal illumination of the great light of all phenomena; the dharani-door of the removal of the darkness of delusion from all phenomena; and the dharani-door of the purification of the mental faculty regarding all phenomena.
The dharani-door of the non-apprehensibility of all phenomena; the dharani-door of universally scattering all manner of exquisite jewel-flowers;
the dharani-door of the manifestation of the intrinsic nature that gives birth to all phenomena; and the dharani-door of being far removed from all illusory and conjured phenomena.
The dhāraṇī door of producing images from a mirror-like clarity; the dhāraṇī door of producing the vocal sounds of all sentient beings;
the dhāraṇī door that causes all sentient beings to experience supreme joy; and the dhāraṇī door of skillfully conforming to the vocal sounds of all sentient beings.
The dhāraṇī door of producing various sounds, phrases, and syllables; the dhāraṇī door of being without obstruction;
the dhāraṇī door of natural skillful means; and the dhāraṇī door of liberation from afflictions.
The dhāraṇī door of being free from all defilements, the dhāraṇī door of discerning the meanings of syllables,
the dhāraṇī door of understanding all phenomena, and the dhāraṇī door of the unimpeded limit of all phenomena.
It is like the *dhāraṇī* gate of empty space; it is like the *dhāraṇī* gate of the vajra.
It is the *dhāraṇī* gate of the King of Proximate Radiance, which attains the most supreme and honored *dhāraṇī* gate.
The Dharani-gate of the Non-retrogressive Eye, the Dharani-gate Born of the Dharma-realm,
the Dharani-gate of Constant Bestowal of Consolation, and the Dharani-gate of the Lion’s Roar.
The dharani-door of surpassing the merit of sentient beings; the dharani-door of being free from all sorrow and affliction;

the dharani-door of being free from all faults and evils; the dharani-door of adornment with exquisite flowers; the dharani-door of shattering the net of all doubts; and the dharani-door of all dharmas conforming to suchness.
The dhāraṇī gate of the manifestation of all phenomena, the dhāraṇī gate of the Sovereign King of Great Sound and Purity,
the dhāraṇī gate of the inexhaustible jewel casket, and the dhāraṇī gate of the boundless whirlpool.
The Dharani-door of the Ocean Seal, the Lotus Adornment Dharani-door,
the Dharani-door capable of entering non-attachment, and the Dharani-door of gradually penetrating the four types of unimpeded wisdom.
The Dharma-gates of the *dhāraṇī* for being protected and adorned by all Buddhas—
such dharmas as these were foremost—
and immeasurable, incalculable *dhāraṇī* gates all appeared before him.
At that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Sovereign King of All Dharmas addressed the Buddha,
saying: "World-Honored One,
such are these countless dharani-doors."
What are the dharani-gates that enable a bodhisattva to retain all the sublime teachings spoken by the Buddhas without loss or corruption?
What are the dharani-gates?
It enables a bodhisattva to possess inexhaustible eloquence when preaching this Dharma.
What are these dharani-doors that enable a bodhisattva to cause all sentient beings to love, delight in, and rejoice at this Dharma when it is being preached?
The Buddha addressed the Bodhisattva Sovereign King of All Dharmas, saying:
"Good son, there are eight dharani-gates.
If one receives and upholds them, they can enable a bodhisattva to retain all the Buddha-dharmas."
Their eloquence is inexhaustible and beings delight in hearing it.
What are these eight?
They are the dhāraṇī gateways of the Great Voice, the Pure Sovereign King.
The Dharani-gate of the Inexhaustible Treasure Casket;
the Dharani-gate of the Boundless Whirlpool;
the Dharani-gate of the Ocean Seal.
The Dharani-gate of Lotus Adornment;
it enables entry into the Dharani-gate of Non-attachment,
and gradually leads to deep entry into the Dharani-gate of the Four Unhindered Knowledges.
This is the gate of the dhāraṇī of adornment sustained by all buddhas.
If a bodhisattva can receive, uphold, and practice these eight kinds of dhāraṇī gates, [they shall attain this state].
He was then able to maintain in his memory all the sublime teachings spoken by all Tathāgatas;
his eloquence was inexhaustible, and he caused all sentient beings to feel affection, joy, and delight.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Sovereign King of All Dharmas...
He addressed the Buddha, saying, "World-Honored One,
we pray that the Tathāgata, out of compassion for us,
will extensively analyze and explain these eight kinds of dhāraṇī gates."
Upon hearing this, bodhisattvas are able to diligently seek and enter into it.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the Bodhisattva Sovereign King of All Dharmas, saying:
"Excellent, excellent, son of good family!"
Listen attentively, listen attentively, and reflect upon this well; I shall now explain it to you in detail so that all bodhisattvas may enter this gate.
Noble son, what is called the "Gate of the Dharani of the Purification of Great Sound"?
If there is a bodhisattva who cultivates this dharani-gate,
they should abide in reality with unattached, pure, and wondrous mindfulness;
their mind must be free from agitation, and their deportment must be composed and tranquil.
With a resolute mind, he preaches the subtle and wondrous Dharma,
so that all sentient beings within a single buddha-field,
according to their respective species and sounds, may universally hear its voice and fully understand its meaning.
In this way, it may be two buddha-fields,
or three buddha-fields, or ten buddha-fields,
or a hundred buddha-fields, or a thousand buddha-fields.
In two thousand times ten thousand, and even throughout the infinite,
boundless, koṭi-nayuta-hundred-thousand Buddha-fields of the ten directions,
the sentient beings therein likewise each followed their respective kinds.
They hear his voice everywhere and fully comprehend its meaning.
Good son, if this bodhisattva occupies the lion throne within the great assembly,
The height of those seats is one krośa,
adorned with various jewels sustained by the majestic power of the lion king;
likewise, they may measure half a yojana, one yojana, or even a thousand yojanas.
Or again, its size may be equal to Sumeru, the king of mountains;
or its height may reach as far as the Brahma Heaven—
according to whatever beings' hearts desire.
He causes each of them to see their own body and seat according to their respective sizes as he preaches the Dharma for them.
While he is preaching the Dharma, the Buddhas of the ten directions all appear before him and expound the sublime Dharma for this bodhisattva.
Upon hearing this, the bodhisattva is immediately able, through the power of this dhāraṇī,
to hear and retain everything in its entirety at once, never forgetting it.
Deeply penetrating the principles and meanings, they accord with direct realization; body and mind are serene and joyful.
Within each and every phenomenon, they achieve one-pointedness of mind;
regarding each and every word and phrase, they hear them as if hearing nothing at all.
At the very time of hearing such Dharma in this way,
one constantly expounds it without obstruction.
If bodhisattvas enter deeply into such a gateway of the sound of a single syllable, [they attain this].
All dharmas enter entirely into this gate;
they are produced from this very gate,
and all dharmas are expounded therein.

when entering the first letter *a*, they expound all dharmas.

Furthermore, sons of good family, because Bodhisattvas abide in this dhāraṇī, they attain purity of body;
because their deportment is tranquil,
they attain purity of speech.
Because their eloquence is unimpeded,
they attain purity of intent; because they observe with compassion, they attain purity of mind.
One attains purity of giving because one is without stinginess regarding wealth or the Dharma and rejoices in the giving of others.
One attains purity of ethical discipline.
Because it is without breach, without perforation, and without flaw or leakage,
one attains the purity of patience (*kṣānti*).
Because it is without enmity, without opposition, and without obstruction, [it is pure].
One attains the purity of diligence,
because one does not regress from sublime activities;
one attains the purity of meditative concentration.
Because it is without attachment, without pride, and without relish,
one attains the purity of wisdom;
for by opening the eye of wisdom, one pierces the film of delusion.
One attains purity of karma,
because one universally cultivates all supreme and wholesome deeds;
one attains purity of the eye.
Because the divine eye sees all forms from afar,
one attains the purity of the ear;
because the divine ear hears the teachings of all Buddhas from afar.
They attain purity of the nose,
because they universally smell the fragrance of the Tathāgata’s pure precepts;
they attain purity of the tongue.
Because they have attained the flavor of purity that accords with the mind,
they attain physical purity;
for although they currently dwell within a womb, they are not defiled by the womb.
One attains purity of mind because one is well able to discern subtle dharmas;
one attains purity of form.
Because all physical forms are wonderfully adorned,
one attains purity of sound, such that whatever is heard is exclusively sounds in accordance with the Dharma;
one attains purity of fragrance.
Because they are perfumed by the fragrance of generosity, ethical discipline, and learning,

because they transcend all realms of Māra;
