As it is said regarding this single gateway of the letter A, it is immeasurable, boundless, and inexhaustible.
Each and every remaining syllable is likewise so;
they are all entered through gradual cultivation by means of the gateway of unattached wisdom.
Furthermore, good son, what is called the "Inexhaustible Treasure Casket Dhāraṇī Gateway"?
Good son, it means that within a single syllable, all phenomena are explained without end.
What are these phenomena that are without end?
They are what are called form (*rūpa*).
Because it is inexhaustible.
Thus it is said that form is impermanent because it is inexhaustible.
It is said that form is suffering because it is inexhaustible;
it is said that form is non-self.
Because it is inexhaustible:
one speaks of the inexhaustibility of the quiescence of form;
one speaks of the inexhaustibility of the stillness of form.
It is because form is taught as being inexhaustible like a mass of foam;
it is because form is taught as being inexhaustible like an illusion; it is because form is taught as being inexhaustible like a mirage;
and it is because form is taught as being inexhaustible like the moon reflected in water.
It is because form is taught to be inexhaustible like a dream;
it is because form is taught to be inexhaustible like an echo;
it is because form is taught to be inexhaustible like a reflection in a mirror.
It is taught that form is inexhaustible because it lacks intrinsic nature;
it is taught that form is inexhaustible because it is fundamentally non-existent;
it is taught that form is inexhaustible because it lacks conditions for its arising.
Because the gate of the emptiness of form is inexhaustible;
because the signlessness of form is inexhaustible;
because the wishlessness of form is inexhaustible.
It is because form is taught as being without activity and inexhaustible;
it is because form is taught as a dharma of arising and inexhaustible;
it is because form is taught as being without arising and inexhaustible.
It is because form is said to be inexhaustible in its prior limit;
it is said to be inexhaustible in its middle limit;
and it is said to be inexhaustible in its posterior limit.
It is because they speak of the inexhaustibility of the quiescence of form;
they speak of the inexhaustibility of the intimacy with the tranquility of form;
and they speak of the inexhaustibility of the absence of mental activity within form.
It is said that form is inexhaustible because it transcends the path of language;
it is said that form is inconceivable because it is inexhaustible;
it is said that form is immeasurable because it is inexhaustible.
It is because he teaches that form is selfless and inexhaustible;
he teaches that form is devoid of sentient beings and inexhaustible;
he teaches that form is devoid of a life-principle and inexhaustible.
It is said that form is inexhaustible because it is without nourishment;
it is said that form is inexhaustible because it is without a person (pudgala);
it is said that form is inexhaustible because it is without cognition.
It is taught that form is inexhaustible because it is without fabrication;
it is taught that form is inexhaustible because it is like grass, trees, tiles, pebbles, stones, and walls;
it is taught that form is inexhaustible because it cannot be sought or attained.
It is because form arising from the great elements is said to be inexhaustible;
it is because form without sound is said to be inexhaustible;
and it is because form without informative intimation is said to be inexhaustible.
It is because form is taught as being inexhaustible in its ineffability;
it is because form is taught as being inexhaustible in the purity of its fundamental flavor;
and it is because form is taught as being inexhaustible in its arising from causes and conditions.
It is because form is taught to be inexhaustible due to its lack of interruption;
it is taught to be inexhaustible due to its lack of sound;
it is taught to be inexhaustible due to its lack of a creator.
It is taught that form is inexhaustible because it is devoid of a recipient;
it is taught that form is inexhaustible because it is devoid of karmic fruit;
it is taught that form is inexhaustible because the dharma-realm is equal.
It is because it is taught that form abides in the inexhaustibility of *tathatā*;
it is taught that form abides in the inexhaustibility of the *bhūtakoṭi*;
and it is taught that form is inexhaustible due to being without "mine-ness."
It is taught that form is inexhaustible because it is without a master;
it is taught that form is inexhaustible because it is without appropriation;
it is taught that form is inexhaustible because it is inconceivable.
It is said that form is inexhaustible because it is ineffable;
it is said that form is inexhaustible because it is immeasurable;
it is said that form is inexhaustible because it is boundless.
It is because form is said to be the inexhaustible nature of bodhi;
it is because form is said to be the inexhaustible equality of emptiness;
and it is because form is said to be the inexhaustible nature of nirvāṇa.
In this way, it is extensively taught that all Buddha-dharmas— the dharmas of the aggregates, elements, sense-bases, and so forth, as well as the collections of names, phrases, and syllables—
all enter into this gateway of wisdom consisting of the sound of this single syllable.
Just as the four great elements are contained within a single body-casket,
so too is this profound Dharma-gate of the single-syllable sound-door, which encompasses and gives birth to inexhaustible jewels of wisdom.
Therefore, it is called the "Inexhaustible Jewel Casket.
I have above briefly explained a small portion of the meaning within this single gate,
like a single speck of dust from the earth.
If explained in detail,
it would be inexhaustible throughout immeasurable, boundless, and incalculable *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas.
Furthermore, son of good family:
What is called the "Dhāraṇī Door of Boundless Revolving"?
Good son, that which is called "extremes" refers to annihilationism and eternalism.
The twelve links of dependent origination are as follows: ignorance conditions volitional formations;
volitional formations condition consciousness;
consciousness conditions name-and-form.
Name-and-form conditions the six sense bases;
the six sense bases condition contact;
contact conditions feeling.
With feeling as condition, craving arises;
with craving as condition, clinging arises; with clinging as condition, existence arises.
With birth as condition,
there is aging, death, sorrow, lamentation, suffering,
and despair. As for the term "boundless":
That is to say, within the secret realm there is neither annihilation nor permanence;
entering into such profound depth is called "revolving.
Therefore, it is named the "Dhāraṇī Door of Boundless Revolving."
Furthermore, "extremes" refers to grasping and rejecting;
"revolving" refers to neither grasping nor rejecting.
Furthermore, "extremes" refers to the teaching of arising and ceasing;
"revolving" refers to the teaching of non-arising and non-ceasing.
Moreover, "extremes" refers to afflictions and birth-and-death.
"Revolution" (xuan) refers to the inherent purity of one's fundamental nature.
"Extremes" (bian) refer to the presence of marks and the absence of marks.
"Revolution" refers to the total absence of any movement.
"Extremes" refers to coarse and subtle conceptualization;
"revolving" refers to the absence of applied and sustained thought;
and "extremes" also refers to causes and various views.
"Revolution" (*āvartana*) refers to the cause of insight through discernment.
"Extremes" (*anta*) refers to name-and-form (*nāma-rūpa*).
"Revolution" refers to the absence of representation.
"Extremes" refers to the conditioned and the unconditioned.
"Revolution" refers to the purification of the three wheels.
"Extremes" refers to the internal and the external.
"Revolution" (xuan) refers to the fact that the substance of consciousness has no fixed abode;
"extremes" (bian) refers to karma and its fruit;
"revolution" refers to the absence of a substantial entity of karma and its fruit.
"Extremes" refers to the wholesome and the unwholesome;
"revolving" refers to the absence of any substantial entity of activity.
"Extremes" also refers to transgression and non-transgression.
"Revolution" (kṣaṇa) means that its essence is non-dual.
"Limit" (anta) refers to karma and afflictions.
"Revolution" means that its essential nature is luminous.
"Extremes" refers to self and non-self;
"revolving" refers to the purity of their essential nature.
"Extremes" also refers to saṃsāra and nirvāṇa.
"Revolving" means that the intrinsic nature of all phenomena is itself nirvāṇa.
Son of good family, this is a brief explanation;
if explained extensively, there are infinite gateways to its limits.
The exposition of this "Revolutionary" [dhāraṇī] also comprises immeasurable gateways. If bodhisattvas abide in this "Revolutionary" dhāraṇī gateway,
they will accord with all boundless and profound dharmas.
Wisdom is inexhaustible, and both its letters and its meanings are likewise inexhaustible.
One gradually enters the dharani-door of the Boundless Revolving Wheel because it accords with the light of wisdom.
Because it accords with the fundamental purity of the nature of awakening;
because it opens the light of wisdom to pierce through the film of delusion;
and because it accords with the liberated essence of the body of awakening.

Chapter Two on Dhāraṇīs, Part Three.
Furthermore, son of good family,
what is called the gateway of the ocean-seal dhāraṇī?
Good son, it is like the great ocean, which reflects the manifestations of all things—
namely, all forms and appearances within the four continents,
whether they be the forms of sentient beings or the forms of non-sentient beings.
Mountains, marshes, plains, and hills; trees and groves;
medicinal herbs and the hundred grains;
the sun, moon, and stars; mani-jewels, clouds, and lightning.
Villages, hamlets, towns, cities, and royal capitals;
as well as the palaces of gods and goddesses;
all requisites, fragrant groves, and ponds.
The streams and springs of the Qushui River are magnificent and exquisitely adorned;
all such forms and appearances, whether superior, middling, or inferior,
are reflected with equal clarity within the great ocean.
Therefore, it is said that the great ocean is the foremost seal (*mudrā*).
It is the most excellent, wondrous, marvelous, extraordinary, peerless, and unsurpassed seal.
The bodhisattva mahāsattva is likewise so.
Abiding in this profound Samādhi of the Ocean Seal,
one attains the seal of equality with the bodies of all sentient beings;
one attains the seal of equality with the speech of all sentient beings.
They obtain the seal of equality with the minds of all sentient beings.
The verbal activities of all Buddhas throughout the worlds of the ten directions, which turn the wondrous wheel of Dharma,
all flow forth from the Ocean Seal Samādhi.
They preach with impartiality from the gateway of their speech;
whatever they say is never in contradiction with the Dharma-seal of all Buddhas, nor is there any doubt in it.
They are able to cause all sentient beings throughout the entire dharma-realm to fully awaken to and understand it.
Therefore, it is said that this seal is the most supreme among all seals;
that is to say, the seal of the short syllable Aḥ,
because the nature of all phenomena is non-arising.
The seal of the letter *ra* is so called because all phenomena are free from defilement and attachment.
The seal of the letter *pa* is so called because...
Because the gateway of ultimate truth is unattainable;
the syllable *ja* (者) mudrā is because the eyes and all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) are utterly pure;
the syllable *na* (娜) mudrā is—
Because the nature and characteristics of name-and-form (nāmarūpa) cannot be apprehended.
As for the seal of the syllable *la*,
it signifies that the continuous succession of the causal conditions of the link of craving (*tṛṣṇā*) does not manifest.
The *ṇa* seal (with the initial vowel *a* in the rising tone) is for the purpose of awakening to and entering the gateway of the ten pure powers (*daśabala*).
The *ma* seal is...
Because the powers and the factors of enlightenment are all purified;
as for the seal of the heavy letter NA,
it is because one is free from all enemies and afflictions.
The seal of the syllable *Śa* signifies that the six supernormal powers (*ṣaḍabhijñā*) are perfected and free from all hindrances.
The seal of the syllable *Va* signifies...
The Way of non-duality transcends verbal expression;
the seal of the many characters with the rising tone is for the purpose of awakening to the true meaning of all phenomena.
The seal of the syllable *ya* is so called because it expounds the teaching in accordance with the principle of reality (*yathābhūta*).
The seal of the syllable *ṣṭa* is... [so called because...]
Because subduing and maintaining [the world] cannot be apprehended.
As for the seal of the letter KA,
it is because one is far removed from worldly discourse and there is no creator.
The seal of the syllable *Sa* (pronounced with the high tone) is so called because one realizes that the Four Noble Truths are all equal.
The seal of the syllable *Maṅ* (pronounced lightly) is so called because...
Because it awakens one to the path of the purity of all phenomena;
as for the syllable Ga mudrā,
it is because one enters the profound dharma that is without activity or grasping.
The *ṣṭha* syllable mudrā reveals that power is unattainable;
as for the *jra* syllable mudrā...
Because it transcends that which is produced by aging and death;
the seal of the syllable *śva* is because all activities of the afflictions are utterly abandoned.
The seal of the syllable *ḍha* is so called because the essential nature of the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*) is not disordered or confused.
The seal of the syllable *śa* is so called because...
Because one enters into and fully perfects profound śamatha and vipaśyanā.
As for the seal of the syllable Kha,
it is because one awakens to the inexhaustible dharma that is like space.
The mudrā of the syllable *kṣa* (pronounced as a conjunct) is for entering into the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*) and the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*).
The mudrā of the syllable *svadhā* (pronounced as a conjunct) is...
Because it is far removed from the obstacles of torpor and indolence;
the syllable- seal *kṣi* is the essence of the wisdom of all sentient beings.
The seal of the letter *Ha* signifies that both the destruction of evil and the advancement of good are fundamentally detached from substantiality.
The seal of the letter *Va* (with the vowel *u*) signifies...
Because it is the habitual observation that realizes the essence,
the syllable *ccha* (pronounced as two joined syllables) is the mudrā;
because it is the nature of being far removed from greed, hatred, delusion, and obscuration.
The seal of the syllable *saṃ* is for the sake of mindfulness that is undistracted and free from forgetfulness.
The seal of the syllable *hava*— [is for the sake of...]
Because it is the essence for summoning and requesting [the deities],
the *Tsa* (Ṭsa) syllable mudrā is the essence for valiantly expelling all afflictions (*kleśa*).
The *ga* syllable seal is for the purpose of dispersing and extinguishing the dense clouds of ignorance and the cataracts of the mind.
The *ḍha* syllable seal is...
Because it exhausts the essence of all accumulated conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*).
The seal of the syllable *pra* conforms to the essence of supreme quiescent illumination.
The seal of the syllable Pha represents the essence of the universally perfect fruition.
The seal of the compound syllable Ska represents...
Because it realizes the essential nature of all aggregates;
as for the syllable *yaṃ*, it is the mudrā that can eliminate all diseases of old age and death.
The seal of the syllable *śva* (pronounced as a conjunct) is so called because it brings about the realization of that which has never before been realized.
The seal of the syllable *ṭha* (with the acute accent on the vowel) is so called...
Because it severs the path of birth and death and attains nirvāṇa;
the seal of the syllable *ṣṭra* is for the purpose of awakening to and understanding the infinite and inexhaustible essence.
"Good son, by means of these various kinds of dharma-characteristics,
the bodhisattva analytically explains the gateways of all syllables and seals.
Good son, this is called the gateway of the dhāraṇī of the Samādhi of the Deeply Penetrating Ocean Seal."
Furthermore, good son,
what is called the Lotus Adornment Dhāraṇī Gate?
Good son, when a bodhisattva dwells in this dhāraṇī gate, [he...]
As he preached the sublime Dharma within that immeasurable great assembly,
a vast and wondrous lotus throne immediately manifested before him,
adorned with various colors and forms of exquisite beauty.
Those who behold it find no satiety in their hearts;
as soon as this seat appears,
their bodies are immediately settled within it.
Immediately, a rain of various precious flowers fell from the sky;
from within these various flowers issued various sounds,
and within these various sounds were expounded various dharmas.
That is to say: either the extremely profound and immeasurable Dharma;
or the Dharma of skillful names and phrases;
or the teaching of various gates of similes.
Thus, some speak of the sūtra, geya, vyākaraṇa, gāthā, and udāna.
The Nidānas, the Itivṛttakas,
the Jātakas, the Vaipulyas,
the Adbhutadharmas, and the Upadeśas.
He teaches such twelvefold divisions of the Dharma and various gateways,
all for the purpose of severing the afflictions of all sentient beings; meanwhile,
the Bodhisattva’s mind dwells securely in great equanimity.
In tranquil meditative absorption, they are able to enter equanimity;
thus, they preach the Dharma with unceasing sounds,
extinguishing the suffering of sentient beings and performing the works of all Buddhas.
Furthermore, from every pore of the Bodhisattva’s body, various kinds of light radiate forth.
From within each ray of light, various wondrous jewel lotuses emerge.
Upon each flower sits a Bodhisattva.
He travels everywhere throughout the infinite and boundless worlds of the ten directions to perform the Buddha-work.
This is the initial entry into the Lotus Adornment Dharani Gate.
If explained in detail, it would be inexhaustible.
Furthermore, son of good family,
what is called "the gateway of the dhāraṇī for entering non-attachment"?
Good son, when a bodhisattva dwells in this dharani-gate,
his mind has no attachment to even a single dharma-gate;
likewise, he is without attachment to two or three.
Whether ten, or a hundred, or a thousand, or a hundred thousand, or a koṭi, or a nayuta,
up to asaṃkhyeya, immeasurable, boundless, unequaled,
incalculable, incomparable, inconceivable, and ineffable dharma-gates.
Their minds are entirely equanimous and free from attachment.
Even regarding Dharma-gates as numerous as the sands of the Ganges,
they likewise maintain an equanimous mind without any attachment.
In this way, they are likewise without attachment to dharmas as numerous as the atoms in Jambudvīpa,
dharmas as numerous as the atoms in the four continents,
or even dharmas as numerous as the atoms in a trichiliocosm.
Whether it be the dharmas of one buddha-field, ten buddha-fields,
a hundred, a thousand, or as many as the atoms within buddha-fields as numerous as the sands of the Ganges,
even up to dharmas as numerous as the atoms within all buddha-fields.
They are likewise all equal, with minds free from attachment.
If one were to explain a single gateway that encompasses all the dharma-gates as numerous as the atoms in all the Buddha-fields mentioned above,
they would all enter into that one gateway and be expounded simultaneously.
As it is with one gate, so it is with two, three, or even immeasurable and boundless Dharma-gates;
within each single gate, all gates are subsumed and expounded simultaneously.
When speaking in this way, the mind has no attachment and no dwelling place;
it benefits and brings peace and happiness to all sentient beings.
Its meaning is profound and far-reaching, corresponding to the principle of reality as it truly is.
It is sequential, unconfused, and complete in both words and meaning.
Noble son, this is called the "dhāraṇī door of entering non-attachment.
Furthermore, noble son:
What is called the "Dhāraṇī Door of Gradually Entering the Four Unimpeded Knowledges"?
Noble son, if bodhisattvas abide in this dhāraṇī door, [they shall attain it].
They attain inexhaustible wisdom regarding the gateway of subtle distinctions;
they attain inexhaustible wisdom regarding the gateway of subtle and profound meanings;
they attain inexhaustible wisdom regarding the gateway of subtle terminology.
One attains the inexhaustible wisdom of the gateway to subtle and boundless eloquence.
Because one has attained this wisdom,
all sentient beings in the eastern direction share a single site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa).
Each, through skillful means and in voices appropriate to their respective kinds, asked about the Dharma.
All sentient beings in the southern direction shared a single site of enlightenment;
each, through skillful means and in voices appropriate to their respective kinds, asked about its meaning.
All sentient beings in the western direction share a single site of enlightenment;
each, according to their respective species, asks questions through skillful means using their own voices.
All sentient beings in the northern direction likewise share a single site of enlightenment.
With skillful means, he answered their inquiries using the appropriate languages for each species.
In this way, all sentient beings from the four directions simultaneously posed questions concerning various Dharma gates.
The Bodhisattva is able to receive and comprehend them all in a single thought-moment;
with a mind free from confusion, he clearly remembers them without loss.
From a single vocal action, he produces various sounds.
Each and every sound expounds all dharmas;
according to the different species of sentient beings and their various inclinations,
all are able to understand and comprehend them, leaping for joy with hearts full of gladness as their aspirations are fulfilled.
Good son, this is how a bodhisattva gradually enters deeply into the dhāraṇī gate of the four kinds of unimpeded knowledge (*catasraḥ pratisaṃvidaḥ*). Furthermore, good son,
what is called the dhāraṇī gate of the adornment of being protected and sustained by all Buddhas?
Noble son, because the bodhisattva has attained this dhāraṇī,
he occupies the great Dharma throne within the great assembly;
at the very center of his uṣṇīṣa, where the cranial bones intersect.
Suddenly, the body of the Tathāgata appeared, with a complexion like refined gold and adorned with the marks and signs of excellence.
He then stroked the crown of the Bodhisattva’s head with his right hand;
immediately, the Bodhisattva attained a physical body fully endowed with the marks and signs of excellence, equal in perfection to that of the Buddha.
Furthermore, they attain the complete perfection of the Tathāgata’s adornment of vocal action.
They also attain the complete perfection of the Tathāgata’s adornment of mental action.
Thus, they attain the complete perfection of these various kinds of Buddha-dharmas.
Having attained this,
he taught various dharmas according to the different mental dispositions and diverse inclinations of all sentient beings present in this great assembly,
resolving their various doubts through diverse explanations.
Whether for one day and night, or two or three;
for half a month, a month, a year, a hundred years;
or even for hundreds of thousands of years.
According to the duration and extent of their mental inclinations,
he constantly preached the sublime Dharma without end.
While speaking in this manner, he neither drank nor ate.
Neither weak nor emaciated, their body and mind are free from fatigue;
this is due to the inconceivable power of the Tathāgata’s majestic virtue and protective sustenance.
Furthermore, the bodhisattva attains four kinds of great wisdom.
What are the four? They are:
the wisdom that minutely understands the various differences in the mental activities of sentient beings;
and the wisdom that minutely discerns all phenomena without end.
He is well able to discern the wisdom of the successive stages of practice of the three vehicles.
He is fully endowed with the perfected wisdom that accords with and is capable of expounding the Dharma.
Good son, this is called, in brief, the dhāraṇī gate of the adornment of the protection and sustenance of all Buddhas.
If explained in detail, they are immeasurable and boundless, equal to the realm of empty space and without end;
they are all equal to the Tathāgatas for the sake of benefiting all sentient beings.
Good son, these are the eight kinds of dhāraṇī gates.
If there is a bodhisattva who dwells securely in these eight dhāraṇī gates,
they will be able to retain all the sublime Dharma spoken by all Tathāgatas and all bodhisattvas.
It causes the eloquence of all bodhisattvas to be inexhaustible;
and if any sentient beings hear it, they will love,
delight in, and rejoice with it, never feeling satiated.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Sovereign King of All Dharmas,
having heard this Dharma, felt his heart leap with joy and praised it in verse:
The Sugata has taught the eight dhāraṇī-dharmas, Which definitively cause one to attain the subtle and wondrous vehicle.
He expounds hundreds of thousands of billions of sūtras, Without attachment to either their meaning or their phrasing.
His great voice is pure and boundless, And is heard throughout hundreds of thousands of immeasurable lands.
It can bring about the tranquil mind of sentient beings; this is called the meaning of the purity of the Great Sound.
To expound all dharmas through a single syllable, there is no time of exhaustion even throughout many kalpas;
each and every gateway of syllables is likewise so. This is abiding on the ground of the Mantra of the Precious Casket.

Far removed from all extremes, one attains purity; Equanimous and unattached, like the Tathāgata, In a single moment of right mindfulness, afflictions are eliminated. This is called the place of the whirlpool of the Dharma’s meaning.
Among all forms and appearances within the four continents, The great ocean reflects them all, leaving nothing out.
Expounding this gate of non-conceptual inexhaustibility, it is called the ocean-seal mantra;

endowed with the virtues of a great being, he dwells amidst the great assembly. Seated upon a lotus throne, he rains down celestial flowers as he expounds tens of millions of sublime Dharma gates; this is the application of the lotus-adorned dhāraṇī.
Entering into a single phrase of the Dharma without attachment, so it is with phrases as numerous as the atoms of billions of lands;

in every phrase they expound inconceivable gateways, possessing mastery over non-attachment, dhāraṇī, and the eloquence of both doctrine and terminology. Beings from the four quarters all simultaneously raise their doubts.
The nets of doubt regarding self and others are all severed; this is the power of the dhāraṇī of the four analytical knowledges.
As the Bodhisattva ascends the great Dharma throne, a Buddha appears upon his crown like a mountain of gold.
Then, extending his right hand in a majestic and dignified gesture, he reverently strokes the crown of the Bodhisattva’s head.
One attains subtle and wondrous eloquence equal to that of a Buddha; this is called "The Adornment of Mindfulness of the Buddha.
By attaining entry into the gate of the supreme dhāraṇī, one immediately acquires inconceivable and inexhaustible virtues.
Like a lotus, one is unstained by the three realms; unmoved by the five sensory objects, one is equal to Mount Sumeru.
Having attained this most supreme dhāraṇī, one possesses peerless wisdom that transcends the three realms and turns the fearless lion’s roar;
one crushes all non-Buddhists and shatters the mountains of heterodoxy.
Having attained this most supreme dhāraṇī, one remains far removed from the karmic fruits of rebirth.
Like the earth, it gives rise to all wholesome dharmas; like water, it washes away defilements until none remain;
like fire, it burns without discriminating among the fuel; like the wind, it blows and stirs without abiding anywhere.
Like a physician who skillfully knows the medicines of the Dharma, it removes the illnesses of sentient beings and brings them peace and security.
Having attained this most supreme dhāraṇī, wisdom expounds all phenomena without wavering;
like the full moon, bright and pure without a speck, its radiance shines everywhere with impartiality.
Having attained this most supreme dhāraṇī, those in the assembly who behold it can never look upon it enough.
Like the orb of the sun shining impartially, it destroys the darkness of birth and death and awakens the deluded masses.
Having attained this most supreme dhāraṇī, one can eliminate all the cravings of sentient beings.
Like a wheel-turning monarch who teaches the ten wholesome paths, it is like Vaiśravaṇa in the abundance of Dharma and wealth.
Having attained this most supreme dhāraṇī, one regards all sentient beings with compassion and brings down the rain of Dharma;
like a dragon raising clouds, it manifests majestic power, with thunder shaking and lightning flashing, all without volition.
Having attained this most supreme dhāraṇī, one is tranquil, mindless, and free from attachment.
Adorned with subtle majesty like Śakra, The one of great wisdom expounds the Dharma-gates according to capacities;
Having attained this most supreme dhāraṇī, He stands amidst the great assembly like a bull-king,
Or like the Great Brahmā King dwelling in the samādhi of loving-kindness, Surveying the entire world and transcending it all.
Having attained this most supreme dhāraṇī, one constantly attains the five supernormal powers without regression;
one wanders throughout the inconceivable realms of the Dharma-realm, just as the Brahmā King pervades the Brahma palaces.
Having attained this most supreme dhāraṇī, one makes offerings to the oceans of Buddhas of the ten directions.
All Buddhas gaze upon them as their eldest sons, simultaneously praising their inconceivable virtues.
Having attained this most supreme dhāraṇī, they shall before long acquire all the merits of a Buddha;
their eloquence shall be vast and inexhaustible, as they expound profound and extensive sūtras.
Having attained this most supreme dhāraṇī, one’s wondrous eloquence is like a garland, uninterrupted;
with wisdom and intelligence free from delusive thoughts, one’s boundless skillful means become equal to space.
Having attained this most supreme dhāraṇī, arrogance, flattery, and deceit are all severed.
Concentration and wisdom flow together without interruption; Compassion and kindness arise simultaneously, never separated.
Having attained this most supreme dhāraṇī, One forever severs all worldly faults.
One skillfully knows the languages and ways of sentient beings, Their mental activities, faculties, and desires, leaving nothing behind.
Having attained this most supreme dhāraṇī, one’s exposition of the Dharma is without the slightest error;

the foundations of mindfulness, the right efforts, and the bases of psychic power, as well as the faculties, powers, factors of enlightenment, the path, and meditative concentrations, are all perfected.
Having attained this most supreme dhāraṇī, one immediately acquires the sublime and pure knowledge of the Dharma.
Following the various perfections to reach the other shore, Thoroughly mastering the four means of attraction without exception,
One who attains this most supreme dharani Is able to know all the realms of the Sugata;
Spontaneously drawing near to the Buddha’s profound stillness, They establish the myriad practices to harmonize and guide sentient beings.
Having attained this most supreme dhāraṇī, one is never confused at any time;
one attains the stainless aggregates, elements, and sense-bases, remaining unstained within the womb and free from ignorance.
Having attained this most supreme dhāraṇī, one beholds the Buddha like a lotus, the mind unattached.
The three karmas always follow the turning of wisdom; In movement and stillness, they are unimpeded as they benefit sentient beings.
Having attained this most supreme dharani, They preach the Dharma constantly protected by all Buddhas.
With great wisdom, they can act as lords of sentient beings; Even after praising them for many kalpas, one could never reach the end.
At that time, the World-Honored One praised the Bodhisattva Sovereign King of All Dharmas, saying:
"Excellent, excellent, son of good family!
You are able to praise and expound this dhāraṇī."
I now rejoice in what the Buddhas have taught, which is entirely without difference.
Good son, within this assembly there are sixty billion nayutas of renunciant bodhisattvas.
Together with countless hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of lay bodhisattvas,
upon hearing this dharani gateway, they all attained the patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).
There were also immeasurable devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, humans, and non-humans.

The Birth from the Matrix of Great Compassion *Mahāsaṃnipāta-ratnaketudhāraṇī-sūtra*, Chapter Three: The Birth from the Matrix of Great Compassion. At that time, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Mañjuśrī...
He immediately rose from his seat, bared his right shoulder,
knelt with his right knee on the ground, paid homage to the Buddha,
and with palms joined in reverence, addressed the Buddha, saying:
World-Honored One, as the Buddha has taught, the mind, space, dhāraṇī, and bodhi are non-dual and without distinction,
all having great compassion as their root.
But what dharma, in turn, serves as the root of this great compassion?
The Buddha addressed the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī, saying:
"Excellent, excellent, son of good family! It is well that you have posed this question, for it is out of a desire to bring benefit and happiness to many sentient beings."
Listen attentively, listen attentively, and reflect upon it well;
I shall analyze and explain it for you.
Noble son, this is the root of great compassion.
Furthermore, [the Buddha] stated that the suffering of sentient beings is fundamental.
Mañjuśrī again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One, what dharma serves as the basis for the suffering of sentient beings?"
The Buddha said, "They arise from afflictions.
He asked again, "What is the root of afflictions?
The Buddha said, "They arise from various kinds of inverted views and false perspectives."
He asked again, "What is the root of all various inverted views and false perspectives?
The Buddha replied, "They arise from unreal conceptualization.
He asked again, "What is the root of unreal conceptualization?"
The Buddha said, "This false discrimination has no root.
It possesses no phenomenal characteristics; it is difficult to know and difficult to sever.
Good son, for this reason," [he spoke thus].
For the sake of all sentient beings, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva gives rise to great compassion,
laboring with humility and forgetting weariness,
just like sugarcane or sesame seeds.
When pressed with an object, the oil in the gruel appears;
so it is with the Bodhisattva.
With profound and heavy great compassion, he again gives rise to the sixteen aspects of great compassion and reflects as follows:
Alas for sentient beings!
They are constantly bound by the view of a self and take various false views as their dwelling place.
I shall expound the sublime Dharma for them so that they may completely sever [these views].
Alas for sentient beings!
They cling to and establish themselves in the extremes of annihilationism and eternalism.
Mañjuśrī addressed the Buddha, saying,
"World-Honored One, what is meant by the view of annihilation and the view of permanence?
The Buddha said, "Good son,"
To speak of the view of nihilism (*ucchedadṛṣṭi*): it holds that giving and making offerings bear no fruit;
that virtuous and non-virtuous actions have no results in this world or in future lives;
and that parents, transformations, and all such things are utterly non-existent.
Why is this? It is like knowing that when wood is burned, it has already become ash and can never again undergo the process of growth;
this is called the view of annihilationism (*ucchedadṛṣṭi*).
As for the view of eternalism (*śāśvatadṛṣṭi*), it is to say: "A king shall always remain a king, and the noble shall always remain noble."
The rich and the poor, men and women, the handsome and the ugly, as well as elephants, horses, and other such classes, never undergo change. Why is this?
It is because they are like seeds that follow their own respective natures.
Each sprout grows separately, never becoming confused or intermingled.
Son of good family, for these sentient beings who hold such views and find no fruit of their actions,
the Bodhisattva gives rise to great compassion.
He revealed and expounded the gateway of dependent origination, causing sentient beings to believe in and enter into the retribution of causes and conditions.
The Bodhisattva further reflected: "Alas! Sentient beings have given rise to the four inversions."
They perceive the impermanent as permanent, suffering as pleasure,
the non-self as self, and the impure as pure.
For their sake, I shall preach the profound Dharma to eliminate these inversions.
Alas! Sentient beings, amidst that which is without self and without what belongs to a self, calculate "self" and "what belongs to a self.
I shall preach the subtle and wondrous Dharma for them, so as to cause them to sever and abandon the views of self and what belongs to a self.
Alas for sentient beings!
Covered and obscured by various hindrances and obstructions, with the arrow of craving lodged in their hearts,
the fire of hatred blazes so fiercely that both body and mind are consumed by flame.
They are intoxicated and deluded by lethargy and drowsiness;
they are entangled and unable to abandon restlessness and remorse;
and they constantly harbor doubts regarding the profound Dharma.
I shall preach the subtle and wondrous Dharma for them,
so that they may tear asunder the net of all hindrances.
Alas for sentient beings!
Attached to the six sense bases, as soon as the eye sees forms,
one gives rise to attachment according to the names and signs of those forms;
the ear hears sounds, and the nose smells fragrances and odors.
The tongue tastes flavors, the body touches subtle textures, and the mind discriminates dharmas;
all these give rise to attachment following after names and signs.
I shall now expound for them the profound and wondrous Dharma.
He causes them not to take pleasure in or become attached to the six sense bases, which are like empty villages.
Alas for sentient beings!
They give rise to manifold forms of pride.
There are pride, excessive pride, pride beyond pride, the pride of "I am," overweening pride, inferiority pride,
and false pride. What is pride?
That is to say, regarding inferior sentient beings, one conceives of oneself as superior to them;
this is called "excessive pride" (adhimāna).
Regarding those who are equal to oneself, one says, "I am superior to them."
Regarding "conceit beyond conceit" (*mānātimāna*):
it is the estimation that one is superior to others who are actually superior to oneself. Regarding "the conceit of self" (*asmimāna*): [it is the notion of "I am"].
To conceive of a self in relation to form, and even to conceive of a self in relation to consciousness, thereby causing the mind to become uplifted—
this is called "overweening pride" (*adhimāna*).
It refers to one who has never actually attained any superior noble dharma, yet claims to others that they have attained such noble dharmas.
Regarding "inferiority pride" (*ūnamāna*):
it is when one says of those who are for the most part superior to oneself, "I am slightly inferior.
Regarding "false pride" (*mithyāmāna*): [it is when...]
To claim for oneself that which is wrong view and devoid of virtue as being correct,
while conversely denouncing others as being wrong—
such [attitudes] constitute pride.
I shall preach the profound Dharma for them,
so that they may sever [their afflictions] and abide in equanimity.
Alas for sentient beings!
They are heading toward wrong paths and turning away from the noble path.
I shall preach the Dharma of the right path for them so that they may distance themselves from evil ways.
Alas for sentient beings!
They become slaves to affection and love, subject to its commands;
wives, concubines, sons, and daughters serve as their shackles and fetters.
Bound by these restraints, they remain stained by attachment and addicted to sensual flavors, unable to relinquish them.
They cause the body, speech, and mind to lack self-mastery;
I shall preach the Dharma of detachment from craving for them,
so that their three karmas— whether moving or still— shall be free from agitation.
Alas! Sentient beings further engage in mutual strife and contention;
bound by anger and resentment, they act as enemies toward one another.
I must preach the Dharma for them so that they may sever and abandon these tendencies.
Alas for sentient beings!
They distance themselves from spiritual friends and follow after evil companions, never parting from them.
Just as the finger and the nail are joined and dependent upon one another,
they commit various evil deeds without a moment’s rest.
You should preach the Dharma for them so that they may abandon evil friends and draw near to virtuous spiritual friends.
Alas! Sentient beings greedily pursue fame and profit without ever reaching satiety;
like the ocean swallowing rivers, the more they obtain, the more their craving increases.
Like adding fuel to a fire, they distance themselves from the wisdom of the stainless true reality (*dharmatā*).
I shall now expound for you the Dharma of ultimate truth, so that you may sever fame and profit and attain pure wisdom. Alas!
Sentient beings are shrouded in the darkness of ignorance.
Within the dharma of non-self, they perversely give rise to the view of a self,
sentient beings, a life-span, and a person (pudgala).
For their sake, one should preach the Dharma to sever such various false views.
May they be made to remove the cataracts [of ignorance] and open the eye of pure wisdom.
Alas! Sentient beings are imprisoned within the fortress of birth and death, bound in the cycle of saṃsāra, and slaughtered by the bandits of the five aggregates.
I shall preach the Dharma for them so that they may transcend the three realms.
Alas! Sentient beings are bound by the snares of Māra;
ensnared by the five desires, they are unable to achieve liberation.
I shall now expound for you the Dharma that transcends Māra,
so that the snares of Māra may be severed and the fetters of the five desires cut asunder.
Alas for sentient beings!
They close the gate of nirvāṇa and open the path of birth and death.
You should preach the Dharma for them so that they may close the three evil realms and enter the gate of nirvāṇa.
Son of good family, this is the bodhisattva-mahāsattva’s arousal of the sixteen kinds of great compassion.
At that time, the World-Honored One again addressed the youth Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva, saying:
"Good son, this gate of great compassion is the mother of all bodhisattvas."
When a bodhisattva abides within this great compassion,
they are able to establish the thirty-two kinds of uncommon activities, practicing them diligently day and night so that they may swiftly attain perfection.
What are called the thirty-two kinds of uncommon activities? They are as follows:
when a bodhisattva sees all sentient beings who are ignorant, steeped in the heavy darkness of folly, and slumbering in the great night of lack of wisdom.
One first uses wisdom to awaken oneself,
and then uses wisdom to enlighten all deluded sentient beings;
this is called the Bodhisattva’s first unique undertaking.
If a bodhisattva sees sentient beings who delight in the two vehicles and whose minds are narrow and inferior,
they then give rise to a vast mind,
causing those beings to dwell securely within the Mahāyāna teachings.
This is called the second unique activity of a bodhisattva:
when they see sentient beings who delight in what is not the Dharma,
indulging their three karmas and lacking any desire for wholesome dharmas.
The bodhisattva personally dwells in the garden of the true Dharma and further causes sentient beings to dwell within the true Dharma;
this is called the third unique activity of a bodhisattva.
If one sees sentient beings who live by wrong livelihood, practicing deceit and greedy seeking,
one first establishes oneself in right livelihood and then causes those sentient beings to abide securely in the pure dharma of right livelihood.
This is called the fourth unique activity of a bodhisattva:
when they see sentient beings who deny cause and effect and give rise to great false views regarding all phenomena.
Abiding themselves in right view,
they further cause sentient beings to dwell securely within the dharma of stainless right view.
This is called the fifth unique activity of a bodhisattva.
If one sees sentient beings who, being ignorant, accumulate afflictions through evil thoughts,
one should personally settle the mind in right mindfulness with the eye of wisdom,
and further cause those sentient beings to abide in right mindfulness.
To shatter the darkness of ignorance and open the light of wisdom—
this is called the sixth unique activity of a bodhisattva.
If they see sentient beings who have abandoned the true Dharma and dwell in what is not the true Dharma, [they act to remedy this].
First establishing oneself within the True Dharma,
and then causing sentient beings to understand and realize the True Dharma—
this is called the seventh unique activity of a bodhisattva.
If he sees sentient beings shrouded by stinginess,
the bodhisattva himself gives rise to a mind free from stinginess and relinquishes everything;
furthermore, he causes those sentient beings to diligently cultivate the practice of relinquishment.
This is the eighth unique activity of a bodhisattva:
when they see sentient beings who have violated the pure precepts and are unable to practice the manifest or unmanifest forms of discipline.
He then adorns his own body with pure precepts and causes sentient beings to firmly uphold pure precepts as well;
this is called the ninth unique activity of a bodhisattva.
If one sees sentient beings whose anger and resentment burn fiercely as they accumulate various evils,
one adorns oneself with the power of loving-kindness and patience,
and further causes those sentient beings to dwell securely in this Dharma.
This is called the tenth unique activity of a bodhisattva:
if they see sentient beings whose bodies and minds are indolent and who have abandoned diligence,
they themselves adorn their bodies with the armor of diligence.
Furthermore, he causes sentient beings to abandon the mind of indolence and to be diligent, courageous, and untiring.
This is called the eleventh unique activity of a bodhisattva.
If he sees sentient beings who are distracted and possessed of false thoughts, [he acts accordingly].
The Bodhisattva himself abides in samāhita tranquility and observes with discernment,
and likewise causes sentient beings to abandon distraction and abide in meditative concentration.
This is called the twelfth unique activity of a Bodhisattva.
If one sees sentient beings with corrupt wisdom and a lack of knowledge,
one adorns oneself with wisdom and further causes those sentient beings to abandon their corrupt wisdom.
Being fully endowed with the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā) is called the thirteenth unique activity of a bodhisattva.
If they see sentient beings practicing on a wrong path through improper mental attention (ayoniśomanasikāra), [they act accordingly].
The Bodhisattva then employs skillful means to contemplate according to reality,
causing sentient beings to abandon what is irrational and abide in the right path.
This is called the fourteenth unique activity of a Bodhisattva.
If he sees sentient beings who are deluded, ignorant, and afflicted by the defilements,
the bodhisattva himself abides in mindfulness and engages in various types of discrimination and subtle discrimination.
To remain free from afflictions regarding all objects of experience,
and further to cause sentient beings to sever their afflictions and abide within the True Dharma—
this is called the fifteenth unique activity of a bodhisattva.
If one perceives that sentient beings are bound by the prison of the view of a self and the view of existence,
yet through wisdom realizes that one's own person is not bound by such views,
and further causes sentient beings to distance themselves from the view of a self.
Not reckoning on abiding in existence through right wisdom—
this is called the sixteenth unique activity of a bodhisattva.
If they see sentient beings whose faculties are unrestrained and dissolute...
Though unable to restrain the currents flowing toward sensory objects,
he remains naturally gentle and his mind is free from negligence;
furthermore, he causes sentient beings to abide securely in moral discipline.
Skillfully guarding the gates of the sensory faculties and harmonizing the three types of action—
this is called the seventeenth unique activity of a bodhisattva. Furthermore,
if they see sentient beings who are shameless and lack a sense of propriety, who do not recognize or repay kindness, and who have severed their roots of goodness;
They then adorn themselves with a sense of shame and remorse;
knowing gratitude and repaying kindness, they cultivate all roots of goodness and further preach the Dharma for sentient beings to reveal and instruct them.
Causing them to possess a sense of shame and remorse, to be able to recognize kindness and virtue, and to bring their roots of goodness to fulfillment—
this is called the eighteenth unique activity of a bodhisattva.
If they see sentient beings submerged by the waves of a great torrent, [they rescue them].
Driven by karma, beings drift and drown, unable to exert themselves to escape;
the Bodhisattva, manifesting himself as one who has crossed the torrential flood to reach the other shore,
further causes sentient beings to sever and eliminate their evil karma.
To cross the stream of birth and death and reach the shore of nirvāṇa—
this is called the nineteenth unique activity of a bodhisattva.
If they see sentient beings who are stubborn and difficult to transform, [they act accordingly].
Furthermore, by personally practicing humility, benevolence, and deference while following one's teachers and elders,
and causing other sentient beings likewise to abide in humility and respect—
this is called the twentieth unique activity of a bodhisattva.
If one sees sentient beings harboring jealousy and creating many obstacles for those who cultivate goodness,
one should then adorn one's own body with roots of goodness.
Furthermore, they cause sentient beings to abandon hearts of suspicion, jealousy, and obstruction, and to dwell securely in the True Dharma.
This is called the twenty-first unique activity of a bodhisattva.
If a bodhisattva sees sentient beings who are impoverished, suffering, and lacking the wealth of the Dharma,
he manifests an abundance of material resources and the seven noble riches;
furthermore, he causes those sentient beings to be free from all lack and to abide within the noble riches.
This is called the twenty-second unique activity of a bodhisattva:
when they see sentient beings constantly afflicted by the suffering of illness,
as the four great poisonous snakes mutually conflict with and injure both body and mind.
The Bodhisattva adorns himself with the merit of being free from illness and establishes sentient beings in the state of the Dharma of peace and happiness, free from all sickness and affliction.
This is called the twenty-third unique activity of a Bodhisattva.
If he sees sentient beings who are foolish and ignorant, far removed from the light of wisdom,
the bodhisattva adorns his own body with the light of wisdom and further causes those sentient beings to dwell securely within the dharma of non-deluded wisdom.
This is called the twenty-fourth unique activity of a bodhisattva:
when they see sentient beings who take pleasure in and are attached to the foul and evil deep pit of the triple world and the saṃsāra of the five destinies.
The Bodhisattva is skillfully able to emerge from the triple world by himself,
and furthermore, through skillful means, he leads all sentient beings out of the path of the triple world;
this is called the twenty-fifth unique activity of a Bodhisattva.
If one sees sentient beings who turn their backs on the right path and travel along deviant ways,
one establishes oneself in the true Dharma and further causes sentient beings to abide within the true Dharma.
This is called the twenty-sixth unique activity of a bodhisattva:
when they see sentient beings who are attached to their bodies and lives,
adorning themselves and providing for their sustenance in the hope that they may endure forever.
Not realizing that this body is impermanent and impure,
lacking a sense of shame or remorse, and ignorant of the kindness [received],
the Bodhisattva then manifested a state of revulsion toward his own person and cast aside his splendor and beauty.
Furthermore, he causes sentient beings to contemplate impermanence and give rise to the thought of weary detachment.
This is called the twenty-seventh unique activity of a bodhisattva.
If he sees sentient beings who are distant from the Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha, [he causes them to draw near].
The Bodhisattva personally continues the lineage of the Triple Gem and further causes sentient beings to continue the lineages of the Buddha, Dharma,
and Sangha so that they are never severed. This is the twenty-eighth unique activity of a Bodhisattva.
If a bodhisattva sees sentient beings falling away from wholesome dharmas,
he adorns his own body with wholesome dharmas and further causes those sentient beings to abide within wholesome dharmas.
This is called the twenty-ninth unique activity of a bodhisattva.
If a bodhisattva sees sentient beings who distance themselves from their teachers and elders and fail to practice the six recollections (*ṣaḍ-anusmṛti*),
the bodhisattva then adorns himself with these six recollections.
Furthermore, they cause sentient beings to constantly cultivate the six recollections (*ṣaḍ-anusmṛti*) through the wisdom of contemplation as it truly is (*yathābhūta-parijñā*).
This is called the thirtieth unique activity of a bodhisattva.
If they see sentient beings enmeshed and covered by the net of karma and afflictions (*kleśa*), [they act accordingly].
The Bodhisattva then manifests the tearing asunder of the net of karma and delusions,
and causes sentient beings to sever the causes of birth and death and abide securely in the True Dharma.
This is called the thirty-first unique activity of a Bodhisattva.
If a bodhisattva sees sentient beings possessed of various unwholesome states and devoid of roots of goodness,
they personally eliminate their own evils and become adorned with virtues;
furthermore, they cause those sentient beings to be fully endowed with roots of goodness and to distance themselves from the unwholesome.
This is called the thirty-second unique activity of a bodhisattva.
Son of good family, these are the thirty-two kinds of unique activities of a bodhisattva.
If bodhisattvas abide in these activities, [they shall attain enlightenment].
All wholesome dharmas constantly increase of their own accord, becoming fully perfected and complete.
Furthermore, son of good family,
the bodhisattva has further immeasurable activities.
Why is this? It is because sentient beings are infinite, and the afflictions of sentient beings are likewise immeasurable and boundless.
The bodhisattva accords with all those distinctions among the afflictions of sentient beings.
It is also because it explains the boundless gates of liberation.
Good son, even if all the worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges were filled with sentient beings,
and one were to consider all the practices of those beings;
The activities of all śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas are not comparable to the activities of this bodhisattva’s initial generation of the mind of enlightenment.
A hundredth part does not equal it; a thousandth part does not equal it.
Likewise, a hundred-thousandth part, a koṭi-th part, a hundred-koṭi-th part, or a thousand-koṭi-th part does not equal it.
It does not equal even a fraction, a *kalā*, a portion, a comparison, or even a *upaniṣad* part. Why is this?
Because the followers of the two vehicles strive only for their own severance of afflictions.
The activities of a bodhisattva are not for their own sake,
but are universally for the purpose of severing all the afflictions of all sentient beings; therefore,
whatever activities a bodhisattva undertakes [are for this end].
It is the most preeminent compared to the two vehicles;
the merit obtained is immeasurable and boundless.
Why is this? Because the activities practiced by ordinary beings—
All are associated with every form of perversion.
The activities of those of the two vehicles are narrow and inferior;
the deeds of Bodhisattvas are immeasurable and boundless, being far removed from perversion.
Therefore, the merit attained by a bodhisattva is likewise immeasurable and boundless;
for this reason, they surpass all ordinary beings and those of the two vehicles.
At that time, having heard this Dharma, the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī leaped for joy;
his entire body was refreshed and serene, and his mind attained a state of cool clarity.
And he spoke these words: "Rare, World-Honored One! Rare, World-Honored One!
You have skillfully distinguished the various gateways of dhāraṇī and the gateways of great compassion of the bodhisattvas—gateways that are profoundly deep and subtle."
And the gateway of uncommon activities.
Having heard what the Buddha spoke, I received it with joy upon my head and shall practice it according to the Dharma.

Chapter Four: Entering the Inconceivable Great Compassion of the Tathāgata. Chapter Four: Entering the Inconceivable Great Compassion of the Tathāgata.
At that time, the youth Mañjuśrī rose from his seat, bared his right shoulder,
knelt with his right knee on the ground, and joined his palms in reverent salutation.
He addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One,
I only pray that the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha,
will expound for my sake how the great compassion of all the Tathāgatas, the Buddhas, operates in accordance with all sentient beings."
World-Honored One, Tathāgata, how many kinds of great compassion are there?
What are its characteristics, what is its cause,
what are its conditions, and upon what does it abide?
“Excellent, World-Honored One! We pray that you will fully expound this for us, as well as the activities of the Tathāgata’s direct realization of the knowledge of all modes.
At that time, the Buddha addressed the youth Mañjuśrī, saying:
Excellent, excellent, son of good family!
You have skillfully inquired about such a profound meaning.
Listen attentively, listen attentively, and reflect upon it well.
I shall now analyze and explain for you the characteristics of a single drop from the ocean of the great compassion of all Buddhas and Tathāgatas.
Noble son, the great compassion that all Tathāgatas have toward all sentient beings is neither produced nor extinguished.
Why is this? Because the Great Compassion of the Tathāgata is constant and eternal, never ceasing and never failing at any time;
it has already been so for immeasurable asaṃkhyeya kalpas.
Because they have accumulated and perfected all merits, they neither go nor come, yet they never abandon any sentient beings;
for they protect, mindfully regard, and embrace them all.
The great compassion of the Tathāgata is immeasurable, boundless, and inexhaustible;
it is profoundly deep, inconceivable, firm, sharp,
difficult to understand, and difficult to enter.
It cannot be proclaimed by means of words.
Why is this? Good son, [it is because...]
Just as the Tathāgata attains great enlightenment (mahābodhi),
so too does he give rise to great compassion (mahākaruṇā) toward all sentient beings.
How does the Tathāgata attain enlightenment?
Good son, when a Buddha attains bodhi,
it has no root and no place of abiding.
What is the root? What is the abode? The view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) is the root.
Fictitious conceptualization is its dwelling place;
yet, the conceptualization of the view of a self and awakening are equal and identical.
Therefore, it is said that bodhi has no root and no place of abiding;
it is by relying on this meaning that the Buddha attains bodhi.
All sentient beings do not awaken to or know that they have no fundamental basis and no place of abiding.
Desiring to cause them to awaken to reality as it is,
the Tathāgata universally takes all sentient beings as his object and gives rise to great compassion.
Furthermore, son of good family,
awakening is quiescent and approaches quiescence.
That which is called "quiescence" refers to the internal.
To draw near to tranquility is to be "external. Why?
Because the eye is empty, the self is empty, and that which belongs to the self is also empty.
Since its nature is thus, it is called tranquility.
The ear is empty, the nose is empty, the tongue is empty, the body is empty, the mind is empty; the self is empty, and that which belongs to the self is also empty.
Because its nature is thus, it is called "quiescence.
Due to the emptiness of the eye, one does not engage with the realm of forms.
Therefore, this is called "approaching tranquility.
Because the ears, nose, tongue, body, and mind are empty,
one does not engage with the objects of sound, fragrance, taste, touch, or mental phenomena.
Therefore, it is called "approaching tranquility.
Thus, for those who do not know how to approach such tranquility,
one desires to make them know it.
Therefore, the Tathāgata’s great compassion functions in accordance with all sentient beings.
Furthermore, good son,
the intrinsic nature of bodhi is pure and luminous.
Why is this? Because the true nature of the mind is fundamentally pure.
In what way is it pure?
Because its nature is without conjunction;
because its nature is pure like space;
and because it is without characteristics, just like space.
Furthermore, because its nature is equal to that of space,
bodhi is called the most supremely pure radiance.
This pure radiance cannot be perceived by ignorant ordinary beings.
Because they are shrouded by adventitious afflictions,
the Tathāgata’s great compassion operates toward all sentient beings in order to cause them to awaken to reality as it truly is.
Furthermore, son of good family, awakening is without grasping or abandoning.
Why is this? To abandon the shore of birth and death and cross the torrential stream to reach the other shore is what is called grasping and abandoning.
The Tathāgata has deeply entered the ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya).
He perceives neither this shore nor the other shore,
because all phenomena are devoid of "this" and "that."
Therefore, in bodhi there is neither grasping nor abandoning.
Ordinary beings do not know this absence of grasping and abandoning;
[the Buddha] desires to cause them to know it.
Therefore, the Tathāgata’s great compassion functions in accordance with all sentient beings.
Furthermore, son of good family,
awakening is without marks and without observation.
What is signlessness?
It is because visual consciousness cannot be apprehended.
What is meant by "absence of observation"?
Because visual consciousness does not conceptualize forms,
and likewise because auditory consciousness cannot be apprehended, it is called signless (*animitta*).
Because auditory consciousness does not conceptualize sounds, it is called non-examination (*anirīkṣaṇa*).
Because olfactory consciousness cannot be apprehended, it is called signless.
Because olfactory consciousness does not discriminate regarding odors, it is called non-examination.
Because gustatory consciousness cannot be apprehended, it is called signless.
Because tongue-consciousness does not discriminate regarding tastes, it is called "without observation.
Because body-consciousness cannot be apprehended, it is called "without signs.
Because body-consciousness does not discriminate regarding tactile objects, it is called "without observation."
Because mental consciousness cannot be apprehended, it is called signless (*animitta*).
Because mental consciousness does not conceptualize phenomena, it is called non-examination (*anirūpaṇa*).
Thus, being signless and without examination is the domain of the noble ones (*ārya*).
Because it transcends the three realms,
it cannot be known by ordinary or inferior beings;
it is intended to cause them to know and awaken to it as it truly is.
Therefore, the Tathāgata’s great compassion functions in accordance with all sentient beings.
Furthermore, noble son,
because bodhi is neither of the past, nor of the present, nor of the future.
The three time periods are equalized and the three spheres are severed.
What is meant by severing the three spheres?
It is because the mind does not arise with respect to the past.
Because future consciousness does not function therein,
and because the present mind does not act herein,
this mind-consciousness has no place of abiding.
What is meant by the equality of the three periods?
The events of the past are inconceivable;
the consciousness of the future cannot be fully described.
Because the present mind cannot be expressed,
this profound equality of the three periods and purity of the three spheres is unknown to sentient beings.
Desiring to cause them to awaken to reality as it is,
the Tathāgata accordingly turns toward all sentient beings with great compassion.
Furthermore, son of good family:
Awakening is bodiless and unconditioned. Why is it bodiless?
It is because visual consciousness cannot be known.
In this way, because the consciousnesses of the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind cannot be known,
how could they be unconditioned?
They are unconditioned because they are without arising, without cessation, and without abiding.
Therefore, it is said that the unconditioned (asaṃskṛta) is free from the three marks.
Just as the characteristics of the unconditioned are so, the characteristics of the conditioned (saṃskṛta) are likewise.
Why? Because the nature of all phenomena (dharmas) is thus.
The nature of non-nature is not non-existent;
this non-duality of the two is the nature of bodhi.
Thus, it is without body and without the marks of the unconditioned.
Ignorant and immature ordinary beings do not perceive or know [this].
Desiring to cause them to perceive and know it,
the Tathāgata accordingly manifests great compassion toward all sentient beings.
Furthermore, son of good family,
awakening is indestructible and leaves no trace of realization.
Why is it that which is realized, and why is it indestructible?
What is called *tathatā* (suchness) is the track that has been realized;
because it is non-abiding, it is indestructible.
The *dharmadhātu* (dharma-realm) is what is realized.
Because it is devoid of manifoldness, it is indestructible;
the reality-limit (bhūtakoṭi) is that which is realized.
Because it is immovable, it is indestructible.
Emptiness is that which is realized;
because it cannot be apprehended, it is indestructible.
Signlessness is that which is realized.
Because it is non-conceptual, it is indestructible.
Non-aspiration is that which is realized;
because it is not to be sought, it is indestructible.
There are no sentient beings to be realized,
for they are indestructible due to their lack of intrinsic nature.
Space is that which is realized.
Because it cannot be grasped, it is indestructible;
non-arising is that which is realized.
Because there is no cessation, it is indestructible.
The unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) is that which is realized;
because it is devoid of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*), it is indestructible.
Awakening (*bodhi*) is that which is realized.
Because it is peaceful and approaches peace, it is indestructible.
Nirvana is that which is realized;
because it is originally unarisen, it is indestructible.
Such is the path realized and its indestructibility;
yet sentient beings do not know it.
[The Buddha] desires to bring them to awakening.
Therefore, the Tathāgata’s great compassion functions in accordance with all sentient beings.
Furthermore, son of good family,
bodhi cannot be attained by means of the body.
It cannot be attained through the mind.
Why? Because the body is devoid of cognition and the mind is like an illusion.
To know this correctly is called attaining bodhi.
In accordance with conventional truth, one speaks of the existence of bodhi;
yet one should know that the essence of bodhi is unattainable and there is no one able to speak of it. As for what is unattainable:
it is unattainable in its very nature.
Whether body or mind, whether principle or non-principle,
whether non-existent or existent, whether real or false— all are unobtainable.
Why is it that they cannot be spoken of?
Because this bodhi cannot be manifested or explained through any of the various skillful means of all dharmas,
there is not even the slightest portion that abides within any dharma.
Because it is non-abiding,
it is not an object of words or verbal expression;
it is like space, which has no place of abiding and cannot be described.
Bodhi is likewise without abiding and without expression.
Thus, the Tathāgata observes all phenomena as they truly are, finding them all to be inexpressible.
Why is this? Because within all phenomena there is no speech.
Because there is also no dharma within all languages,
all sentient beings do not perceive or know this sublime Dharma; [the Buddha] desires to cause them to perceive and know it.
Therefore, the Tathāgata’s great compassion operates in accordance with all sentient beings.
Furthermore, son of good family,
bodhi is ungraspable and has no basis.
How is it that they are ungraspable? How is it that they are without a basis?
Because the Tathāgata knows and sees phenomena as they truly are:
namely, because the eye cannot be apprehended, it is ungraspable.
Because form cannot be apprehended, it has no locus of dependence.
Because the ear cannot be apprehended, it cannot be grasped.
Because sound cannot be apprehended, it has no locus of dependence.
Because the nose cannot be apprehended, it cannot be grasped;
because odors cannot be apprehended, they have no locus of dependence;
because the tongue cannot be apprehended, it cannot be grasped.
Because taste cannot be apprehended, it has no basis;
because the body cannot be apprehended, it cannot be grasped;
because tangibility cannot be apprehended, it has no basis.
Because the mind cannot be apprehended, it cannot be grasped;
because phenomena cannot be apprehended, they have no basis.
Thus, the Tathāgata is without grasping and without reliance.
Therefore, one manifests perfect enlightenment regarding bodhi.
Because the eye does not grasp forms and has no place of dependence, consciousness has no support.
Because the ear does not grasp sounds and has no place of dependence, consciousness has no support.
Because the nose does not apprehend odors and lacks a basis, consciousness has no support.
Because the tongue does not apprehend tastes and lacks a basis, consciousness has no support.
Because the body does not apprehend tangibles and lacks a basis, consciousness has no support.
Because the mind has no grasping and phenomena have no basis, consciousness has nothing upon which to rely.
Because it has nothing upon which to rely, consciousness has no place of abiding.
All sentient beings falsely and erroneously cling to the notion that consciousness has a place of abiding.
What are the dwelling places of the consciousness-mind of sentient beings?
There are four kinds: namely, the aggregate of form, and the aggregates of sensation, perception, and formations.
This is precisely the dwelling place of the consciousness of sentient beings.
The Tathāgata thoroughly knows that the dwelling place of sentient beings is a non-dwelling place, reaching the ultimate limit of non-dwelling;
yet all sentient beings neither perceive nor know this.
Desiring to bring about awakening and understanding,
the Tathāgata accordingly turns toward all sentient beings with great compassion.
Furthermore, son of good family:
That which is called "bodhi" is designated as empty of intrinsic nature.
Because it is empty of intrinsic nature, bodhi is empty;
because it is empty of intrinsic nature, all phenomena are empty.
In this way, the Tathāgata, according to the emptiness of his own essence,
has attained manifest perfect enlightenment regarding all phenomena.
For this reason, he does not awaken to emptiness by means of an awakening that is itself empty.
This is precisely what is called the single wisdom of *ekābhisambodhi*.
That is to say, whether it be emptiness or a portion of awakening, they are non-dual;
emptiness and awakening cannot be distinguished.
It is likewise with all phenomena: they are non-dual and devoid of dual characteristics.
Upon careful and thorough observation, one finds that all phenomena are without name and without mark;
there is neither an agent who acts nor an object of action, and no destination toward which one proceeds.
Without speech, without discourse, without grasping, and without appropriation—this is called emptiness.
Within the ultimate truth, even emptiness cannot be apprehended; it exists only as a verbal designation.
As it is said that space is merely a word for emptiness, yet emptiness is not the objective domain of words;
likewise, to speak of emptiness as "ineffable" is called the gateway to entering all dharmas.
It means that all phenomena have no names;
within this namelessness, one forcibly employs names to speak of them.
Such names have no place of abiding within any phenomenon.
Why is this? Because names are provisionally established based on all marks (*lakṣaṇa*).
Since the intrinsic nature of marks is empty, upon what could a name be established?
In this way, the Tathāgata knows all phenomena through his knowledge of reality as it is (*yathābhūtajñāna*).
How is this known? It is known that from the very beginning it is unborn, unarisen, unoriginated, and unceasing;
it is without obstruction, without hindrance, without marks, and unconditioned.
Apart from mind, intellect, and consciousness, there is no name and no sound.
To know and see in this way is to attain liberation.
Such liberation is neither bound nor unbound.
Why is this? Because their nature is equal.
Yet ordinary beings do not perceive or know this;
[the Buddha] desires to cause them to perceive and know it as it truly is.
Therefore, the Tathāgata’s great compassion functions in accordance with all sentient beings.
Furthermore, son of good family,
awakening is equal and perfectly equal to space.
Yet that space is neither equal nor unequal;
awakening is likewise neither equal nor unequal. Why is this?
Because all phenomena, in accordance with reality, are without arising and without cessation.
All phenomena are neither equal nor unequal.
The Tathāgata, knowing and seeing all phenomena thus as they truly are— neither equal nor unequal—
therefore manifests perfect enlightenment regarding all phenomena.
Therefore, within this, there is not even the slightest dharma that can be said to be equal or unequal.
One should know all dharmas as they truly are.
How should one know them?
One knows that all phenomena have no fundamental basis, being neither born nor extinguished.
All dharmas are originally non-existent and now exist; having existed, they return to non-existence.
That which is unborn likewise has no extinction.
Thus, arising and ceasing arise from causes and conditions and proceed from causes and conditions;
herein, not even the slightest dharma exists that can proceed.
It is for the sake of severing the long and perilous path of birth and death that the Tathāgata [teaches this].
Therefore, I have preached such dharmas as they truly are:
that all sentient beings, failing to awaken to or understand them, sever the path to birth and death;
nor do they know the equality or inequality of the dharma-nature.
Desiring to cause them to know and awaken to reality as it is,
the Tathāgata accordingly manifests great compassion toward all sentient beings.
Furthermore, son of good family:
That which is realized as bodhi is precisely suchness (tathatā).
As is the suchness of bodhi, so too is that of form;
in the ultimate sense (paramārtha), they are neither identical nor distinct.
Just as with the suchness of awakening,
it is neither identical to nor separate from the suchness of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness.
Just as with the suchness of awakening, it is neither identical to nor separate from the suchness of the earth element, nor the water, fire, or wind elements.
Just as with the suchness of awakening,
the suchness of the eye-element, the form-element, and the eye-consciousness-element is neither identical to nor separate from it;
just as with the suchness of awakening.
The suchness of the ear element, the sound element, and the ear-consciousness element,
up to the suchness of the mind element, the mental-object element, and the mind-consciousness element, is neither identical to nor separate from them.
It is the same for these aggregates, elements, and sense-bases.
All phenomena do not depart from suchness;
the Tathāgata knows all phenomena by means of suchness.
Therefore, he manifests the realization of perfect enlightenment before him.
Because it is correctly awakened to as being identical to the nature and characteristics [of phenomena].
As it is in the present, so it was in the past and will be in the future:
unborn in the prior limit, not yet arrived at in the subsequent limit, and quiescent in the middle limit.
Such equality is precisely the true realization of bodhi.
This realized single dharma is not different from all dharmas,
and all dharmas are not different from this single dharma.
Within suchness, whether one, two, or many dharmas are all unobtainable;
yet ordinary beings, regarding that which is thus realized, neither awaken to it nor know it.
"I shall cause them to awaken.
For this reason, the Tathāgata acts in accordance with great compassion toward all sentient beings.
Furthermore, son of good family:
Awakening is signless, yet it skillfully enters into all signs.
What is a sign? What is signlessness?
In this context, a "sign" refers to the initial cultivation and arising of all wholesome dharmas.
To speak of "signlessness" (animitta) means that all phenomena (dharmas) are unattainable.
Furthermore, a "sign" is the locus where the non-abiding mind dwells;
to speak of "signlessness" is precisely the liberation of the signless samādhi.
Furthermore, "characteristic" refers to the mind and mental factors that weigh and examine all phenomena.
"Absence of characteristic" refers to that which transcends such weighing and functions in accordance with consciousness.
