Furthermore, "characteristics" refers to the detailed observation of conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*),
while "signlessness" (*animitta*) refers to the direct realization and correspondence with unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*).
Such is the profound gateway of characteristics and signlessness.
Ordinary beings do not realize this; I shall cause them to realize it.
For this reason, the Tathāgata’s great compassion functions in accordance with all sentient beings.
Furthermore, son of good family:
Awakening is without outflows and without the aggregates of affliction.
In this context, what constitutes "outflow" and "without outflow"?
There are four kinds of outflows: namely, the outflow of desire, the outflow of existence, the outflow of ignorance, and the outflow of views.
Because one is completely detached from these four outflows (*āsrava*), it is called "outflow-free" (*anāsrava*).
Why is it called "free from the aggregates of affliction"?
Because one is detached from the four kinds of aggregates of affliction (*kleśa-skandha*).

That is to say: being far removed from the aggregate of desire, far removed from the aggregate of wrong views, far removed from the aggregate of the view of self, and far removed from the aggregate of attachment to precepts and observances.
These four afflictions are all shrouded by the darkness of ignorance.
Blind and lacking the eye of wisdom,
they are parched and withered by the thirst of desire and craving;
because they are accumulated and established, they are called "aggregates" (skandhas).
The Tathāgata knows that these delusions, such as the view of a self, have no fundamental basis and are primordially pure;
he also knows, in accordance with reality, that sentient beings are pure.
Whether it be the purity of the self or the purity of sentient beings, they are non-dual and devoid of dual characteristics.
This absence of dual characteristics is the meaning of non-arising;
this meaning of non-arising is the meaning of non-ceasing.
Within this state of neither arising nor ceasing,
The mind, intellect, and consciousness do not arise at all.
In this state where the mind, intellect, and consciousness do not arise, conceptual discrimination does not occur.
If there were conceptual discrimination, the phenomena of birth and death would arise.
If there is no conceptualization, the dharma of liberation arises.
If the dharma of liberation arises, ignorance does not arise.
If ignorance does not arise, the twelve links of existence do not arise.
If the twelve links of existence do not arise,
that is non-arising; if there is non-arising, that is liberation.
That which is liberation is the definitive meaning (*nītārtha*).
The definitive meaning is the ultimate truth (*paramārthasatya*). What is called the ultimate truth?
That which is called "non-self" cannot be described if it were truly non-existent.
That which cannot be described is precisely the meaning of the harmony and conjunction of causes and conditions.
The meaning of the harmony of such causes and conditions is the meaning of all dharmas;
the meaning of all dharmas is the meaning of the Tathāgata.
For this reason, [it is so].
If one sees the phenomena that arise from the conjunction of causes and conditions, one sees all phenomena;
if one sees all phenomena, one sees the Tathāgata.
Such is true seeing within the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*).
Upon careful and thorough observation, not even the slightest portion is seen.
What is this "slightest portion"? It refers to the observation itself.
When the observing mind perceives reality according to its investigation, that is called the vision of reality.
Thus one knows the equality of all phenomena;
for this reason, the Tathāgata has realized perfect enlightenment.
This is the untainted, affliction-free aggregate.
Ordinary beings are neither awakened nor aware;
I shall cause them to awaken.
For this reason, the Tathāgata’s great compassion functions in accordance with all sentient beings.
Furthermore, son of good family,
awakening is pure, stainless, and has no location.
In this regard, what dharma is called "pure"?
What is "stainless," and what again is called "having no location"?
It is said that emptiness is purity,
and signlessness is stainlessness.
The wishless is without location;
the unborn is purity; the unconditioned is stainless.
That which is unarisen has no locus;
the intrinsic nature of all phenomena is purity itself.
To thoroughly investigate this purity is to realize it is stainless.
The intrinsic luminosity has no location;
its essence is ineffable, which is purity;
its essence is non-conceptual, which is stainlessness.
The ineffable silence has no location;
the true reality, the pure *dharmatā*, the stainless limit of truth, has no location.
To know the purity of the aggregates (*skandha*) and to know the intrinsic nature of the elements (*dhātu*) is itself to be stainless.
To know that entry into seclusion is without location;
to know that the wisdom of the exhaustion of the past is pure, and the wisdom of non-arising regarding the future is stainless.
Knowing that the dwelling place of the present dharma-realm is itself without location— such meanings of purity, stainlessness,
and non-locality as these are all entirely subsumed within a single realization.
That which is realized is itself tranquility;
tranquility is itself cessation;
cessation is itself direct realization.
That which is directly realized is signlessness;
signlessness is the ultimate truth;
the ultimate truth is the characteristic of space.
As is the characteristic of space, so too is the characteristic of bodhi;
as is the characteristic of bodhi, so too is the characteristic of all phenomena;
as is the characteristic of all phenomena, so too is that of all sentient beings.
As it is with all sentient beings, so it is with all buddha-fields;
as it is with all fields, so it is with the Great Parinirvāṇa.
Therefore, I say that all dharmas are themselves the characteristic of nirvāṇa.
This is the characteristic of the ultimate reality-limit, the characteristic of non-opposition.
It is primordially pure from the beginningless past,
inherently stainless, and from the very outset has no location.
In this way, the Tathāgata perceives no marks of form within these various marks of form;
thus, he attains manifest, perfect enlightenment regarding all phenomena.
Having attained manifest, perfect enlightenment, he surveys the ten directions.
Seeing all sentient beings dwelling in impurity,
giving rise to defilement and attachment to their abodes,
he universally arouses the great compassion of playful mastery toward them.
Employing skillful means, he desired to turn the wheel of Dharma,
yet he reflected that the Brahma King had not yet come to make a formal request.
At that time, the Great Brahma King Śikhin, knowing the Buddha’s thoughts, [approached].
Surrounded before and behind by eight billion devas who were his Brahma-retinue,
he vanished from the Brahma palace and appeared before the Tathāgata.
Prostrating at the Buddha’s feet, he addressed the Buddha, saying:
“I pray only that the World-Honored One will turn the wheel of Dharma;
I pray only that the Sugata will turn the wheel of Dharma.”
Then he spoke these verses:
“The Tathāgata’s realization is most tranquil, Pure, stainless, and wondrously luminous;
It cannot be expressed and is beyond names and words— Only the Buddha’s pure wisdom can fully fathom it.”
For this sutra, throughout many billions of eons, they have undergone every difficult practice and ascetic hardship;
they have caused sentient beings who are inverted by beginningless ignorance, craving, and latent tendencies to attain awakening.
The sentient beings in this assembly possess abundant merit and benefit; in the past, at the presence of the Buddhas, they have already cultivated the causal conditions.
I only pray that you shall widely open the gate of ambrosia and turn the most supreme wheel to benefit all sentient beings;
may they awaken to the most exalted Dharma and utterly destroy the armies of Māra without remainder.
May you guide all those who have strayed onto evil paths and cause them to abide in the Tathāgata’s true and correct Way.
The Tathāgata’s great compassion is supreme; for the sake of benefiting all beings in an inconceivable way,
I now entreat the Teacher of Gods and Humans to turn the most excellent and subtle Dharma,
just as K Krakucchanda Buddha turned it, and as K Kanakamuni did.
Kāśyapa, Sugata, turned the wheel of Dharma; now we entreat the World-Honored One to turn it likewise.

Just as a great cloud sends down sweet rain, causing medicinal herbs, grasses, and trees to all flourish, may the Buddha raise the great cloud of compassion and send forth everywhere the inconceivable rain of the sublime Dharma.
At his first birth, the Tathāgata let out a lion’s roar, vowing to universally liberate all sentient beings;
may he now rain down the water of the Dharma in accordance with the time, to satisfy the profound thirst and longing of gods and humans.
After the noble son Śirīṣa Brahmā had spoken these verses in request, [the Buddha responded].
At that time, having accepted the invitation of the Brahma King,
I did not abandon the Tathāgata’s playful exercise of great compassion;
[I went] to the Deer Park at Ṛṣipatana in the city of Vārāṇasī.
At first, he turned the unsurpassed wheel of Dharma,
which cannot be turned by any ascetic, brahmin, god, Māra, Brahmā, or anyone in the world.
When he turned the wheel of Dharma, there arose the sound of impermanence.
It was heard throughout the trichiliocosm.
At that time, Ājñātakauṇḍinya was the first to hear the Dharma, attain realization, and obtain the fruit.
On that occasion, I spoke these verses:
Ineffable and profoundly deep, the ultimate truth is without letters;
yet I say it is not without fruit. O son of good family, when I first attained realization, as I turned the wheel of Dharma, I spoke thus.
Furthermore, there were immeasurable and innumerable sentient beings who were all tamed by the Tathāgata’s playful exercise of great compassion.
Moreover, there were immeasurable and innumerable sentient beings who gave rise to the bodhicitta.
Therefore, the Tathāgata constantly turns the great compassion toward all sentient beings.
Good son, this is the Tathāgata’s fulfillment and perfection of the sixteen great compassions;
he dwells eternally within them, turning them spontaneously and effortlessly without requiring any exertion.
For the sake of a single sentient being, one may undergo all manner of sufferings in the great hells throughout kalpas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges;
yet this sentient being may be either tamed or untamed.
One must bring them to subdual and establish them within the True Dharma of the Tathāgata.
As one does for a single sentient being, so it is for all sentient beings without exception.
Thus one proceeds throughout immeasurable kalpas.
He experiences the sufferings of hell without weariness or fatigue,
and his heart of great compassion likewise never diminishes.
Therefore, toward all sentient beings, the Tathāgata—
Great compassion is profound, heavy, and inconceivable.
The compassion of those of the Two Vehicles is like cutting the skin;
the compassionate heart of a Bodhisattva is like cutting through fat and flesh.
The great compassion of the Tathāgata penetrates deeply to the very marrow of the bones.
Furthermore, compassion that conforms to the Buddha's wisdom is the compassion of the śrāvaka;
compassion that exhorts all sentient beings to resolve upon bodhicitta is the compassion of the bodhisattva.
Bestowing the prediction of future Buddhahood is the compassion of the Tathāgata;
arising from a mind of loving-kindness is the compassion of the Śrāvaka;
transforming sentient beings is the compassion of the Bodhisattva.
Because it brings sentient beings to ultimate maturity, this is the great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*) of a Buddha.
Seeking the cessation of birth and death is the compassion of a *śrāvaka*.
Transporting sentient beings to the other shore is the compassion of a Bodhisattva.
The ability to universally deliver all beings from birth-and-death and all afflictions to the other shore is the Great Compassion of the Buddha.
Therefore, one should know that the Great Compassion of the Tathāgata is the most supreme and honored.
For the sake of taming all sentient beings,
he may remain in the world for one kalpa,
or a hundred kalpas, or even a hundred thousand kalpas.
He did not enter ultimate nirvana without remainder.
Son of good family, in the distant past, beyond incalculable eons (*asaṃkhyeya-kalpa*),
there appeared a Buddha in the world.
He is named Candanaśa Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha.
His world is named Sugandhā,
and his eon is named Varagandhā.
The lifespan of that Buddha was one hundred and sixty-eight thousand four thousand years.
His assembly of śrāvaka disciples numbered one hundred and sixty-eight thousand four thousand.
From every pore of that Tathāgata’s body, a sublime fragrance constantly flowed forth.
It pervades the trichiliocosm; it universally perfumes all things without any impurity or foulness,
including walls, houses, dwellings, trees, mountains, and rivers.
There are no diverse forms and appearances that are not fragrant;
therefore, this world is named "Possessing Fragrance.
Any sentient beings therein who encounter this fragrance [attain...]
With the three karmas purified and all virtues fully perfected,
he left home to cultivate the Way and entered deeply into the four dhyānas.
Within this world, ten thousand Tathāgatas appeared in succession.
They all shared the same name, Candanaśa;
therefore, this eon was named Most Excellent Fragrance (Varagandha).
When the Tathāgata Candanaśa had completed his buddha-work, the time for his parinirvāṇa arrived.
Furthermore, with the pure and wondrous divine eye that transcends all humans and devas, he surveys all sentient beings, considering: "Which sentient beings are to be tamed by other Buddhas?
Which sentient beings am I to tame?"
Then he saw a sentient being in the Heaven of Neither Perception nor Non-Perception who,
having planted roots of goodness in past lives,
delighted in hearing the Mahāyāna and possessed a pure mind— one whom he should subdue.
Yet these sentient beings shall remain in that heaven for eighty-four thousand kalpas;
only after this period has passed will they descend from the heavens and be born among humans, where they do not yet know the five desires.
Upon hearing the praise of the Mahāyāna, they immediately gave rise to the mind of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* and shall never again regress from that great enlightenment.
At that time, the Tathāgata Candanaśa—
Having observed all with skillful means and great compassion, he addressed the bhikṣus:
"Tonight, I shall enter parinirvāṇa.
He then entered the samādhi of great compassion and pity.
Having entered samādhi, he manifested parinirvāṇa.
After the Buddha’s extinction, his relics were distributed,
and the humans and devas of the ten directions paid them respectful homage and made offerings.
The True Dharma shall remain in the world for eighty-four thousand years,
benefiting and bringing peace and happiness to immeasurable sentient beings,
transforming people solely through the single flavor of the True Dharma.
No longer will the semblance-dharma circulate in the world.
Although that Buddha, the World-Honored One, has manifested parinirvāṇa,
he sustains it through the power of his great compassion, pity, samādhi, and supernormal faculties.
He remained further in the world for eighty-four thousand kalpas;
concealing his physical marks and signs, no one in the world was able to behold him.
After eighty-four thousand kalpas had passed,
That single sentient being who dwells in the realm of non-perception is now born among humans into a family of great wealth and nobility,
at the age of eight.
Then that Tathāgata arose from samādhi and went to the youth’s house.
Manifesting his body adorned with the marks and signs of excellence, he stood before the youth;
there was only this youth and twelve thousand devaputras present.
Those who were to be disciplined were able to behold the Tathāgata, while others could not see him at all.
At that time, the Tathāgata first inspired the Great Vehicle in them as children,
and further expounded for them the faults and afflictions of the five desires.
And he addressed him, saying: "Good son,
the faults and evils of the five desires are truly terrifying,
like five great and tall venomous serpents."
A single venomous snake can immediately harm a person;
how much more so five such snakes?
It is also like a collection of five types of poisonous drugs.
If even a small portion can harm a person,
how much more so when one eats the five aggregates?
Therefore, you should not give rise to greedy attachment.
At that time, having heard these words,
the youth surveyed his house, his means of livelihood,
and all that he possessed, whether male or female.
Regarding all [phenomena] as being like venomous snakes,
they develop a profound sense of weary detachment; they then give rise to a deep and heavy resolve for *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* and attain the stage of non-retrogression.
The Buddha, knowing that the youth’s body and mind were pure and clear and fully endowed with manifold virtues,
bestowed upon him a prediction of enlightenment and addressed the devaputras,
saying: "In the future, after seventy-two asaṃkhyeya kalpas have passed, this youth..."
When he attains *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*,
he shall be known as the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Most Victorious Jewel appearing in the world.
At the time the Buddha grants this prophecy, others do not hear it.
Only this youth and the twelve thousand devaputras,
who were all capable vessels for the Dharma, were able to hear it.
At that time, all those devaputras resolved their minds upon anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
They made this vow, saying: "When that Most Victorious Jewel Tathāgata attains Buddhahood, we shall be born in his Buddha-land.
Then, the Tathāgata Candanaśa told the devaputras: "You shall indeed attain rebirth there."
That Tathāgata Most Victorious Jewel shall bestow upon you the prediction of Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
At that time, the Tathāgata Candanaśa...
Having bestowed the prediction of enlightenment upon that bodhisattva,
he then finally entered parinirvāṇa;
all humans and devas made offerings to his relics.
Good son, for this reason,
all Tathāgatas are fully endowed with profound and heavy great compassion;
it is not within the realm of the Śrāvakas or Pratyekabuddhas.
"Noble sons, this Dharma gate can cause the lineage of the Buddhas to remain unbroken among you.
If there are sentient beings who hear this Dharma gate,"
The roots of goodness obtained from upholding, reciting, copying, and explaining— even down to a single word, a single phrase, or a single verse—
shall continue in succession without interruption until one enters nirvana.
Why is this? Because the causes have not been severed.
While the Tathāgata was preaching this profound Dharma-gate of great compassion within this assembly, [the causes were not severed].
There were sentient beings as numerous as the sands of one Ganges River who resolved their minds upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
Bodhisattvas as numerous as the sands of two Ganges Rivers attained the patience of conformity (*anulomikī-kṣānti*).
Bodhisattvas as numerous as the sands of three Ganges Rivers attained the sixteen great compassions of the Tathāgata,
as well as the dharma-patience of the empowerment of all Buddhas.
At that time, the entire great assembly heard this Dharma-gate.
Leaping for joy, refreshed and serene, with body and mind utterly surrendered, he joined his palms toward the Buddha and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Excellent, Tathāgata! Excellent, Sugata! You have so well explained this meaning."
They immediately presented various offerings of humans and devas,
such as diverse and exquisite jewel necklaces or various kinds of superior and wonderful garments.
Or with various kinds of precious foods and drinks;
or with Dharma robes, banners, flags, and parasols—
bearing such various articles of offering as these.
Reverently honoring, respecting, and making offerings to the Buddha.
*The Dhāraṇī Sūtra of the Sovereign Who Protects the Realm*, Scroll Four;
*The Dhāraṇī Sūtra of the Sovereign Who Protects the Realm*, Scroll Five.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Prajñā of Kaśmīra together with Munisri.
Chapter Five: Entering the Inconceivable and Profound Activities of the Tathāgata, Part One.
At that time, the World-Honored One again addressed the youth Mañjuśrī, saying:
"Good son, how should one understand the deeds of realization of the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha?
Good son, there are thirty-two kinds of deeds of perfect enlightenment performed by the Tathāgata."
What are the thirty-two kinds?
Son of good family, the Tathāgata knows, as they truly are, what is possible and what is impossible.
Son of good family, what is possible and what is impossible?
To speak of what is impossible means that sentient beings lack the skillful means;
yet through their physical, verbal, and mental actions, they perform unwholesome deeds and still obtain things that are agreeable, pleasing, and to their heart's content.
Thus, it is impossible for one who seeks the fruit [of liberation] to fail;
as for what is called "possibility," it refers to those sentient beings who possess skillful means and perform various virtuous deeds through the actions of body, speech, and mind.
It is possible for one who attains what is pleasing, delightful, and according to their heart to subsequently seek its fruit; this is indeed a possible case.
Furthermore, noble son, as for what is called an "impossible case":
If sentient beings, lacking skillful means,
harbor a mind of stinginess yet attain great wealth and status;
or violate the pure precepts yet obtain the bodies of gods or humans.
One who constantly harbors anger may obtain the retribution of physical beauty;
one whose body and mind are indolent may attain wisdom;
and a person of distracted mind may achieve liberation.
It is impossible for sentient beings of corrupt wisdom to sever the habitual tendencies and various afflictions. However,
if sentient beings possess skillful means and practice generosity,
they will attain great wealth and nobility.
By upholding the pure precepts, one attains birth among humans and devas;
by constantly practicing patience, one obtains the retribution of physical beauty;
by diligently applying vigor, one acquires wisdom.
It is possible for one whose mind is undistracted to attain right liberation;
it is possible for one who has skillfully cultivated wisdom to sever the habitual tendencies and all afflictions.
Furthermore, it is impossible for one who has committed the five heinous crimes to attain peace and happiness of mind.
It is possible for one who purely maintains the prohibitive precepts to attain peace and happiness of mind;
however, it is impossible for a sentient being who clings to the view of existence to attain the patient endurance that accords with reality.
It is possible that one who delights in cultivating emptiness may attain the patience of conformity (*anulomikī-kṣānti*). Furthermore,
it is impossible for sentient beings who dwell frequently in remorse to obtain peace and happiness of mind.
It is possible that a mind free from regret may attain peace and happiness.
Furthermore, it is impossible for a woman to become a Wheel-Turning King who rules over the four continents,
or to become Śakra, or a Great Brahmā King, or to appear as a Buddha.
If one abandons the female body and attains a male body,
one will become a Wheel-Turning King ruling over the four continents, or become Śakra or Mahābrahmā.
And that one who has attained Buddhahood [should act otherwise]—this is impossible.
Furthermore, it is impossible for a wheel-turning monarch to rule and transform the world through unrighteousness;
it is possible for a wheel-turning monarch to rule and transform the world through righteous Dharma.
Furthermore, it is impossible for kings who are greedy, debauched, arrogant, and extravagant to govern the affairs of state;
it is possible for kings who are free from greed and are simple and straightforward to govern the affairs of state.
If human kings adhere to the views of nihilism or eternalism, it is impossible for their state administration to be orderly.
If human kings clearly believe in cause and effect, it is possible for their state administration to be orderly.
If the hearts of human kings are not impartial,
it is impossible for them to govern the affairs of state effectively;
if the hearts of human kings are free from partiality and characterized by equality, [they can do so].
That one who is capable of governing a state could fall into the three evil realms after casting off their life and body in the northern continent of Uttarakuru is impossible. Furthermore,
that such a person would fall into the three evil realms after casting off their life and body in Uttarakuru is impossible.
If one says that after dying in the northern continent (Uttarakuru), one is reborn in the heavens—
this is possible. Furthermore, if one who commits acts of killing attains long life,
or even one who holds wrong views and practices perverted dharmas [attains such results]— this is impossible.
It is impossible for one who has attained the Noble Path to [commit such acts].
If one refrains from taking life, they will attain long life;
and so on, up to: by practicing right view, one receives and practices the True Dharma.
It is possible for one who has attained the Noble Path to do so.
Furthermore, it is impossible that one who is a candidate for Arhatship (Arhattvaphalapratipannaka) should not definitely attain the fruit;
however, it is possible that one who is a candidate for Arhatship will definitely attain the fruit.
Furthermore, it is impossible for a stream-enterer (srotāpanna) to undergo an eighth birth;
it is only possible that a stream-enterer does not have an eighth birth.
Furthermore, it is impossible for a once-returner (sakṛdāgāmin) to undergo a third birth.
If a sakṛdāgāmin does not have a third birth,
it is possible that in one more life among humans or devas he can reach the end of suffering.
Furthermore, it is impossible for an anāgāmin to be reborn again in the desire realm.
It is possible that an Anāgāmin, without being reborn in the desire realm,
may exhaust the limits of suffering and attain Nirvāṇa.
Furthermore, it is impossible for an Arhat to undergo the body of birth and death.
It is possible that an Arhat, not undergoing further birth and death, enters nirvana. Furthermore,
it is impossible for anyone to say that, apart from the Great Teacher, the Buddha, there is another noble one who surpasses the Buddha.
If it is said that the Buddha alone is the Teacher of Gods and Humans and that there is no one superior to him, this is possible.
Furthermore, if someone should say that one who has attained the patience of non-arising (anutpattika-dharmakṣānti) can fall back, this is impossible.
It is possible for one who has attained the non-arising [of dharmas] to be non-retrogressive.
Furthermore, it is impossible for anyone to say that they sit at the seat of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa) and yet do not attain perfect awakening.
If one sits at the site of enlightenment and is certain to achieve perfect awakening, such a thing is possible.
Furthermore, if anyone were to say that the Buddhas still possess the habitual tendencies of afflictions, such a thing is impossible.
If it is said that the Buddhas have no habitual tendencies of affliction, this is possible.
Furthermore, if anyone should say that the wisdom of all Tathāgatas has obstructions, this is impossible.
If it is said that the Tathāgata’s wisdom is without obstruction, this is possible.
Furthermore, if anyone should say that they are able to see the cranial protuberance (uṣṇīṣa) of the Tathāgata, this is impossible.
If one says that there is anyone capable of seeing the Tathāgata’s crown, such a thing is impossible.
Furthermore, if anyone says they can know where the Tathāgata’s mind dwells without the Buddha bestowing his power upon them, such a thing is impossible.
If one says that it is only through the Buddha’s empowerment that one comes to know the place where the Tathāgata’s mind abides, such a thing is possible.
Furthermore, if anyone were to say that the Tathāgata also possesses a non-abiding samādhi or samāhita state, such a thing is impossible.
If it is said that the Tathāgata always abides in samādhi and the merit of meditative equipoise, this is indeed possible.
Furthermore, if someone were to say that the words of all Tathāgatas are false, [this would be impossible].
It is impossible for the Tathāgata to have errors or omissions.
If one says that the Tathāgata’s speech is without falsehood and without error, this is possible.
Furthermore, if anyone were to say that the actions performed by the Tathāgata can be mistaken, this is impossible.
If one says that all the deeds performed by the Tathāgata are free from error, this is indeed possible.
Son of good family, because of such statements,
the immeasurable gateways regarding the Tathāgata’s knowledge of what is possible and what is impossible are beyond the reach of words.
Just as there is no alteration in the ultimate truth,
this is the Tathāgata’s first deed of perfect awakening.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:
The great earth may be made to move, The void may be shaken;
But the Tathāgata would never declare That what is impossible is possible.
The void may become a body, Possessing the five colors of a mortal man.
The Tathāgata never declares that which is not a proper basis to be a proper basis;
yet he has fully proclaimed the distinctions among all bases, their differences as superior,
middling, or inferior, which are definitively without discrepancy.
The Tathāgata has already proclaimed that all things are distinguished by what is not possible, differing as superior, middling, or inferior;
he knows with perfect reality whether something is impossible or possible.
In accordance with the inclinations and desires of sentient beings, he teaches them in their full perfection.
Śramaṇas and brahmins, who do not know what is possible and what is impossible, falsely race through various objects of perception; there is nothing that the Buddha’s wisdom does not know.
Sentient beings harbor various attachments, seeking liberation in what is not the proper place;
though they have attained that which is honored by the world, I preach the true place for them.
Because those who cling to such [false] things are not vessels for the Dharma, the Buddha abandons them.
When the faculties have matured and it is time for liberation, one should further proclaim this to them;
this is the Buddha’s foremost and most excellent gateway of activity,
which is free from all faults and non-virtues, and is able to deliver sentient beings from suffering.
The phenomena of what is possible and what is impossible are immeasurable and boundless;
they are invincible and cannot be defeated. This is called the power of the Great Sage.
Furthermore, son of good family:
The Tathāgata’s past, present, and future karmic actions and vows differ according to various locations and various causes and conditions.
He knows, exactly as they are, the various phenomena, their diverse maturations, and their infinite distinctions.
How does he know them?
Good son, herein, past karma, vows, and roots of goodness serve as the causes for abandoning unwholesomeness and attaining results in the future.
If there is past karma, vows, and [roots of goodness],...
Taking unwholesome roots as their cause,
they distance themselves from wholesome roots and fail to attain future fruits.
The Tathāgata knows each and every such variety exactly as it is.
Furthermore, there are those whose practices and vows gradually diminish in the future;
those whose practices and vows gradually increase in the future;
and those whose practices and vows gradually diminish in the present but gradually increase in the future.
If there are practices and vows that increase in the present but gradually decrease in the future;
or if there are practices and vows that gradually decrease in both the present and the future;
or if there are practices and vows that gradually increase in both the present and the future.
One knows all such various things as they truly are.

Furthermore, if there are practices and vows where a small cause in the present leads to a vast result in the future, or where a vast cause in the present results in a minute outcome in the future; [one knows these as they truly are].
Whether they initially arise subtly and later gradually increase in excellence,
or whether they are initially vast and later gradually become subtle—
such various modes he knows all as they truly are.
Furthermore, he knows as it truly is: if there are practices and vows that shall result in the attainment of the state of a śrāvaka;
if there are practices and vows that shall result in the attainment of the state of a pratyekabuddha;
and if there are practices and vows that shall become the cause for attaining Buddhahood.
Furthermore, there are some practices and vows whose cause is suffering while their fruit is happiness;
some whose cause is happiness while their fruit is suffering;
and some whose cause and fruit are both suffering.
There may be those whose practices, vows, causes, and fruits are all equally joyful;
he knows them all as they truly are.
Good son, such is the case for the past, present, and future.
The various karmas and the resulting maturations (vipāka) are in accord with their causes and effects,
like a shadow following a form or an echo following a sound;
the Tathāgata knows each and every one of these exactly as they truly are.
Having known this, he teaches the Dharma to them according to what is appropriate for each.
This is the Tathāgata’s second deed of perfect enlightenment.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, [spoke these verses].
And he spoke in verse:
The Tathāgata’s skillful wisdom Knows the karmic fruits of sentient beings throughout the three times without omission; His eye of wisdom is entirely free from attachment.
Wholesome causes shall bring happiness; The ripening of which occurs among humans and gods.
Evil is the cause that brings about suffering; The Tathāgata fully knows and sees both wholesome and unwholesome karma, And how each respective fruit shall come to fruition.
The Sugata knows them all completely, like a mani jewel held in the palm of his hand.
There are karmas that are extremely subtle yet will become vast causes;
those that are great at first but subtle later—the Tathāgata perceives and knows them all.
There is karma for the practice of śrāvakas, Karma that is the cause of pratyekabuddhas, And karma that brings about the state of a Tathāgata; The Sugata knows and perceives them all.
Some have causes that are pleasant but results that are painful, While others have causes that are painful but results that are pleasant.
The suffering of cause and effect is identical; Both cause and effect are equally peaceful and blissful.
Karma and the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) Do not contradict one another in cause and effect;
The Tathāgata knows them as they truly are, Having thoroughly investigated both their nature and their characteristics.
The realms of all sentient beings, And the cycles of karma throughout the three periods of time, Are each without exception; The Tathāgata fully understands them all.
Furthermore, son of good family:
All sentient beings have countless varieties of inclinations and desires;
the Tathāgata knows each and every one of these exactly as they are.
How does the Buddha know them?
There are some sentient beings who abide in the practice of sensual desire and take pleasure in ill-will;
there are some sentient beings who abide in ill-will and take pleasure in sensual desire;
and there are some sentient beings who abide in delusion and take pleasure in both sensual desire and ill-will.
The Tathāgata knows each and every case as it truly is:

he knows as it truly is when there are sentient beings dwelling in wholesome dharmas who yet desire what is unwholesome; or when there are sentient beings whose actions are minor yet whose desires are vast.
There may be sentient beings whose actions are vast while their aspiration is slight;
or there may be sentient beings whose aspiration is slight at the stage of the cause,
yet becomes vast by the time they reach the result.
There may be those who have vast aspirations regarding the causes,
yet have only minor aspirations regarding the fruits;
all such various cases he knows as they truly are.
There may be sentient beings who delight in false views and so forth;
though indeterminate during the causal stage, they shall become determinate.

There may be those who delight in the correct [path] and are indeterminate during the causal stage, yet shall become determinate. Or there may be those who delight in the correct causes and are already determinate, and shall attain liberation.
The Tathāgata fully knows each of these various distinctions:
some have the aspiration to transcend the desire realm,
while others have the aspiration to transcend the form realm.
There may be those who desire to transcend the triple world;
each such one, every Tathāgata knows completely.
There may also be those who desire that [their afflictions] decrease day by day.
Later, it will gradually become superior, vast,
and expansive; or, for those who desire the most excellent and vast,
it will later gradually diminish until it becomes disagreeable.
He knows all such various things as they truly are.
There are those who, out of desire and longing, undergo various births,
assume various forms, and enjoy various requisites for life.
The Tathāgata fully knows such distinctions:
some have the aspiration to dwell among humans or in the heavens,
while others have the aspiration to attain liberation.
The Tathāgata knows each of these distinctions exactly as they are.
Having known them thus, he teaches the Dharma according to what is appropriate for each.
This is the third enlightened activity of the Tathāgata.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning,
spoke these verses:
"The various desires of sentient beings, Their inclinations are immeasurable."
The Tathāgata, with all-encompassing wisdom, knows each and every sentient being exactly as they are:
those who dwell in the pleasure of greed and anger, and those who dwell in the pleasure of anger and the darkness of delusion; he knows them all truly, one by one.
Those who dwell in delusion, pleasure, and sensual craving, and those who dwell in the wholesome while delighting in the unwholesome— their minds undergo manifold transformations.
The Sugata fully knows these inferior causes among sentient beings; yet their own minds always delight in the vast.
Abiding in the vast and enjoying the expansive, abiding in the superior, the inferior, or the middling; or furthermore,
there may be sentient beings for whom the cause is inferior yet the fruit is transcendentally superior,
or for whom the cause is superior yet the fruit is middling or inferior— the Tathāgata knows these as they truly are.
Abiding in the midst of the indeterminate and the heterodox, they shall later become certain and dwell in the right path,
liberating themselves from the three realms. The Tathāgata knows them as they truly are—
whether they delight in various births, physical forms, or material requisites.
Abiding in the realm of humans and devas, he understands all sentient beings of the three periods of time who are bound by desire for liberation; knowing their inclinations toward the Buddha,
he teaches the Dharma according to their minds— this is the third gateway of activity.
Furthermore, son of good family,
the Tathāgata knows, as they truly are, the various distinctions of realms within countless worlds.
How does the Buddha know?
It means he knows that among the sentient beings in this world, some cultivate various meritorious virtues,
while others in this world create various evil karmas.
He knows as they truly are that the sentient beings of this realm cultivate the karma of liberation,
and that the sentient beings of this realm shall transcend the world;
he knows all such various matters in accordance with reality.
Furthermore, good son,
the Tathāgata knows the eye-element, the form-element, and the eye-consciousness-element.
How does he know them?
There are three reasons:
namely, because one knows internal emptiness, external emptiness, and internal-external emptiness.
Thus is it thoroughly known.
...up to the knowledge of the mind-element (*manodhātu*), the dharma-element (*dharmadhātu*), and the mental-consciousness-element (*manovijñānadhātu*),
by virtue of their being empty internally, empty externally, and empty both internally and externally. Furthermore,
one knows the earth-element (*pṛthivīdhātu*), and the water, fire, and wind-elements (*abdhātu, tejodhātu, vāyudhātu*).
All are like space.
Furthermore, one knows that the desire realm, the form realm,
and the formless realm arise from conceptual construction and discrimination.
Furthermore, one knows the conditioned realm because its modes of activity manifest as having an end; one knows the unconditioned realm because it is devoid of such modes of activity.
He knows the realm of afflictions as being characterized by adventitious dust;
he thoroughly understands the flow of afflictions.
Because it can be severed;
because one penetrates its fundamental nature,
which is characterized by radiance.
One knows the realm of conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra-dhātu*),
because its characteristic is false conceptualization and ignorance;
one knows the realm of nirvāṇa (*nirvāṇa-dhātu*).
By virtue of the characteristic of wisdom and the characteristic of right mindfulness,
son of good family, the world is established in such and such a manner.

The Tathāgata knows, exactly as they are, each of these distinctions: how the world first manifests and then undergoes dissolution; and how it abides in its activities based on the causes and conditions for rebirth in other worlds.
Having known this, he teaches the Dharma accordingly.
This is the fourth enlightened activity of the Tathāgata.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, [spoke as follows].
And he spoke this verse:

The Buddha is skillful regarding the elements (*dhātu*); Even when staying in a time of decline and diminution, A small amount of goodness achieves great fruit; The Lion among Men is able to understand this.
The realm of merit and the realm without merit, The opening of the gate of merit and the realm of liberation—these realms are not the same.
The Tathāgata, with the clear vision of all-knowledge, perceives the realm of the eye;
The realm of form and the realm of consciousness are both empty.
The elements of the ear, nose, tongue, body, And mind and phenomena are likewise empty;
The elements of earth, water, fire, and wind— One who understands them as they truly are sees them all as empty.
The Lion among Men can thoroughly comprehend The deluded thoughts of the three realms.
The afflictions are empty and like dust; the nature of all phenomena is entirely without activity or non-activity, being like space.
These three characteristics of nirvana arise from the unwholesome world; once formed, they perish and dissolve together.
This realm and those in other directions— though they are empty and boundless throughout the ten quarters,
all known and seen through non-conceptualization— the Buddha alone can know these realms;
the Buddha’s wisdom is supreme and limitless, which sentient beings cannot fathom.
This is the Lord of Purity; through this fourth gate of training beings, one practices without falling back and will certainly realize the fruit of Bodhi.
Furthermore, son of good family:
The Tathāgata knows, exactly as they are, the superior and inferior faculties, the diligence and indolence,
and whether they are sharp or dull among all sentient beings.
How is it that he is able to know this?
Good son, he knows as they truly are sentient beings of dull faculties, those who are ignorant and dark, and those of inferior, middling, or superior faculties.
Furthermore, he discerns how greed arises according to these various faculties.
According to such faculties, discrimination gives rise to hatred;
according to such faculties, discrimination gives rise to delusion;
and by relying on external objects, greed, hatred, and delusion arise.
The Tathāgata knows them all.
Furthermore, he knows how greed, hatred, and delusion arise and progressively expand according to the distinctions among the faculties;
or else, how they arise following the distinctions among those very faculties.
The Tathāgata fully knows that greed, hatred, and delusion do not further increase.
Furthermore, he knows that this faculty is the cause of wholesome roots,
while this faculty is the cause of unwholesome roots.
This faculty is the cause for the path of liberation;
this faculty is the cause for the path that transcends birth and death.
The Tathāgata fully knows all such various [faculties].
Furthermore, son of good family, the Buddha knows, as they truly are, the six sense faculties of the eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind;
the faculties of masculinity, femininity, and life;
the faculties of suffering, pleasure, and equanimity; and the faculties of faith, vigor, mindfulness, concentration, and wisdom.
The faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown," the faculty of "knowing," and the faculty of "one who has known"—the Tathāgata fully knows all such varieties.
Furthermore, the mind abides in the ear-faculty by reason of the eye-faculty.
The mind does not abide in the three faculties of nose, tongue, or body.
Because of the ear faculty, the mind abides in the nose faculty but does not abide in the other faculties;
because of the nose faculty, the mind abides in the tongue faculty.
The mind abides in the body-faculty because of the tongue-faculty;
the mind abides in the eye-faculty because of the body-faculty.
The Tathāgata fully knows all such various faculties.
Furthermore, if there are sentient beings who possess the faculty of generosity and currently maintain pure precepts,
the Tathāgata knows that from time immemorial their various faculties have undergone manifold and successive differentiations.
For this reason, he teaches the *dānapāramitā*.
If there are sentient beings who possess the faculty of pure ethical discipline (*śīlendriya*) yet currently practice generosity,
the Tathāgata knows that their various faculties have undergone manifold distinctions through successive transformations since beginningless time.
For this reason, he teaches the *śīlapāramitā*.
There may be sentient beings who possess the faculty of patience (*kṣānti-indriya*) yet manifest diligence (*vīrya*).
The Tathāgata knows that from beginningless time, their various faculties have undergone successive transformations and possess many differences.
For this reason, he teaches the perfection of patience (*kṣānti-pāramitā*).
There may be sentient beings who possess the faculty of diligence (*vīryendriya*) yet manifest the practice of patience.
The Tathāgata knows that from beginningless time, their various faculties have undergone manifold and successive differentiations.
For this reason, he teaches the perfection of diligence (*vīrya-pāramitā*).
There may be sentient beings who possess the faculty of meditative concentration (*dhyāna-indriya*) and are currently practicing wisdom (*prajñā*).
The Tathāgata knows that from time immemorial, their various faculties have undergone successive transformations and possess many distinctions.
For this reason, he teaches the dhyānapāramitā.
There may be sentient beings who possess the faculty of wisdom and currently abide in meditative concentration;
the Tathāgata knows that from beginningless time their various faculties have undergone successive transformations and possess many distinctions.
Therefore, for their sake, he teaches the profound *prajñāpāramitā*,
causing them to cultivate all the vast factors of enlightenment (*bodhipakṣadharma*).
Furthermore, he knows that these sentient beings possess the faculties of a *śrāvaka*.
He currently practices the conduct of a pratyekabuddha.
The Tathāgata knows that, from beginningless time, his faculties have evolved through successive stages and possess many distinctions, making him capable of being a śrāvaka.
Therefore, for their sake, he teaches the Dharma of the Śrāvaka vehicle.
If there are sentient beings who possess the faculties of a pratyekabuddha yet practice the conduct of a śrāvaka,
the Tathāgata knows that their various faculties have evolved through successive stages since beginningless time.
There are many distinct categories of those capable of hearing the teachings for pratyekabuddhas;
therefore, the Dharma of the pratyekabuddhas is taught for them.
Or there may be sentient beings who possess the faculties of the Mahāyāna yet practice the path of the two vehicles.

The Tathāgata knows that, from beginningless time, their various faculties have developed through successive transitions and possess many distinctions such that they are capable of hearing the Great Dharma;
for them, he teaches the Mahāyāna. Furthermore, there are sentient beings with inferior faculties who currently practice the Mahāyāna.
The Tathāgata, knowing that from time immemorial the various faculties have undergone successive transformations and possess many differences,
teaches the Dharma for them so that they may abandon what is inferior and practice the Mahāyāna.
Furthermore, there are sentient beings who are not fit vessels for the Dharma.
The Tathāgata knows that their faculties have evolved through successive lifetimes since beginningless time,
and due to these many differences, they have long remained unfit.
Therefore, for the time being, I shall set this aside until their faculties have matured;
when they become capable vessels and give rise to a sincere mind,
the Tathāgata will diligently preach the Dharma for them.
Good son, the Tathāgata knows all sentient beings in this way:
whether their faculties are already mature or not yet mature,
and whether they desire to emerge from the triple world or do not so desire.
The Tathāgatas know all such various things.
How do they know them?
They know their root and how they are to be cultivated.
What is their nature? What is their characteristic?
What is their cause? What is their condition?
What is their volition? What is their fruit?
What is the retribution and what is the ultimate consummation?
The Tathāgata knows each of these exactly as they are.
This is the fifth enlightened activity of the Tathāgata.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:

The Buddha’s wisdom of knowing faculties has reached the other shore; He accords with the various differences among sentient beings, Fully understanding all superior, middling, and inferior grades. Exalted karma can bring about the fruit of liberation.
He has realized that the limit of afflictions is merely false; he knows all things—whether thick or thin, heavy or light—and is well-versed in the various gates of remedying delusions.
He knows that evil gives rise to birth and death while goodness leads to liberation;
he knows the faculties of the eye up to the mind, as well as the faculties of femininity, masculinity, and vitality, along with the roots of suffering, pleasure, grief, joy, and equanimity.

One should know that faith, diligence, mindfulness, concentration, and wisdom—namely, the faculty of "I-have-known" and the faculty of "one-who-has-finally-known"—are all fully understood through the faculty of the eye; they abide solely in the ear, and so on, up to abiding in the body.
Among these, for one who practices the root of generosity, one explains giving (*dāna*); for one who practices the root of morality, one explains ethical discipline (*śīla*).
For those cultivating the faculty of patience, he teaches diligence; for those cultivating the faculty of vigor, he teaches patience.
For those cultivating the faculty of concentration, he teaches wisdom and the various dhyānas. For those cultivating the faculty of wisdom, he teaches prajñā while abiding in concentration.
He teaches the practice of the pratyekabuddhas to those with the faculties of śrāvakas, and he teaches the śrāvaka path because of their specific faculties.
Those with the faculties of a pratyekabuddha who abide in the practice of a śrāvaka—knowing their faculties, he teaches them the path of the pratyekabuddha;
for those who are inferior and far removed from the vehicle of the supreme Dharma, he teaches the gates of the various perfections out of great compassion.
Knowing whether their faculties are mature or immature, he teaches what is suitable for those who are vessels and abandons what is not.
The nature of the cultivation of the modes of activity of the faculties, knowing them as they truly are— according to their causes and conditions,
as well as the ultimate fruition of volition— this is the fifth true activity of the Buddha.
Furthermore, son of good family:
The Tathāgata knows all paths leading everywhere as they truly are.
How does he know them? He knows the realm of sentient beings who are fixed in the right [path].
They know the realm of beings who are indeterminate;
they know the realm of beings who are fixed in error.
How do they know those beings who are fixed in the right?
It means that these sentient beings possess the power of great causal conditions and have planted much merit in the past;
their faculties are sharp and acute, and their wisdom is about to unfold.
The Tathāgata, knowing their past virtues as they truly are, [perceives them].
He may preach the Dharma for some and not for others;
according to their capacity as vessels for the Dharma, he brings them all to liberation.
How does he know those beings who are indeterminate?
This means that those sentient beings possess great power of conditions and their faculties are on the verge of maturation;
if they hear the true Dharma according to their mental dispositions, they will immediately attain liberation,
but if they do not hear the Dharma, they will not attain liberation.
For the sake of these beings of indeterminate nature,
the Tathāgata teaches the Dharma of the harmony of causes and conditions;
those beings hear the Dharma according to their respective capacities.
Their minds attained purity, and each realized the fruits of the Path.
It is for the sake of such beings of indeterminate destiny that the Tathāgata appears in the world.
How, then, does one know those beings of false determination?
This means that these sentient beings have their minds shrouded by ignorance and are not vessels for the Dharma;
there is no further skillful means by which they can be transformed or guided,
just as a blind person stands before the sunlight.
Whether he preaches the Dharma for them or does not preach it,
there is no benefit and they lack the factors of liberation;
the Tathāgata knows that they are not vessels for the Dharma.
He then sets them aside and abandons them for the sake of those sentient beings.
For this reason, the bodhisattva dons the armor of great compassion.
Furthermore, son of good family:
The Tathāgata thoroughly knows the all-pervading conduct of the three poisons of sentient beings.
He knows that there are three types of conduct characterized by sensual desire. What are these three?
That is to say, some instances of lust arise from excellent objects;
some instances of lust arise from perceptions of endearment;
and some instances of lust arise from past habitual tendencies.
One should know that there are also three types of angry conduct. What are these three?
They are as follows: there may be the poison of anger that arises from resentment.
There may be the poison of hatred arising from an adverse object, or there may be the poison of hatred arising from past latent tendencies (*anuśaya*).
One should know that the conduct of delusion (*moha*) likewise has three types.
What are the three? They are:
there is delusion arising from ignorance;
and there is delusion arising from the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*).
There may be delusion arising from a doubting mind;
the Tathāgata fully knows all such various states.
Furthermore, the Tathāgata knows that through ascetic practices one may swiftly attain penetration.
Because the faculty of knowledge is sharp;
and because one knows that the practice of asceticism leads to realization slowly due to the dullness of the faculty of knowledge.
One knows that the practice of peaceful conduct leads to swift penetration because the faculties are sharp;
one knows that the practice of peaceful conduct leads to slow penetration [because the faculties are dull].
Because one knows that the faculties are dull;
furthermore, because one knows there is sluggish progress toward penetration due to being far removed from right mindfulness.
Furthermore, one knows that there are practices which are swiftly mastered through the power of being able to maintain them with persistence;
and one also skillfully knows those practices which are swiftly undertaken but mastered only slowly.
Because of the practice of counting the breath,
there is swift activity and swift penetration;
because the mind does not cling.
Furthermore, one skillfully knows the practice of the discernment of dharmas (dharmapravicaya);
that is to say, there may be a practice in which wisdom is predominant and concentration is slight,
or there may be a practice in which concentration is predominant and wisdom is slight.
Whether some lack both concentration and wisdom,
or whether others are fully perfected in both concentration and wisdom—
the Tathāgata knows them all.
Furthermore, there are some whose practice is endowed with mental power but not physical power;
others whose practice is endowed with physical power but not mental power;
and others whose practice is endowed with neither.
Furthermore, there are those whose conduct is fully endowed with both [purity];
the Tathāgata knows each of these exactly as they truly are.
Moreover, there are those whose bodily actions are pure while their speech and mind are impure.
Furthermore, there may be conduct that purifies speech and mind while leaving bodily action impure;
or that brings all three types of action into purity;
or that leaves all three types of action impure.
Whether these conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) are the causes of birth and death within the three realms or the causes of liberation,
the Tathāgata perceives them all through his unimpeded eye of wisdom, following their every movement.
This is the sixth work of perfect enlightenment of the Tathāgata.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning,
spoke these verses:
The Buddha fully knows the conduct in all places: the great causal power of those with right determination,

the signs of ripening faculties in those of indeterminate determination, and the three types of causes for sentient beings who possess compassion yet lack the vessel [of liberation] due to wrong determination— namely, the three types of hatred, delusion, and greed.
The Buddha knows all the various and boundless realms of afflictions, And how they arise from pervasive causes.
He knows those who attain enlightenment quickly through ascetic practice and keen faculties, And those with dull faculties who cannot reach it due to their sluggishness;
he knows those who attain it swiftly through pleasant practice because of keen faculties, And those with dull faculties who are weak and inferior—the Buddha knows them all.
There are those whose practice is slow but gradually becomes clear; there are others who are slow but attain sudden purification.
There are those whose practice is swift yet achieves only meager results; there are those who surpass the swift through the cause of non-attachment.
There are those whose practice increases wisdom, giving rise to the discernment of dharmas; there are those whose practice increases meditative concentration, becoming vessels for the Dharma.
There are those who possess application but lack both [body and mind], being unsuitable vessels for the Dharma;

There are those in whom the union of concentration and wisdom gives rise to the supreme path, possessing the power of application but not the body; There are those who possess the power of the body but lack the mind;
Because of great majesty and virtue, there are those who possess both body and mind— all who see them know this completely.
There are practices that cannot purify speech and mind;
some can purify body and speech but cannot eternally purify the mind;
there are practices that can only purify the mind but cannot purify speech; and there are practices that can purify both mind and speech.
Some are unable to achieve permanent purity of body; some practice the three karmas with stainless purity;
some practice by establishing the causes of birth and death; and some practice by creating the causes for liberation.
Thus, the Buddha fully understands all such universal modes of conduct; this is the sixth most excellent gateway of karma.
Furthermore, son of good family,

the Tathāgata knows, exactly as they are, all the causes and conditions for the arising and the subduing and extinction of afflictions within all meditative concentrations (*dhyāna*), liberations (*vimokṣa*), samādhis (*samādhi*),
and attainments (*samāpatti*).
How does the Buddha know?
It means he knows the arising of afflictions in sentient beings—
by what cause they arise and by what condition they arise.
Regarding the purification through the extinction of afflictions: by what cause can they be extinguished, and by what condition can they be extinguished?
In this context, the causes and conditions for the arising of afflictions are as follows:
improper mental attention serves as the cause, and ignorance serves as the condition.
With ignorance as cause, volitional formations are the condition;
with volitional formations as cause, consciousness is the condition;
with consciousness as cause, name-and-form are the condition.
With name-and-form as cause and the six sense bases as condition;
with the six sense bases as cause and contact as condition;
with contact as cause and feeling as condition.
Feeling is the cause and craving is the condition;
craving is the cause and grasping is the condition;
grasping is the cause and becoming is the condition.
Conditioned phenomena have arising as their cause and becoming as their condition;
birth has arising as its cause and old age and death as its condition;
afflictions have birth as their cause and karma as their condition.
Viewing is the cause and craving is the condition;
latent afflictions are the cause and manifest afflictions are the condition.
This is the causal condition for the arising of afflictions.
What are the causes and conditions for sentient beings to extinguish all afflictions?
There are two kinds of causes and two kinds of conditions. What are these two?
First, hearing the sound of the Dharma from another in accordance with it;
second, giving rise to right mindfulness within one's own mind.
Furthermore, there are two kinds of causes and two kinds of conditions.
It can cause sentient beings to attain purity and liberation;
that is to say, through *śamatha*, the mind is one-pointed,
and through *vipaśyanā*, there is skillful mastery.
Furthermore, there are two kinds of causes and two kinds of conditions:
because of the knowledge of non-coming and because of the knowledge of coming.
Again, there are two kinds of causal conditions.
Because one observes the principle of non-arising with subtlety and because one is close to liberation.
Furthermore, there are two kinds of causes and conditions:
because one is fully endowed with practice and because wisdom and liberation manifest before one.
Furthermore, there are two kinds of causes and conditions:
namely, the knowledge of exhaustion and the knowledge of non-arising.
Furthermore, there are two kinds of causes and conditions.
Because it accords with the awakening to the principle of ultimate truth,
and because it accords with the attainment of the wisdom of ultimate truth;
this is the cause and condition for the purification that eliminates the afflictions of sentient beings.
The Tathāgata knows them all.
Furthermore, son of good family, the causes and conditions of affliction are without measure,
and the causes and conditions of liberation are likewise immeasurable.
There are some afflictions that can serve as the causal conditions for liberation,
because they contemplate the true nature of reality.
There are also some liberations that can serve as the causal conditions for afflictions.
Because they give rise to attachment,
the Tathāgata fully knows such vast and unobstructed conduct.
Son of good family, the Tathāgata is fully endowed with both meditative concentration and wisdom.

That is to say: having abandoned sensual desires and unwholesome states, with directed thought (*vitarka*) and sustained thought (*vicāra*), and experiencing the joy and happiness born of seclusion, one enters the first *dhyāna*.
Upon arising from the first *dhyāna*, directed thought, sustained thought, and so forth cease.
He enters the eight liberations and the *samāpattis* in forward order;
he dwells in and enters the various *samādhis* in reverse order;
or again, he proceeds with unimpeded freedom, leaping over, skipping, moving horizontally, or ascending vertically.
Abiding in meditative equipoise (*samāpatti*), he manifests samādhi.
The Tathāgata knows that there is not the slightest difference between *samāpatti* and the gateways of samādhi;
the Tathāgata’s samādhis and *samāpattis* do not arise from causes and conditions.
Upon entering a single samādhi, all samādhis manifest before him;
upon arising from one samādhi, he is able to immediately enter all samādhis.
The Tathāgata never forms such a thought.
I am now able to enter such a samādhi,
yet my constant samādhi is never a state of non-concentration;
no one at all is able to fathom or know any of the Tathāgata’s samādhis.
The samādhi of the pratyekabuddha surpasses that of the śrāvaka;
the samādhi of the bodhisattva surpasses that of the pratyekabuddha;
and the samādhi of the Tathāgata surpasses that of the bodhisattva.
Furthermore, there is no one who can surpass the Buddha’s samādhi.
The Tathāgata’s wisdom operates without obstruction in all places, and there is no one who can surpass it.
He teaches all śrāvakas in accordance with their needs so that they may give rise to the śrāvaka-concentration;
it is likewise for pratyekabuddhas and bodhisattvas.
Having thus known these various matters, the Tathāgata [acts accordingly].
He teaches the Dharma to them according to what is appropriate for each;
this is the seventh enlightened activity of the Tathāgata.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, [spoke these verses].
And he spoke in verse:
“The Buddhas, the Kings of Dharma, possess true wisdom; They know the causes of the defilement and purification of all sentient beings.
Through such causes and conditions, afflictions arise; Through such causes and conditions, liberation is attained.”
With wrong thought as the cause and ignorance as the condition, with ignorance as the cause and volitional formations as the condition for consciousness,
name-and-form, the six sense bases, and so forth— the causal conditions of the factors of existence are all thus:
with afflictions as the cause and karma as the condition, with various views as the cause and craving as the condition.

With latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) and fetters as the cause, and active afflictions (*kleśa*) as the condition, sentient beings attain liberation through these two causes and conditions. Hearing the voice of another, they give rise to compliance;
within their own minds, they correctly contemplate the dharma of emptiness. Thus liberated from the ocean of existence, they attain transcendence.
The union of śamatha and vipaśyanā mutually support one another; Not the slightest coming or going can be found.
Contemplating with truth that there is neither birth nor cessation, One draws near to liberation and attains the cool state.
Cultivating these three practices, one grows in the three types of clear knowledge (vidyā); Practicing liberation, one remains heedful.
Having attained the knowledge of the exhaustion of outflows and the knowledge of non-arising, he realizes the true truths;
by these causes and conditions, the Buddha enters the samādhi-gate of the pure mind.
Entering and emerging from the meditative absorption of cessation with full mindfulness, the Dharma King’s dhyāna-concentration is peerless; he enters the eight liberations and many samādhis.
Moving through the stages in reverse or forward order, leaping over or skipping intervals;
In one concentration, they manifest infinite concentrations, their minds free from constraint and non-conceptual;

Though they always abide in concentration, they have no fixed concentration such as the *samādhis* of śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas— The bodhisattvas possess hundreds of millions of various kinds of concentrations.
The Buddha’s samādhi surpasses all meditative concentrations; this skillful wisdom of his activity is immeasurable.
Furthermore, son of good family, the Tathāgata, by means of the knowledge of past lives...
He knows the countless past lives of himself and all sentient beings—
namely, one birth, two births, ten births, a hundred births, a thousand births,
ten thousand births, and hundreds of thousands of millions of births.
The eon of formation, the eon of destruction, and the eon of both formation and destruction;
countless eons of formation, countless eons of destruction, and countless eons of both formation and destruction;
myself and sentient beings with such-and-such names.
Such is their lineage; such is their diet;
such is their physical form; such is their appearance;
such is their experience of suffering and pleasure; and such is their dwelling place.
Thus, with such a lifespan and such a cycle of birth and death,
he recollects all the various and countless matters of his former existences, including how he passed away from one place and was reborn in another.
Furthermore, he knows that various sentient beings were born into this world due to such causes in the past;
having known this, the Tathāgata teaches the Dharma to them according to what is appropriate for each.
Furthermore, one knows truly that the past mental activities of all sentient beings are such that the preceding thought-moment,
through its sequential causal cessation, gives rise to a continuous succession,
and so it is with the subsequent thought-moment.
Furthermore, when conditions are lacking, subsequent moments of mind do not arise;
all such various instances the Tathāgata fully knows.
Just as for a single sentient being, such a thought ceases and such a thought arises.
The cycle of rebirth continues without interruption, immeasurable and boundless;
it could not be fully described even in eons as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.
As it is for one sentient being, so it is for all sentient beings.
The arising and ceasing of every thought-moment and the continuous succession of minds are such that they could not be fully described;
yet the Tathāgata knows each and every one of them exactly as they are,
even until the end of the kalpas of the future.
It is said that the Tathāgata’s knowledge of past lives is inexhaustible;
therefore, it is said that the Tathāgata’s wisdom regarding past lives is inconceivable and immeasurable.
Its limits are difficult to fathom and its explanation is inexhaustible.
At that time, the Tathāgata uttered a voice of great compassion,
like a bull king, proclaiming universally to all sentient beings.
You all should, in every thought-moment,
contemplate whether you planted roots of goodness in the distant or recent past,
or whether you ever planted roots of goodness in the presence of a Buddha.
Or, regarding the various roots of goodness planted by those of the two vehicles,
all those sentient beings, through the Buddha's majestic power, remember their past virtues; having known this,
the Tathāgata teaches the Dharma according to their needs.
Once those sentient beings have heard the Dharma,
they attain non-retrogression in their respective vehicles according to their past roots of goodness.
This is the eighth deed of perfect enlightenment of the Tathāgata.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning,
spoke these verses: "The Buddha,
the Lamp of the World, recalls past kalpas numbering in the countless billions of nayutas."
Having clearly realized himself and all sentient beings, as if viewing five *āmalaka* fruits in the palm of his hand,
he discerns their names, surnames, physical forms, and distinctions of lifespan, dwelling place, and birth and death;
for these reasons, knowing the proper time, he preaches the Dharma to those born in this place.
Furthermore, he knows that throughout boundless past kalpas, the minds and mental factors of sentient beings differ;
though they give rise to thoughts of infinite varieties, the Tathāgata’s great wisdom clearly understands them all.
The stream of the past mind flows on without interruption, and the Buddha knows every single instance of each sentient being.
Even if one were to speak for as many eons as there are grains of sand in the Ganges,
throughout all eons until the end of the future, one could never exhaustively describe his boundless conduct;
for the wisdom regarding the causes of the Buddha’s past lives is peerless and limitless, like the great ocean with no shore.
The Buddha abides in superior power through sharp wisdom; He recollects the pure, white causes he cultivated in the past, As well as the roots of goodness planted by those sentient beings.
Through the Buddha’s majestic spiritual power, he causes them to remember The causes of virtuous dharmas they previously performed.
Having reflected thus, he taught and established them in the three vehicles; his pure liberation never regresses.
The Sugata’s past causes were immeasurable, difficult for all sentient beings to fathom.
With this eighth deed as the cause, countless sentient beings have been fully disciplined.
Furthermore, son of good family,
the Tathāgata’s divine eye is pure and surpasses that of the human eye;
he sees all sentient beings dying here and being born there.
That is to say, there are inferior and superior, beautiful and ugly, or fair and foul forms;
in these various ways, beings take birth according to their karma.
There are some sentient beings who possess evil conduct of the body.
There are some sentient beings who possess verbal misconduct;
there are some sentient beings who possess mental misconduct;
or, due to the karmic causes and conditions of slandering the noble ones, holding wrong views, and so forth.
After casting off this body, they fall into hell.
Furthermore, there are sentient beings who possess virtuous conduct of the body;
or there are sentient beings who possess virtuous conduct of speech.
There are some sentient beings who possess virtuous conduct of mind;
because of the karmic causes and conditions of not slandering the noble ones and maintaining right view,
after casting off this body, they are reborn in the heavens.
The Tathāgata’s divine eye knows and sees all such things throughout the ten directions,
as far as the limit of the dharma-realm and the ultimate reaches of the realm of empty space— immeasurable and boundless.
Beyond all worlds that exceed in number,
there may be some worlds among them where the kalpa-fire blazes forth, leaving everything empty and non-existent.
In some worlds, various sentient beings die here and are reborn there;
in others, bodhisattvas travel through various lands;
and in yet others, tathāgatas proceed to the tree of enlightenment.
Having realized great bodhi and turned the wheel of the true Dharma,
he should now conceal his traces and manifest entry into nirvāṇa;
likewise, each of the śrāvakas has manifested the attainment of liberation or entered nirvāṇa.
Those various Pratyekabuddhas manifest diverse supernatural powers,
enabling those who encounter them to increase in merit.
Thus, the Buddha clearly perceives all these various manifestations as if they were right before his eyes.
Furthermore, one sees sentient beings who possess no corporeal form;
they are not visible to the divine eye of those with the five supernatural powers,
nor can they be seen by the eyes of the followers of the Two Vehicles or even Bodhisattvas.
Only the Tathāgata perceives with the clarity of his divine eye that there may be a region the size of a chariot wheel,
filled with sentient beings who possess no physical form.
The Buddha clearly perceives all the humans and devas within the trichiliocosm.
With his purified divine eye, he minutely observes all sentient beings in every world who are capable of being tamed.
He causes each and every one of those beings to see the Buddha’s body appearing before them,
yet those various beings do not know of one another.
This is the ninth enlightened activity of the Tathāgata at that time.
The World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:
With the Tathāgata’s pure divine eye of radiance, His majestic power illuminates boundless kalpas;
Throughout all inconceivable lands in the ten directions, What are the various signs of sentient beings as they take birth?
There are those who have already been born, those currently being born, and those yet to be born; distinguished by various forms, whether with or without form;
or belonging to the realms of humans and devas, or the three miserable paths.
Their births are not of one kind—low, middling, or superior—and as they are about to die or are about to be born, these various differences are all seen by the Seer without exception.
Those who commit evil deeds sink into the miserable realms; those who cultivate merit transcend to the human and celestial worlds.
Some practice the conduct of a bodhisattva, entering and emerging from the cultivation of the roots of enlightenment.
Others sit beneath the tree of awakening to vanquish the hosts of Māra and realize the supreme path of bodhi.
Turning the wondrous wheel of Dharma with total mastery, The measure of the liberation of humans and devas is inconceivable;
Having performed the Buddha-work, they manifest nirvana. With the Tathāgata’s divine eye, all are clearly seen:
Some hear from a teacher and attain right mindfulness, Treading upon cessation and attaining cool serenity.
Some transcend the ocean of existence without relying on a teacher; the Tathāgata beholds their liberation and peace.
There may be countless assemblies of śrāvakas, or others who practice the vehicle of the pratyekabuddhas.
That realm of sentient beings is without limit, yet the Buddha’s pure divine eye perceives it all with clarity.

There may be sentient beings without form or appearance, as numerous as those within the three thousandfold world-systems who are as large as chariot wheels; such subtle beings the Tathāgata perceives,
