seeing each and every realm of sentient beings as they transmigrate through the five paths of existence without end.
The All-Knowing One realizes there are no sentient beings; yet, out of great compassion, he tames them.

To those of sharp faculties who are ready for deliverance, each perceives the Tathāgata appearing before them, preaching the supreme Dharma to satisfy their hearts. This is the ninth karmic activity of the Buddha’s divine eye.
Furthermore, son of good family,
the Tathāgata has exhausted all outflows and is free from further afflictions;
his mind is well-liberated and his wisdom is well-liberated.
With self-awakening manifest before him, fully perfected and complete, he uttered this lion’s roar, saying:
"Birth has been exhausted; the holy life has been established."
Having accomplished what was to be done, he shall not undergo further existence.
The Tathāgata knows this: that all afflictions have been utterly exhausted, and that there is the supremely stainless, pure radiance.
There are no habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) that are not eternally extinguished.
The Śrāvakas, having severed their delusions, possess a cessation that is finite and measurable, yet their habitual tendencies are not removed.
The Pratyekabuddhas, though they exhaust their delusions, likewise have a limit to their attainment.
Far removed from great compassion and lacking unimpeded eloquence,
there is only the Tathāgata’s single moment of mind in equal correspondence with reality.
All afflictions, all characteristics of affliction, the root afflictions, and the latencies of affliction are forever exhausted without remainder.
Great compassion perfectly gathers [beings], and eloquence and fearlessness are entirely fulfilled;
none in all the worlds can surpass them. Why is this?
Because the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas...
Because it eternally extinguishes all habitual tendencies of karma, habitual tendencies of afflictions, and habitual tendencies of lapses in dignified conduct;
it is like space, which is pure by nature and provides no basis for the abiding of any smoke or dust.
The Tathāgata is likewise; having attained the wisdom that brings afflictions to their ultimate end, all karmas, afflictions, and habitual tendencies have no place of abiding.
Yet, the mind of the Tathāgata functions through the characteristic of non-abiding.
Abiding in the subtle and wondrous state of the equality of wisdom where all afflictions are exhausted,
he preached the sublime Dharma for the sake of severing all the afflictions and tainted five aggregates of sentient beings, speaking these words:
Alas! Sentient beings give rise to afflictions amidst matters that are fundamentally non-existent.
You should contemplate, discern, and investigate this according to reality.
Furthermore, for the sake of sentient beings, you should employ various skillful means and diverse analogies.
It is taught that the nature of afflictions is fundamentally non-existent.
When those sentient beings have contemplated this according to reality,
they do not perceive even the slightest phenomenon that can be grasped or clung to.
Various afflictions are spontaneously and eternally extinguished as they enter nirvana;
this is the Tathāgata’s tenth deed of perfect awakening.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, [spoke these verses].
And he spoke these verses:
The World-Honored One of Ten Powers, his strength perfected, Has accomplished the vast and profound gateway;
In accord with the wisdom that exhausts the hindrances of affliction, He has attained supreme enlightenment, the most tranquil state.
The Śrāvakas extinguish delusions and attain the knowledge of exhaustion, yet their limited habitual tendencies remain unremoved;
The Pratyekabuddhas sever delusions and attain enlightenment, yet they lack great compassion and eloquence.
The Buddha is the Lord of the World, supreme among men; Delusions and habitual tendencies are both extinguished, and his virtues are perfectly complete.
Great compassion increases as the limit of afflictions is reached; Infinite eloquence is fully accomplished.

The Buddha abides in the wisdom that exhausts all afflictions; Knowing that the delusions of sentient beings are not real, he pities those beings who travel on wrong paths And fail to tread the tracks of the Tathāgata’s True Dharma.
With fierce and great compassion, he teaches beings the gateway of impermanence, suffering, emptiness, and non-self.
You should contemplate that the fundamental nature is empty; thus you shall always attain the most supreme and wondrous tranquility.
Do not perceive sentient beings, persons, agents, or *māṇavas*.
For the sake of sentient beings who cling to false views, the Great Awakened One gives rise to compassion and preaches liberation;
at all times, he never grows weary, never for a single thought-moment abandoning sentient beings,
remaining eternally in unmoving samādhi, expounding the wondrous Dharma to benefit them.
Such are the signs of the Buddha’s activities; he who abides in the stage of the Ten Powers turns the peerless, most supreme wheel. He can crush enemies and is immovable;
this is the *Dhāraṇī Sūtra of the Protector of the Realm*, Scroll Five.
The Scripture of the Dhāraṇī of the Sovereign Who Protects the Realm, Scroll Six.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Prajña of Kaśmīra together with Munisri.
Chapter Five, Part Two: Entering the Inconceivable and Profound Activities of the Tathāgata.
Furthermore, son of good family,
the Tathāgata abides in the four fearlessnesses and is able to perform the various activities of all Buddhas.
This means knowing that one’s own self is indeed the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
Among all the worlds, whether gods or humans,
there is no one capable of making a reasoned statement saying that the Tathāgata, the World-Honored One, is not perfectly enlightened.
For what reason are the Tathāgatas called "Perfectly Awakened Ones"?
It is because the Tathāgatas have attained equal and perfect awakening regarding all phenomena,
such that there is no distinction of high or low among them.
What are all phenomena? They are the phenomena of ordinary beings, the phenomena of those in training, the phenomena of those beyond training,
the phenomena of pratyekabuddhas, the phenomena of bodhisattvas, and the phenomena of buddhas.
All such phenomena are perfectly awakened to.
Furthermore, there are mundane phenomena and supramundane phenomena;
wholesome phenomena and unwholesome phenomena.
There are tainted phenomena and untainted phenomena;
conditioned phenomena and unconditioned phenomena.
Such phenomena as these have been perfectly awakened to by the Tathāgata.
Because their essence is equal.
In what way are they equal?
It means that they are equal in emptiness.
Because one sees that the intrinsic nature of all phenomena is empty,
they are signless and equal,
for signs are themselves their intrinsic nature.
The equality of wishlessness,
because of the nature of the three realms;
the equality of non-arising.
Because the nature of arising is such,
there is equality in non-activity; because the nature of activity is such, there is equality in non-activity.
It is equal in being without emergence,
because it emerges from its own fundamental nature;
it is equal in being without the ālayavijñāna.
Because it is the intrinsic nature of the mind,
such is the equality of ultimate truth;
because it is the nature of the three periods of time.
Wisdom and liberation are equal,
because their fundamental nature is ignorance and craving.
Nirvana is equal.
Because the very essence of the cycle of birth and death is thus,
the Tathāgata has perfectly awakened to all such equal dharmas.
For these reasons, it is said that the Tathāgata is truly the Unsurpassed Perfectly Enlightened One.
Having attained such perfect enlightenment,
he utters sublime words with a heart of great compassion,
preaching various dharmas for the sake of all sentient beings.
He demonstrates the path of liberation to enable beings to transcend the limits of suffering;
other sentient beings are truly not Great Teachers,
yet they claim for themselves, "I am a Perfectly Awakened One."
For the sake of these sentient beings, the Tathāgata proclaims his own virtuous name, saying:
"I alone, the Tathāgata, am the Truly Perfectly Awakened One."
Causing those who are not vessels for the Dharma to all become vessels for the Dharma—
this is the eleventh deed of perfect enlightenment of the Tathāgata.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to reiterate this meaning,
spoke these verses:
"The one who has attained spontaneous awakening Awakens to the equality of all dharmas."
Therefore, he is called the Tathāgata; with the vision of perfect awakening,
he sees all ordinary beings' dharmas as equal to the Buddha-dharmas,
and likewise for those in training and those beyond training, as well as the dharmas of the pratyekabuddhas.
Mundane and supramundane phenomena—these two are also equal;
wholesome and unwholesome phenomena, as well as nirvana, are equal.
Empty phenomena, signless phenomena, wishless phenomena, and non-arising phenomena are all equal.
The dharmas such as non-action and so forth are revealed in their equality;
the Buddha’s great compassion is extensively proclaimed.
Awakening all sentient beings, they attain liberation upon hearing the Dharma—this is the Buddha’s supreme activity.
Furthermore, son of good family,
the Tathāgata himself knows that all outflows and afflictions have been completely exhausted;
this is known by all in the world, whether gods or humans.
There is no one capable of saying that the Tathāgata’s outflows and afflictions are not yet exhausted;
how could it be that the Tathāgata’s outflows and afflictions have been completely and ultimately extinguished?
This means that the mind attains liberation from the afflictions of desire,
because one realizes the truth of cessation regarding all habitual tendencies and afflictions associated with the sphere of desire.
The mind also attains liberation from the afflictions of existence.
Because the afflictions of the habitual tendencies of all hatred-practices have been realized as extinction,
the mind is liberated from the afflictions of ignorance.
Because the afflictions of the habitual tendencies of all delusion-practices have been realized as extinction, [the mind is liberated].
The mind attains liberation from the afflictions of views;
because one realizes the extinction of all afflictive activities along with their habitual tendencies,
this principle accords with conventional truth.
It is said that for the Tathāgata, all outflows and afflictions have been utterly and eternally exhausted.
With the noble eye of wisdom, which accords with ultimate truth,
he observes and realizes that not even the slightest dharma can be apprehended.

That is to say, whether it be the wisdom capable of extinguishing, the afflictions to be extinguished, the contemplation, or the cultivation—even up to the direct realization—none of these can be apprehended. Why is this?
Because their intrinsic nature is exhausted; there is no time when they are not exhausted.
It is not said to be exhausted through dependence upon causes and conditions or through opposition. Such exhaustion is true exhaustion.
This true exhaustion does not act as a cause or condition for any other dharma.
Therefore, this exhaustion is precisely the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
Within this very dharma, there is neither arising nor ceasing, nor is there any abiding.
This absence of arising and ceasing remains eternally present within the realm of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*), whether a Buddha appears in the world or does not appear.
Just as the dharma-realm is eternal, so too is the accomplishment of this wisdom.
This accomplishment is itself non-accomplishment.
If one can abide in accordance with these instructions, one will attain freedom from afflictions.
It is not that afflictions cease to exist simply because they have been severed;
rather, out of great compassion, the Tathāgata accords with conventional truth and teaches sentient beings the Dharma for extinguishing afflictions.
This is the twelfth deed of perfect enlightenment of the Tathāgata.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning,
spoke these verses:
The Buddha has no habitual tendencies of desire;
therefore, the afflictions of desire and the habitual tendencies of hatred are exhausted.
Afflictions do not arise in the Sugata, for he is free from ignorance by having extinguished the root of delusion.
When the habitual tendencies of all afflictions are exhausted, the afflictions of view no longer arise.
The Buddha speaks of the exhaustion of afflictions by way of conventional truth;
within the ultimate truth, they cannot be found—there is neither decrease nor increase.
The knowledge of exhaustion does not take objects as its conditions;
Noble wisdom is fundamentally exhausted because it is devoid of the three characteristics.
This exhaustion is the unconditioned dharma-realm, eternally immutable; To know this is to reach the other shore.
Having known this, he spoke thus: "The Buddha is able to exhaustively fathom this karma.
Furthermore, son of good family, the Tathāgata is impartial.
He understands, as they truly are, the obstructive factors and the unobstructive factors regarding all hindrances;
and among all the world, whether devas or humans—
There is no one capable of providing a reasoned statement that the dharmas described by the Tathāgata as obstacles are not actually obstacles.
In this context, what are the obstructive dharmas?
It is said that there is one dharma capable of acting as an obstacle,
namely, a turbid and distracted mind.
Furthermore, there are two dharmas capable of acting as obstacles.
That is to say, lack of shame and lack of dread.
Furthermore, there are three factors that act as obstacles:
namely, misconduct of body, misconduct of speech, and misconduct of mind.
Furthermore, there are four things that can act as obstacles:
namely, practicing what is unrighteous out of greed,
or practicing what is unrighteous out of hatred.
There are those who act contrary to the Dharma out of delusion,
and there are those who act contrary to the Dharma out of fear.
Furthermore, there are five factors that can serve as obstacles.
These are killing, stealing, sexual misconduct, false speech, and drinking various intoxicants.
Furthermore, there are six other factors that act as obstacles:
namely, lack of respect for the Buddha and lack of respect for the Dharma.
They do not respect the Sangha, they do not respect the precepts,
and they cannot respect meditative concentration or spiritual friends.
Furthermore, there are seven other factors that can act as obstacles.
That is to say: pride, excessive pride, pride beyond pride, the pride of "I am," overweening pride, inferiority pride, and false pride.
Furthermore, there are eight factors that can act as obstacles.
That is to say: wrong view, wrong intention, wrong speech, wrong action, wrong livelihood, wrong effort, wrong mindfulness, and wrong concentration.
Furthermore, there are nine factors that can act as obstacles.
What are the nine? They are:
those who have harmed me, those who are currently harming me, and those who will harm me;
those who have hated my virtuous friends in the past, those who are currently hating my virtuous friends, and those who will hate my virtuous friends in the future.
Those who were my enemies in the past, those who are my enemies in the present, and those who will be my enemies in the future—
when one’s unwholesome mind increases through recollecting these nine types of objects, it is called an obstruction.
Furthermore, there are ten factors that can act as obstacles. What are these ten?
They are: killing, stealing, sexual misconduct, false speech, divisive speech, harsh speech, and frivolous speech.
Greed, hatred, and wrong view— these are called the ten.
In this way, up to the point of giving rise to unwholesome thoughts and becoming attached to their causes and conditions,
one dwells securely within all afflictions (*kleśa*) and fetters (*saṃyojana*).
They are constantly associated with the obstacles of perversion;
their afflictions of craving and views are firmly grasped and not relinquished.
Whatever actions they perform through body, speech, or mind—
All of these are associated with fame, profit, and various desires;
all such things are called hindrances.
The Tathāgata knows them all and [teaches] for the sake of sentient beings.
To teach the unobstructed dharmas as they truly are,
so that all obstructions are forever severed and do not arise again—
this is the thirteenth deed of perfect enlightenment of the Tathāgata.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke in verse:
The Buddha has awakened to the factors that constitute obstacles; One cannot realize liberation [if one remains bound by them].
That is to say, with a mind that is not pure, lacking both shame and dread of blame,
and devoid of the unmanifest precepts within the actions of body, speech, and mind,
one gives rise to limitless evil conduct driven by greed, hatred, delusion, and fear.
Killing, stealing, and sexual misconduct; False speech and the drinking of various intoxicants—these six;
Lack of respect, the seven types of pride, The constant practice of the eightfold wrong path, The nine afflictions, and the ten causes of evil— The Buddha taught that all these are obstacles.
Cultivating unwholesome thoughts prevents one from attaining the gateway to liberation;
the Buddha, knowing the source of such perversity, teaches the Dharma out of compassion for those who cling firmly to what is non-existent,
so as to cause them to leave behind the causes of obstruction.
Furthermore, son of good family,
the Tathāgata has taught, in accordance with reality, the path that leads to the exhaustion of suffering.
All sentient beings who rely upon this for practice shall all attain liberation.
Regarding this matter, among all those in the world— whether gods or humans—
none are able to speak reasonably, saying that what the Tathāgata has taught is not the path to liberation.
What is called the path of true liberation?
It is said that the Single Path is the path of liberation;
it consists in giving rise to a pure mind toward all sentient beings.
Furthermore, there are two paths that constitute the path of liberation: namely, śamatha and vipaśyanā.
Furthermore, there are three paths that constitute the path of liberation.
This refers to the gateways of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness.
Furthermore, there are four paths that constitute the path of liberation;
these are the four foundations of mindfulness. What are the four?

These are the applications of mindfulness regarding body, feeling, mind, and phenomena. What is the application of mindfulness regarding the body? It is observing the internal body as a body so that the mind attains stability;
it is observing the external body as a body so that the mind attains stability.
Contemplating the body internally and externally,
one dwells observing the body as the body;
this is called the foundation of mindfulness of the body.
What is the application of mindfulness of feelings?
It is said: by contemplating internal feelings, external feelings, and both internal and external feelings in accordance with feelings, the mind attains stable abiding.
What is the foundation of mindfulness of the mind?
It is the contemplation of the internal mind, the external mind, and both the internal and external mind; by thus following the mind in contemplation, the mind attains stable abiding.
What is the application of mindfulness to phenomena?
It refers to contemplating internal phenomena, external phenomena, and both internal and external phenomena, following the observation of phenomena so that the mind attains stable abiding.
Furthermore, there are five paths that constitute the path of liberation. What are these five?
They are the faculty of faith, the faculty of vigor, the faculty of mindfulness, the faculty of concentration, and the faculty of wisdom.
Furthermore, there are six paths that constitute the path of liberation.

What are these six? They are: mindfulness of the Buddha, mindfulness of the Dharma, mindfulness of the Sangha, mindfulness of ethical discipline, mindfulness of relinquishment, and mindfulness of the devas.
Furthermore, there are seven paths that constitute the path of liberation.

What are these seven? They are: the factor of enlightenment of mindfulness, the factor of enlightenment of investigation of phenomena, the factor of enlightenment of energy, the factor of enlightenment of joy, and the factor of enlightenment of pliancy.
The concentration factor of enlightenment and the equanimity factor of enlightenment;
furthermore, there are eight factors of the path which constitute the path of liberation.
What are these eight? They are right view, right intention, right speech, and right action.
Right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness, and right concentration.
Furthermore, there are nine paths that constitute the path of liberation, namely:
the first dhyāna, the second dhyāna, the third dhyāna, and the fourth dhyāna.

The sphere of infinite space, the sphere of infinite consciousness, the sphere of nothingness, the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, and the attainment of the cessation of perception and feeling.
Furthermore, there are ten paths that constitute the path of liberation:
namely, abstaining from killing, abstaining from stealing, and abstaining from sexual misconduct.
Abstaining from false speech, abstaining from divisive speech, abstaining from harsh speech, and abstaining from frivolous speech;
being without covetousness, without ill will, and without wrong views—these are called the ten.
All such wholesome factors conducive to enlightenment (bodhipakṣadharma) are likewise included.
Or it is associated with the aggregate of ethical discipline, associated with the aggregate of concentration,
associated with the aggregate of wisdom, associated with the aggregate of liberation,
and associated with the aggregate of the knowledge and vision of liberation.
Alternatively, all that is associated with the Noble Truths constitutes the path of liberation.
Furthermore, there is the path of liberation known as the true Middle Way,
wherein not the slightest thing can be apprehended, and there is neither increase nor decrease.
Neither grasping nor abandoning, neither collecting nor dispersing,
one attains the true path wherein two thoughts do not arise,
for all dharmas are fundamentally non-dual.
The Tathāgata possesses true knowledge and vision regarding this path of liberation,
and he likewise proclaims it thus for the sake of sentient beings;
those who practice it are able to exhaust the source of suffering.
This is the fourteenth deed of perfect enlightenment of the Tathāgata.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning,
spoke these verses:
Cultivating the pure path, increasing immeasurable bliss,
and being able to enter the way to the deathless nectar—
these are the factors of enlightenment (bodhipakṣa) known spontaneously by the Buddha’s wisdom as all causes for every kind of goodness.
The practitioner attains liberation; there is nothing that can be said to be non-rectitude for extinguishing the afflictions.
Being able to harmonize with what is wholesome and remaining far from what is not, one attains the peace and bliss of nirvāṇa.
Skillfully observing causes and conditions, Like space, they have no objective reality;
Like illusions and like dreams, They are able to escape the stream of birth and death.
Relying on meditative concentration, they give rise to compassion, And thus liberate themselves from the cycle of existence.
This is the deed of the Great Sage, peerless in the world.
Furthermore, son of good family,
the body of the Tathāgata is free from error.
It is impossible for any ordinary person or even a person of superior wisdom to find even the slightest fault in the Tathāgata. Why is this?
Because of the Tathāgata’s physical actions (kāyakarma).
His deportment was dignified and majestic, and his movements were without glancing about. Wearing the saṃghāṭī robe, with his robes and bowl in hand, whether walking,
standing, sitting, or reclining, or in any movement, advancing, retreating, or turning, he remained composed.
Entering and leaving villages, or traveling to and from towns and cities—
in all such instances, he was discerning and composed;
his feet did not touch the ground.
Furthermore, the mark of the thousand-spoked wheel appeared clearly upon the ground;
moreover, there were lotuses, pure and fragrant with exquisite beauty, that supported his feet.
All living beings who came into contact with the Tathāgata’s footprints [experienced great benefit].
For seven days and seven nights, he remained peaceful and composed.
Thereafter, he was reborn among humans and devas, experiencing supreme and wondrous bliss.
The Tathāgata’s kāṣāya robe remained four inches away from his body without falling.
Even the violent winds of the whirlwind cannot shake it.
His body is constantly radiant; wherever its light touches, even those as low as the Avīci Hell are relieved of their suffering and become cool and refreshed.
For these reasons, it is said that the Tathāgata’s bodily actions are without fault.
Furthermore, son of good family, the Tathāgata’s verbal actions are free from error.
This applies to all ordinary beings, whether they be ignorant or wise.
It is impossible that one could find any fault [in this].
Why? Good son, it is because the Tathāgata speaks words only when he knows the proper time.
At that time, his speech was truthful, real, and meaningful;
he acted exactly as he spoke without error.
He did not speak twice, and all sentient beings who heard him were filled with joy.
He adorns his speech with the profound meaning of syllables;
through a single sound he teaches the Dharma, which is understood equally by beings of diverse kinds.
For this reason, it is said that the Tathāgata’s speech is without error.
Furthermore, son of good family,
the mental karma of the Tathāgata is free from error.
This applies to all ordinary beings, whether they be ignorant or wise.
It is impossible to find any fault [in this].
Why? Because the Tathāgata constantly abides in samādhi;
he practices the conduct of all Buddhas and is always free from distraction.
By means of unattached wisdom, he knows all phenomena;
therefore, the Tathāgata’s mental karma is without fault.
Son of good family, the Tathāgata abides spontaneously in the state of being free from error and transgression.
He also teaches such a Dharma to sentient beings,
enabling them to attain the Tathāgata’s quality of being free from error.
This is the fifteenth enlightened activity of the Tathāgata.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:
"Uniquely Honored throughout the Three Realms, free from error; The actions of body, speech, and mind are pure and without blemish."
The World-Honored One is inwardly free from afflictions and is universally able to benefit all sentient beings;

desiring to sever the various faults of living beings, he proclaims the most supreme gate of tranquility so that they may be without error and become equal to the World-Honored One— this is the fifteenth activity of the Tathāgata.
Furthermore, son of good family,
the Tathāgata has no distinct characteristics such as sounds of suffering or pleasure;
therefore, among all humans, devas, non-Buddhists, Māras, or Brahmās, [he is peerless].
No one can say that the Buddha’s voice has any fault.
What kind of voice does it lack?
It is the so-called Tathāgata’s voice, which is free from both sorrow and joy.
Why is this? Because he is free from attachment and aversion.
Even when all sentient beings offer him various kinds of offerings, respect, and praise, he does not give rise to a heart of joy, nor does he become elated.
When all sentient beings fail to practice respectful service and instead slander,
revile, or insult him, the Tathāgata gives rise to neither anger nor dejection;
thus, the Tathāgata possesses a voice free from regret or resentment.
Why is this? Because the tasks he has undertaken have been brought to ultimate completion without the slightest difficulty.
The Tathāgata possesses a voice free from contention;
why is this? Because in the past, he always delighted in dwelling in *araṇya* (forest hermitages).
Free from "I" and "mine," without grasping or seeking,
for they have already been liberated from the fetters and bonds of affliction.
Good son, the Tathāgata abides in a voice that is free from differentiated characteristics.
He also teaches such a Dharma to sentient beings,
causing them to be free from such sounds of divergent characteristics.
This is the sixteenth deed of perfect enlightenment of the Tathāgata.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke in verse:
"When respectfully praised, the mind does not become elated; when treated with contempt or reviled, the mind does not sink."

Because he is far removed from craving, hatred, and unrighteousness, And because his sublime conduct in past lives was beyond reproach, The Buddha dwelt in forest hermitages (āraṇya) practicing in former times; All fetters of grasping at "mine" are non-existent in him.
Abiding in such a Dharma, he speaks thus: "This most supreme activity belongs only to the Tathāgata."
Furthermore,
son of good family,
the Tathāgata possesses no loss of mindfulness.
Therefore, there is not the slightest phenomenon that he does not clearly remember.
Regarding what he does not forget:
it refers to all the dhyānas, liberations, samādhis, and samāpattis.
Within such dharmas, there is no forgetting or loss. Furthermore,
he knows the mental activities, movements, glances, and comings and goings of sentient beings,
and he expounds the Dharma according to what is appropriate without ever forgetting.
Within the fearlessnesses of the Dharma, its meaning, its phrasing, and his eloquence, there is likewise no loss of mindfulness.
The Tathāgata, abiding in unattached wisdom, possesses no loss of mindfulness regarding the phenomena of the three periods of time.
He also teaches such a Dharma to sentient beings,
causing them to attain mindfulness without forgetfulness.
This is the seventeenth enlightened activity of the Tathāgata.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:
The Supreme Dharma King has no forgetfulness; In meditative concentration and the knowledge of dharmas, nothing is left behind.
He fully knows the mental activities of all sentient beings and teaches them according to their needs without fear.
Regarding all dharmas of the various vehicles throughout the three periods of time, his unattached wisdom is never forgetful;
his teaching likewise follows this state of non-forgetfulness—this is the deed of the Supreme Being.
Furthermore, son of good family,
all Tathāgatas possess no unconcentrated mind; that is to say, whether walking,
standing, sitting, or reclining, eating, drinking, speaking, or remaining silent.
During such times, he constantly abides in profound samāhita;
entering all samādhis, he reaches the further shore,
remaining unimpeded in all meditative concentrations.
Among all the beings of the world, whether gods or humans,
not a single one was able to perceive the Tathāgata’s state of meditative equipoise (samāhita),
except for those who were enveloped by the majestic power of the World-Honored One.
The Tathāgata always abides in a state of non-distraction and also teaches such Dharma to sentient beings so that they may abandon distraction;
this is the eighteenth enlightened activity of the Tathāgata.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke in verse:
The Tathāgata constantly abides in samādhi, At all times— whether walking, standing, sitting, or reclining.
Whether eating, drinking, speaking, or remaining silent, he benefits sentient beings;
Always abiding in samādhi without wavering, the classes of beings throughout the worlds of the ten directions Cannot fathom the Buddha’s mind of samādhi.
He also explains this gateway for the sake of sentient beings; Such is the inconceivable activity of the Buddha.
Furthermore, son of good family,
all Tathāgatas have no manifold conceptions;
because they are free from various and diverse conceptions, their minds are without high or low.
How is it that the Tathāgata has no notion of diversity?
It is because he has no notion of diversity regarding all buddha-fields;
for the essential nature of buddha-fields is identical to space and is inexhaustible.
One has no notion of diversity regarding all sentient beings,
because the fundamental nature of sentient beings is equally selfless.
One has no notion of diversity regarding all Buddhas.
Through the wisdom of equality, one realizes the true dharma-realm;
because it is of a single characteristic, unmixed and indestructible,
there is no notion of diversity within the Buddha-dharma.
Because the nature of all phenomena is undefiled,
one does not give rise to attachment upon seeing those who uphold the precepts,
nor does one give rise to aversion upon seeing those who violate the prohibitions.
When one gains benefit for oneself or others, the mind does not become inflated; when one suffers loss for oneself or others, the mind does not diminish.
One neither shows excessive respect toward those with right views nor treats those with wrong views with contempt.
Why is this? Because the Tathāgata abides in the state of equality.
The Tathāgata himself dwells in the equality of all phenomena and has no notion of diversity;
he also teaches such a Dharma to sentient beings so that they may be free from all notions.
This is the nineteenth deed of perfect enlightenment of the Tathāgata.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to reiterate this meaning,
spoke these verses:
The Sugata is equal and free from all conceptual distinctions; within the Buddha-dharma for the sake of benefiting sentient beings, such notions as these are forever absent.

The one of great renown maintains an equal mind toward those who observe the precepts and those who break them, toward gain and loss, and toward those who are easy to train and those who are difficult to train.
The Honored One among Two-Legged Beings, for the sake of all sentient beings, has taught the Dharma so that they may be liberated from all false attachments.
Furthermore, son of good family,
there is nothing that the Tathāgata’s perfect awakening does not discern or relinquish.
Why is this? It is because the Tathāgata practices and relinquishes all wholesome paths;
it is not that he relinquishes anything without having practiced them.
That is to say, he relinquishes by practicing physical discipline, mental discipline, and wisdom in this manner.
The equanimity of the Tathāgata is associated with wisdom;
it is not a state of ignorance, for it is the supramundane path.
This noble liberation and equanimity is not of the mundane world.
It is not through a non-noble liberation that there is anything to be relinquished.
One who relinquishes in this manner does not relinquish great compassion, is able to turn the Brahma-conduct,
and naturally accomplishes the benefit of sentient beings.
It is not achieved through the conjunction of dependent causes and conditions; rather,
it is the Tathāgata’s relinquishment of all distinctions of high and low,
abiding in equanimity and remaining unshakable.
Its essence is non-dual and far removed from dualistic characteristics;
it completely transcends both the finite and the infinite.
It relinquishes [conditioned states] in accordance with the timing, yet does not exceed that timing; it is not a realm of mental activity, consciousness, or the movement of thought.
It is not a provisional designation, nor is it a conceptual construction;
it is not an accumulation, nor is it a view of differentiation.
Such relinquishment is the true ultimate truth—eternal and unchanging.
This is the Tathāgata’s perfection of great equanimity;
he also teaches such a Dharma to sentient beings,
enabling them to attain this same perfection of great equanimity.
This is the twentieth work of perfect enlightenment of the Tathāgata.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to reiterate this meaning,
spoke these verses:
The Tathāgata has no relinquishing that is not preceded by discernment; having cultivated the supreme path through the causal conditions of body,
precepts, mind, and wisdom in successive order, he is the most excellent among men, free from attachment and aversion,
without false discrimination yet beyond all conceptualization, and his relinquishing is never conjoined with the accumulation of conditioned things.
Within the true, unchanging, and great equanimity, he thus speaks extensively for the sake of sentient beings.
Furthermore, son of good family,
the aspiration of all Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, never diminishes.
This refers to the desire for wholesome dharmas. What is meant by the desire for wholesome dharmas?
It is the non-diminishment of the Tathāgata’s desire for great loving-kindness (*mahāmaitrī*), and the non-diminishment of his desire for great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*).
The desire to teach the Dharma does not diminish;
the desire to discipline sentient beings does not diminish;
the desire to bring sentient beings to maturity does not diminish.
The desire to dwell in tranquility does not diminish;
the desire to exhort all sentient beings to resolve upon bodhicitta does not diminish;
the desire to cause all sentient beings to perpetuate the lineage of the Triple Gem does not diminish.
The Tathāgata has no evil desires that follow the mind;
all his wholesome desires are preceded by wisdom,
and he himself fulfills these wholesome desires.
He also teaches such a Dharma to sentient beings,
causing them to attain the desire for the Tathāgata’s most supreme and perfect omniscience.
This is the twenty-first deed of a perfectly awakened Tathāgata.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to reiterate this meaning, spoke in verse:
The Buddha’s aspiration for wholesome dharmas is already perfected; With compassion ever turning, he delivers all sentient beings.
Maturing others and exhorting them to generate the bodhicitta, Ensuring that the lineage of the Triple Gem is never severed;
Disregarding desire, hatred, delusion, and fear, With wisdom as the precursor to all that is desired—
The most supreme of sages knows this, Out of compassion for sentient beings who are largely indolent.

Lacking desire for wholesome dharmas and possessing many evil desires, they are taught to cultivate wholesome desires through right diligence, to perform the work of peerless wisdom, and to benefit sentient beings; by this means, all sentient beings are brought to subdual.
Furthermore, son of good family:
The Tathāgata’s diligence never diminishes.
In what respect does the Tathāgata’s diligence not diminish?
It is said that his diligence never diminishes in the thorough and discerning observation required to discipline sentient beings.
If there are sentient beings who listen to the Dharma with single-minded devotion,
he expounds it for them without shrinking from toil, his diligent effort never diminishing.
If there are sentient beings who listen to the Dharma for an entire eon, his body and mind remain free from weariness.
The Buddha likewise remains for one eon or even more than one eon,
without rising from his seat and without drinking or eating, preaching the Dharma without interruption.
This extends even beyond worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.
If there is a sentient being capable of being tamed,
he immediately goes to teach and transform them, causing them to practice correct conduct;
yet the Buddha’s body and mind experience no weariness or fatigue.
Attaining noble liberation through personal diligence in peace and tranquility,
and likewise praising diligence for the sake of sentient beings—
this is the twenty-second work of perfect enlightenment of the Tathāgata.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:
"Vigor gives birth to the Lions among Men; Therefore, I always praise vigor."
In every thought-moment, his valor never diminishes; he is always capable of hearing the Dharma and constantly proclaims it.
The Sugata’s diligence knows no rest; his actions of body, speech, and mind are untiring.
Naturally firm and fierce, he is free from all that is improper, and he also exhorts sentient beings to arouse diligence.
Furthermore, son of good family,
the Tathāgata’s perfect awakening is such that at all times and in all places, his right mindfulness never diminishes.
In what way do time and place not cause his right mindfulness to diminish?
Good son, from the moment immediately following the path of uninterrupted realization,
the Tathāgata attained anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
He then contemplates the mental activities of all sentient beings throughout the three periods of time as they continue in succession, arising and ceasing in a flowing stream.
Having known this, he maintains it in mind without forgetting.
Because he does not seek nor does he regress, he is eternally without decrease.
The Tathāgata is universally able to observe the three groups [of beings] with unimpaired right mindfulness;
that is to say, he deeply penetrates the faculties, mental activities, and conduct of sentient beings.
Although he is without movement of thought, investigation,
or conceptual discrimination, he preaches the Dharma without any error;
therefore, the Tathāgata’s mindfulness never diminishes.
He also teaches such a Dharma to sentient beings so that their mindfulness shall not diminish.
This is the twenty-third enlightened activity of the Tathāgata.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, [spoke these verses].
And he spoke in verse:
The Buddha’s mindfulness is not a thought and never diminishes; He knows the realms of sentient beings without exception.
Since his own awakening to great bodhi, He has known all three times with no further recollection.
He skillfully knows the distinctions in the mental activities of sentient beings, and that their faculties, inclinations, and desires are each different;
he dwells in effortless activity constantly and perpetually, and further teaches the supreme Dharma for the sake of sentient beings.
Furthermore, son of good family:
The Tathāgata’s samādhis never diminish.
How is it that the Tathāgata’s samādhis do not diminish?
It is because the Tathāgata’s samādhi regarding all phenomena...
It is equal, non-dual, without high or low, just like the true meaning of all phenomena (dharmas).
Why is this? It is because samādhi is equal.
This is the equality of the intrinsic nature of all phenomena.
This equality of nature is the equality of samādhi.
The equality of samādhi is the Tathāgata.
For this reason, it is said that the Buddha’s samādhi attains the nature of equality of all phenomena.
What is the nature of equality of all phenomena?
It means that the limit of passion is equal to the limit of freedom from passion.
The equality of the limit of hatred is itself the equality of being free from the limit of hatred;
the equality of the limit of delusion is itself the equality of being free from the limit of delusion;
the equality of the limit of the conditioned is itself the equality of the limit of the unconditioned; and the equality of the limit of birth-and-death is itself the equality of the limit of nirvana.
He enters this equanimity;
therefore, it is said that the Tathāgata’s samāhita-samādhi never diminishes.
Why does it not diminish?
Because it is equal to this, without increase or decrease.
Furthermore, the Buddha’s samādhi does not conjoin with the eye, nor does it conjoin with the ear;
it does not harmonize with the nose, tongue, body, or mind.
Because the Tathāgata has no discriminating faculties,
the Tathāgata’s samādhi likewise does not combine with the earth element,
nor does it combine with the water, fire, or wind elements.
Furthermore, it does not conform to the three realms or the three periods of time.
This non-conformity is equal in its essential nature, neither increasing nor decreasing.
Therefore, it is said that the Tathāgata’s samādhi neither increases nor decreases.
He also teaches such a Dharma to sentient beings,
causing them all to attain this samādhi without diminution.
This is the twenty-fourth deed of perfect enlightenment of the Tathāgata.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:
"The Tathāgata’s samādhi neither increases nor decreases; He is ever in meditative equipoise, benefiting sentient beings."
The essential nature is equal, without high or low; it does not combine with any phenomena.

When observing the elements of earth, water, fire, and wind, as well as the realms of desire, form, and formlessness, it is likewise always taught as neither diminishing nor combining. Therefore, the Tathāgata is certainly without diminution.
Furthermore, good son,
the Tathāgata’s wisdom is without decrease.
What is meant by "wisdom without decrease"?
It is the wisdom that directly realizes the intrinsic nature of all phenomena;
it is the wisdom of all phenomena that is universally revealed and expounded for the sake of all diverse sentient beings.
The wisdom that is skillful, unimpeded, subtle, profound, and inexhaustible;

the wisdom that analyzes a single phrase and enters into countless phrases; the inexhaustible wisdom of upholding and expounding [the Dharma] for hundreds of thousands of billions of eons; the wisdom that severes doubts one by one through individual inquiries; and the wisdom that is entirely without attachment in all circumstances.
It is the wisdom capable of explaining the sequential continuity of the distinctions among the three vehicles;

it is the wisdom capable of knowing the eighty-four thousand variations in the mental activities of sentient beings and teaching the eighty-four thousand aggregates of Dharma according to their individual capacities.
It is the wisdom that tames sentient beings without missing the proper time. For this reason,
it is said that the Tathāgata’s wisdom is boundless, limitless, inexhaustible, and possesses immeasurable doors.
This is the Tathāgata’s wisdom, which never diminishes;
he likewise proclaims it thus for the sake of sentient beings,
so that they may attain the inexhaustible wisdom of the Tathāgata.
This is the twenty-fifth deed of perfect enlightenment of the Tathāgata.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning,
spoke these verses:
In all teachings, wisdom manifests before you; Unimpeded and sovereign, you have reached the further shore.
Spontaneously preaching the Dharma to benefit sentient beings, A single phrase, according to their faculties, enters the infinite.
The conduct of beings is difficult to measure; For them, you preach eighty-four thousand dharmas.
Wisdom is boundless and cannot be diminished; the activities of the supreme ten powers are inconceivable.
Furthermore, son of good family, the liberation of the Tathāgata, the World-Honored One, is without diminution.
What is the Tathāgata’s undiminished liberation?
It is that the liberation of the śrāvaka is attained by following after sounds.
The liberation of the pratyekabuddha consists in awakening to dependent origination;
the liberation of the Tathāgata is [the same].
It is far removed from all that arises from attachment;
it does not take the past as its object, does not enter into the future, and does not cling to the present.
Regarding the eye and forms, it does not cling to the two characteristics.
The same applies to the ear and sounds, the nose and odors, the tongue and flavors, the body and tangibles, and the mind and mental phenomena.
Because one does not cling to these two characteristics, it is called liberation.
Furthermore, there may still be subtle forms of grasping, attachment, or mental conceptualization.
By remaining far removed from these three, one attains liberation.
One perceives the luminosity of wisdom, which is the intrinsic nature of the mind;
therefore, this liberation is itself wisdom.
Therefore it is said that when a single moment of mind is conjoined with wisdom,
one immediately attains *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
Having thus awakened to such perfect enlightenment, the Tathāgata [is established].
He also teaches such Dharma to sentient beings so that they may attain liberation;
this is the twenty-sixth deed of perfect enlightenment of the Tathāgata.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to reiterate this meaning, [spoke as follows].
And he spoke these verses:
"Śrāvakas attain liberation by following sounds; Pratyekabuddhas awaken to dependent origination.
The Sugata’s liberation is like space— Stainless, unattached, most supreme."
Fully understanding the flow of past minds, one realizes that their fundamental nature is liberated and free from all fetters;
knowing them as they truly are—unbound—one therefore says that liberation cannot be diminished.
Furthermore, son of good family:
The bodily actions of the Tathāgata are preceded by wisdom and follow the course of wisdom;
that is to say, the bodily actions of the Tathāgata are fully perfected.
There are sentient beings who are tamed merely upon seeing the Buddha’s body.
Some are tamed by hearing their speech;
some are tamed by seeing their silence;
and some are tamed by receiving food and drink.
In this way, he may manifest one of the four postures,
or display his physical marks and signs, or reveal his invisible crown;
or he may look back, or emit rays of light.
Whenever he lifts his foot or sets it down, entering or leaving cities and villages,
all sentient beings who see him are brought to discipline; therefore,
there is not the slightest degree of deficiency in the Buddha’s majestic deportment.
He is unable to discipline all sentient beings.
Therefore, it is said that the bodily actions of the Tathāgata are preceded by wisdom and follow after wisdom; this is the twenty-seventh enlightened activity of the Tathāgata.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning,
spoke these verses:
"If one sees the most excellent body and its majestic deportment— whether emerging or entering, or its various marks and signs..."
Some see the mark of the *uṣṇīṣa*, all established among the most supreme and honored of those who discipline sentient beings;
or they emit light, whereby immeasurable sentient beings are all brought to peace and happiness.
Those touched by the light are all disciplined; the deeds of the Honored One Among Two-Legged Beings are supreme and immeasurable.
Furthermore, son of good family,
all verbal actions of the Tathāgata are preceded by wisdom and accord with the activity of wisdom.
What is meant by "accordance with the activity of wisdom"?
The Tathāgata’s teaching of the Dharma is without obstruction;
he is able to explain both the words and their meanings in full and without deficiency.
The sounds of his speech enter the minds of sentient beings and give rise to wisdom.
That is to say: a voice that is neither too loud nor too low;
a voice that is upright and not timid;
a voice that is not stammering and not coarse or harsh; and a voice that is free from the density of a thicket.
The voice is extremely supple and possesses adaptability;
it is not harsh or broken, but is always steady and composed;
it is neither too rapid nor too slow.
The voice that is without confusion; the voice that skillfully analyzes;
the voice of exquisite diction; the voice of exquisite profundity;
the voice of exquisite vastness; the voice like a surging spring.
The uninterrupted voice, the soothing and ripening voice,
the profound and beautiful voice, the harmonious voice,
the adorned voice, and the beneficial voice.
A voice that is pure and translucent, a voice free from dust,
a voice without affliction, a voice without defilement,
a voice without delusion, and a voice of supreme brilliance.
The sound of non-attachment; the sound of excellent liberation;
the extremely pure sound; the sound free from deviousness;
the sound without inferiority; the sound without hardness; and the sound without laxity.
It is the sound that can produce peace and bliss; the sound that purifies the body;
the sound that gladdens the mind; the sound that leads with joy;
the sound that first inquires after one's welfare; and the sound that can purify lustful desire.
It is the sound that does not give rise to anger, which can extinguish the sound of delusion;
it is the sound that swallows all Māras, which can crush the sound of evil karma;
it is the sound that burns away external treatises, which accords with the sound of awakening.
Like the sound of a celestial drum, the wise hear it as a joyful sound;
it is like the voice of Śakra Devānām Indra, the voice of Mahābrahmā,
the roar of the great ocean’s tides, and the universal thundering of clouds and lightning.
The sound of a great earthquake; the voice of the kalaviṅka bird; the voice of the kokila bird;
the voice of the jīvajīvaka bird; the voice of the king of deer; the voice of the king of oxen;

the voice of the king of geese; the cry of the crane; the voice of the peacock; the sound of the vīṇā lute; the sound of the pi-pa; the sound of the pipa; the sound of the zheng; the sound of the flute; the sound of the conch; and the sound of the drum.
A voice that is easy to understand and distinct;
a lovely voice and a voice pleasant to hear;
a profound voice and a never-tiring voice.
The sound that brings peace and bliss to the ears; the sound that can generate roots of goodness;
the sound of perfected syllables and phrases; the sound of exquisite words, phrases, and letters;
the sound of beneficial harmony; and the sound of harmony with the Dharma.
The sound of knowing the proper seasons; the sound that is appropriate at all times;
the sound that never speaks at an improper time; the sound of explaining how the various faculties have successively continued from the past;
the sound of adorning generosity; and the sound of being able to maintain pure ethical discipline.
The sound that gives rise to patience; the sound of fierce and sharp diligence;
the sound of being capable in meditative concentration; the sound of vast wisdom;
the sound of the harmony of great loving-kindness; and the sound of tireless great compassion.
The sound of the light of Dharma-joy, profound, vast, and great equanimity;
the sound of abiding in the three vehicles, the sound of the non-interruption of the Three Jewels;
the sound of discerning the three groups, and the sound of purifying the three gates of liberation.
The sound of cultivating the various truths; the sound of cultivating the various forms of knowledge;
the sound of being endowed with wisdom; the sound of praise from the noble ones;
the sound that accords with space; the sound that is without measure; the sound that is fully endowed with all marks.
Good son, because the Tathāgata’s vocal karma is endowed with such immeasurable sounds,
it is said that all the Tathāgata’s vocal karma is preceded by wisdom and proceeds in accordance with wisdom; this is the twenty-eighth work of a perfectly awakened one.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:
"The Buddha’s speech is peerless, pure, and without blemish; All merits and virtues are perfectly fulfilled."
A single sound pervades infinite lands, Each hearing it according to their own kind:
Some hear the voice of the Śrāvakas, Some hear the Dharma of the Pratyekabuddhas,
Or hear the great majestic power of the Tathāgata, And immediately resolve upon unsurpassed Bodhicitta.
The meanings of all words and phrases are perfectly complete, arranged in sequence without any obstruction;

yet the mind is free from any conceptual discrimination. Such a one can expound the inconceivable and wondrous Dharma-gate, possessing the most excellent voice among men, whose uttered sounds are like echoes in a valley.
Without effort and without thought, universally responding; the soundless sound that delights the hearts of beings.
*The Dhāraṇī Sūtra of the Sovereign Who Protects the Realm*, Scroll Six.
*The Dhāraṇī Sūtra of the Sovereign Who Protects the Realm*, Scroll Seven.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Prajñā of Kaśmīra together with Munisri.
Chapter Five, Part Three: On the Inconceivable and Profound Deeds of the Tathāgata.
At that time, the World-Honored One...
Again, he addressed the youth Mañjuśrī, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva, saying:
"Good son, the mental karma of the Tathāgata is preceded by wisdom and proceeds in accordance with wisdom."
What is meant by mental karma following after wisdom?
Good son, the Tathāgata has no faults of mind, thought, or consciousness. Why is this?
Because the mind, thought, and consciousness of the Tathāgata are all unknowable.
Because it manifests solely from the Buddha’s wisdom,
and because the Tathāgata’s wisdom is its sovereign.
Son of good family, the Tathāgata’s wisdom turns in accordance with the minds of all sentient beings.
They accord with and enter into the mentalities of all sentient beings;
they accord with and understand the consciousnesses of all sentient beings;
and they give rise to all dharmas and all samādhis.
Therefore, no one can know the Tathāgata’s mind, thought, consciousness, and so forth;
he transcends the stage of causes, is far removed from dependent origination,
and does not belong to the three realms of existence.
It liberates one from all forms of pride and the activities of Māra;
from flattery, deception, and delusive illusions;
and from the cataracts of the darkness of ignorance, folly, and the grasping at "I" and "mine."
They skillfully cultivate the factors of enlightenment without distraction;
free from conceptual discrimination, they enter into the state of equality like space.
Such are their immeasurable activities.
Each and every one of these is preceded by wisdom.
This is the twenty-ninth enlightened activity of the Tathāgata.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, [spoke as follows].
And he spoke these verses:
The mind of the Honored One among Two-Legged Beings is immeasurable; Through the causes and conditions of pure wisdom, the Buddha’s wisdom is supreme in the world.
Equal to the dharma-realm, it accords with and universally enters the minds of sentient beings.
Meditative concentrations and liberations are all perfected; the mind’s conceptualizations are unshakable.
Transcending the realms and activities of Māra, it is stainless and immutable like space.
Furthermore, son of good family:
The Tathāgata’s perfectly awakened vision of the past proceeds with unattached and unimpeded wisdom.
How does this wisdom proceed?
It is said to be regarding the various Buddha-fields of the past.
The Tathāgatas fully know the immeasurable and innumerable manifestations of formation and destruction;
within those lands, the Tathāgatas fully know all the herbs, trees, forests, creepers, and medicinal plants.
All classes of sentient beings in that land—whether born from eggs, from wombs, from moisture, or by transformation;
whether with form or without form; with perception, without perception, or neither with nor without perception.
All such things the Tathāgatas know fully.
The various sounds of sentient and non-sentient beings within those lands, the Tathāgatas know them all.
Furthermore, the various teachings proclaimed by the Tathāgatas appearing in those lands, they know them all.
The Tathāgata fully knows all the various assemblies— monks, nuns, laymen, and laywomen— and all sentient beings,
each of whom attains discipline within the Three Vehicles;
he fully knows their various lifespans and the duration of their respective dharmas.
Those sentient beings have various inhalations and exhalations,
various foods and drinks, various requisites,
various physical appearances, and various faculties.
The Tathāgata fully knows all various modes of conduct and understanding, as well as the various natures of the mind;
how one dies here and is born there in a momentary flow,
with birth and cessation continuing in succession.
All such things are obtained through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) and are not known through inference (*anumāna*).
What is direct perception?
It is knowing reality as it is without moving the mind.
The flowing mind does not enter the past;
knowing time in this way, one is fully endowed with wisdom and teaches the Dharma in various ways according to the minds of sentient beings.
This is called the thirtieth deed of perfect enlightenment of the Tathāgata.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning,
spoke these verses:
The Buddha’s wisdom is immeasurable and unattached; he knows the names, characteristics, and distinctions of the great assemblies where Buddhas and sentient beings preached the Dharma in past lands.

He perceives the many differences in mental activities, faculties, and desires, and according to each, brings them to subdual through the three vehicles, so that they ultimately all return to the source of liberation.
And knowing the mind that flows through arising and ceasing, the seer of all things attains true awakening.
Furthermore, son of good family,
the Tathāgata’s wisdom perceives future worlds.
It is unattached and unimpeded, seeing as if it were the present. How is this seen?
It means that all future various sentient beings, various phenomena, and various lands are seen.
The Tathāgata fully knows all that is to arise and to cease, that which has dwelt and that which will dwell; likewise,
he knows all realms and eons that are to be consumed by fire and brought to exhaustion.
They shall be established and remain;
within those lands, they shall become all the various grounds,
trees, groves, and the myriad flowers, herbs, and medicinal plants.
They know coarse forms and subtle forms, the sun, moon, and stars,
down to the finest atoms, all as they truly are;
they also know which Buddhas will appear in each and every world-system.
There shall be śrāvakas, there shall be pratyekabuddhas,
there shall be bodhisattvas, and there shall be the requisites for their sustenance;
there shall be the exhaling and inhaling of breath, and the coming and going, the advancing and stopping.
The Tathāgata fully knows their adoption and rejection of dignified conduct (*īryāpatha*).
Among such sentient beings within various buddha-fields,
he knows those who shall attain liberation through the three vehicles (*triyāna*).
The Tathāgata fully knows the distinctions of liberation.
Furthermore, he knows all the aggregates, sense bases, and elements of all sentient beings within that buddha-field.
The Tathāgata fully knows all mental states and mental factors as they arise and cease;
although he knows them all exactly as they are,
the mind of the Tathāgata does not flow or enter into the future.
To cause sentient beings to realize the nature of the future, he teaches such a Dharma.
This is the thirty-first enlightened activity of the Tathāgata.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, [spoke these verses].
And he spoke these verses:
The Buddha’s stainless eye in future ages Sees all that shall be accomplished by all Buddhas throughout all lands;
There is not the slightest thing it does not know or fail to exhaust.

In each and every matter, he is without error; furthermore, through subtle observation, he perceives the causes of the future and teaches the Dharma-gates according to the minds of sentient beings. This is the surpassing karma of the Honored One among Two-Legged Beings.
Furthermore, son of good family:
The Tathāgata’s knowledge and vision function in the present without attachment or obstruction.
How do they function?
It means that regarding all Buddha-fields currently manifest throughout the ten directions:
One knows with subtle insight through three kinds of causes; that is,
one knows their characteristics, whether they arise or cease,
and one knows which phenomena they are.
That is to say, the Tathāgata fully knows all Buddhas, all Bodhisattvas, all Śrāvakas,
all Pratyekabuddhas, and all subtle forms as well as all coarse forms.
The entire earth element is minutely analyzed to determine that it is composed of a certain number of atoms;
the entire water element is known by its quantity through drops measured by a hair.
He fully knows the number of all instances of the arising and ceasing of flames within the entire fire element;
he perceives the colors, forms, and gusting impacts of the entire wind element;
and he discerns the various motes of dust within the empty space of the ten directions.
One measures them exhaustively with the tip of a single hair to know their limits.
In this way, one knows the characteristics of all such objects;
one knows their arising and one knows their cessation.
Furthermore, by means of these three kinds of knowledge, one knows the realm of sentient beings:
one knows the hell realm, the causes for birth in hell, and the causes for emergence from hell;

one knows the animal realm, the causes for birth as an animal, and the causes for abandoning the animal state; and one knows the Yāma realm, the causes for birth in the Yāma realm, and the causes for the cessation of the Yāma realm.
He knows the causes for birth in the human realm and the causes for losing the human realm;
he knows the causes for birth in the various celestial realms and the causes for the decline and passing away from those heavens.
All such things as these, the Tathāgata fully understands through direct presence.
He knows the flow of the minds of all sentient beings—
whether their minds are afflicted by defilements or free from them—
and he knows how the faculties of various sentient beings are disciplined.
The Tathāgata fully knows the untrained faculties of various sentient beings.
Thus, regarding objects present before him,
the Tathāgata’s non-dual wisdom functions such that duality does not manifest.
He likewise proclaims this for the sake of sentient beings.
This is the thirty-second deed of perfect enlightenment of the Tathāgata.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to reiterate this meaning, [spoke these verses].
And he spoke in verse:
"The realm of the Tathāgata is boundless, inconceivable, incomparable, and without equal, like space; how could all sentient beings ever fathom it?"

All classes of sentient beings throughout the ten directions, And the diverse activities within the manifest realm— The Tathāgata is able to know them all; Such is the supreme, spontaneous activity of wisdom.
O son of noble family, these thirty-two are the profound activities of the Tathāgatas.
All Buddhas are fully and perfectly endowed with these [qualities].

Desiring to discipline all sentient beings and cause them to awaken and enter [the truth], they briefly explain a small portion; yet in reality, such is the entirety of the Tathāgata’s enlightened activity.
It is immeasurable, boundless, and cannot be fully described.
Son of good family, the Tathāgata further possesses a true activity that is without measure and inconceivable.
It cannot be fathomed by any world;
it cannot be proclaimed by any words;
it cannot be understood by any consciousness.
All wisdoms cannot penetrate it;
it pervades all established buddha-fields and accords with the equal wisdom of all Buddhas.
It transcends all worldly activities;
though engaged in various deeds, it performs no action.
Its essential nature is equal to space.
The dharma-realm manifests before one without conceptual differentiation.
Why is this? Son of good family, because the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, reveal that the nature of the dharma-realm is non-dual.
The various dharmas and various sentient beings;
the various lands and various consciousnesses;
the various liberations and various nirvanas.
Because all such phenomena— whether in their essence or their characteristics— are ultimately empty, son of good family,
the Tathāgata has thus personally realized that the Dharma-realm is of a single flavor, signless, and free from the laws of causes and conditions.
Desiring to cause all sentient beings to equally awaken to and enter the unimpeded Dharma which is like space,
he turns for all sentient beings the irreversible, unsurpassed wheel of Dharma.
Good son, it is like a skilled craftsman who is well able to polish and refine a wondrous maṇi jewel.
He knows the nature of the gem and extracts it from the mountain rock;
he then uses the yakṣa-rasa medicine mixed with water to rub and polish it.
Wipe it with a garment made of black sheep’s wool;
having wiped it repeatedly, moisten it with a special medicinal liquid called "vinegar-flavor" mixed with water,
and polish it with a soft wooden tool.
When the work was still not yet finished, he again used mahāviśeṣaka medicine to polish it with a fine cloth;
as it still did not possess radiance, he placed it in a blazing fire and burned it for seven days.
All other stones, ores, and impurities are completely eliminated;
knowing it is not a counterfeit gem, it is named the priceless *mahā-vaiḍūrya-maṇi* wondrous jewel.
Son of good family, the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, are also like this.
Knowing that sentient beings delight in birth-and-death, which is impure and defiled,
he preaches for them the teachings of impermanence, suffering, emptiness, non-self, and impurity in order to engender world-weariness and detachment.
Having entered the noble Dharma and disciplined body and mind,
the Tathāgata’s diligence does not yet cease;
he next teaches them emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness.
Therefore, he causes them to know, see, awaken to, and realize the Buddha-eye.
The Tathāgata’s diligent effort has likewise not yet ceased;
next, he further turns the wheel of non-retrogression for them.

The Tathāgata’s diligence likewise never ceases; finally, for their sake, he expounds the realm of the Tathāgata, which is pure in the three spheres, so that all sentient beings may clearly understand dependent origination and perceive the fundamental nature of phenomena.
"Up until the point of universally entering the equal dharma-body of all Tathāgatas.
Good sons, for this reason,
you should understand the inconceivable activities of the Tathāgata in this way."
If bodhisattvas abide in these inconceivable activities of the Tathāgata,
although they attain equanimity of mind regarding all phenomena,
they nonetheless accord with the knowledge that all phenomena are free from all faults.
Although they accord with the equality of the three periods of time,
they do not sever the lineage of the Three Jewels;
although they know that the nature of the body is like empty space, fundamentally without movement.
Yet they manifest their bodies throughout all Buddha-fields in the ten directions;
although they know that the essence of all phenomena is inexpressible,
they nevertheless employ language to produce sounds according to the capacities of beings and teach all dharmas.
Although the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, speak of various causes and conditions according to the differing mental activities of sentient beings,
they remain free from the marks of both sentient beings and all phenomena.
Good son, the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas...
He appears in the world for the sake of purifying the minds of bodhisattvas;
yet in reality, the Tathāgata is without change and remains eternally established in this inconceivable activity.
Without relinquishing diligence, he bestowed the prediction of enlightenment upon the bodhisattvas and taught the Dharma without interruption.
At that time, the World-Honored One, having finished expounding this profound Dharma gate of the inconceivable deeds of the Tathāgata, [remained silent].
Throughout the ten directions, in immeasurable and incalculable *asaṃkhyeya* Buddha-fields, the earth shook in six ways;
great radiance was emitted, and a rain of various celestial flowers fell.
Within this great assembly were bodhisattvas of immense majesty and power, as well as the gods of the desire realm,
the sixteen great kingdoms of Jambudvīpa, and various minor kings.
Nāgas, devas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, humans, and non-humans,
as well as bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, and upāsikās.
Upon hearing this Dharma-gate, their minds became pure, and they rejoiced with immeasurable exultation.
They made offerings to the Buddha with various requisites,
namely, diverse exquisite flowers, various kinds of renowned incense, ointments, and powdered incense.
They made offerings with robes, necklaces, banners, streamers, garlands, and canopies;
or they offered worship with reverence through various subtle and wonderful sounds, singing hymns of praise.
Some used the bright jewel from the topknot on their heads, the bright jewel on their foreheads, ear-ornaments, or necklaces as offerings;
others used exquisite maṇi jewels, pearl necklaces, or crescent-shaped necklaces.
They adorned their various limbs with diverse necklaces,
jeweled chains, jeweled seals, jeweled bracelets, jeweled rings, jeweled mirrors, jeweled girdles, jeweled caskets, and jeweled crowns;
as well as with many exquisite garments, various ornaments, and numerous wonderful bells.
They all gathered at the site of enlightenment to pay respectful homage and make offerings, using various kinds of exquisite jewels,
such as vaidūrya gems and jambūnada gold.
The *aśmagarbha* jewel, the *śrīgarbha* jewel, the *indranīla* jewel,
the red *sphatika* jewel, the fire-colored jewel, the flame-light jewel, and the infinite-colored jewel.
Such treasures as these were offered to the Buddha as an act of worship.
Furthermore, there were sentient beings who made offerings using various powdered jewels, such as gold and silver.
Or with aloeswood, tagara, seasonal incenses, exquisite sandalwood,
nāgapuṣpa filaments, and red pearl incense—
with various powdered incenses such as these, they were scattered as offerings.
Furthermore, some scattered various celestial flowers as an offering,
namely: pāriyātraka flowers, māndārava flowers, and mahāmāndārava flowers.
Mañjūṣaka flowers and great Mañjūṣaka flowers;
Rucaka flowers and great Rucaka flowers;
Sātalā flowers and great Sātalā flowers; Cakrā flowers and stainless Cakrā flowers.
There were flowers with a hundred petals, flowers with a thousand petals, and flowers with a hundred thousand petals;
flowers of universal radiance, flowers of universal fragrance, flowers of blazing light, and most excellent flowers;
flowers of boundless color, flowers of great pervasiveness, and flowers delightful to behold, which they used for offering; or there were sentient beings who scattered land-grown flowers.
These are the vārṣikī flowers, sumanā flowers, kusuma flowers, atimuktaka flowers,
campaka flowers, and aśoka flowers.
There are *dhānuṣkārī* flowers, *pāṭala* flowers,
*mucilinda* flowers, and *mahāmucilinda* flowers;
there may also be sentient beings who offer worship by scattering water-born flowers.
That is to say, they scattered various kinds of exquisite flowers— such as the *utpala*, *padma*, *kumuda*, and *puṇḍarīka*— as offerings to the Buddha.
All the devas in the void played various celestial music,
making offerings with sounds that were refined, pure, resonant, and subtle.
These included flutes, pipes, *konghou*, lutes, conch shells, and various kinds of celestial drums and drums of exquisite sound.
They honored, praised, and made offerings to the Buddha with various songs and dances.
Furthermore, they rained down various celestial and exquisite flowers,
various powdered incenses, various wonderful jewels, various necklaces, and various garments.
Thus, with these exquisite celestial offerings, they made worship to the Buddha.
At that time, the great assembly of Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas from all worlds throughout the ten directions gathered together.
Furthermore, the various bodhisattvas within this assembly,
in order to make offerings to the Buddha, all ascended into the void;
each transformed their body into the form of a celestial being.
As soon as he had transformed his body, by the power of the Bodhisattva, a net of various jewels covered the entire great assembly.
This net encircled the Bodhi tree on all sides,
extending four *yojanas* in each of its four directions and being eight paces thick throughout.
Various pearl necklaces hang down in all directions;
numerous nets, bells, and jeweled chimes are suspended, chiming in harmony;
and it is adorned with lotus flowers made of various precious gems.
Within each and every pearl of those pearl necklaces,
there appeared simultaneously immeasurable and innumerable bodhisattvas;
having appeared, they reverently circumambulated the Buddha seven times.
Having completed the circumambulation of the Buddha,
he manifested for each of the bodhisattvas a lion throne made of various precious lotuses.
At that time, each Tathāgata in the immeasurable Buddha-fields of the ten directions likewise [manifested such thrones].
All were due to the power of their sovereign spiritual authority,
which caused each to manifest wish-fulfilling jewel trees, jeweled nets,
and various rare and extraordinary articles of offering.
They arrived equally and universally at the Bodhi tree in the Sahā world,
where they arranged rows of precious trees surrounding it on all sides;
they distributed various offerings to adorn the site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa) in order to make offerings to Śākyamuni Tathāgata and this sutra.
At the time of making these adorned offerings,
immeasurable and innumerable sentient beings in this assembly resolved their minds upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
Immeasurable bodhisattvas attained the patience of the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).
At that time, the World-Honored One surveyed the entire assembly of bodhisattvas and spoke these words:
"O sons of the Buddha, who among you is able to give rise to a vast and great vow?"

By means of his great majestic power, he was able to cause this inconceivable array of various wonderful jewels adorning the site of enlightenment—the necklaces and nets that covered the dwelling place of the Bodhisattva, as well as the wish-fulfilling trees from the ten directions with their flowers and fruits arranged in rows—to remain here.
Radiating flames and containing brilliance, it remains forever without change.
It awaits the time when Maitreya Buddha descends to be born;
at the age of sixteen, he shall sit in the place of enlightenment, and his perfect awakening will finally be fulfilled.
While preaching this *Rāṣṭrapālaparipṛcchā-sūtra* and revealing and expounding this dhāraṇī,
one should at that time offer worship.
"Even until the appearance of the thousand Buddhas of the Bhadrakalpa,
he likewise made offerings in this manner.
While these words were being spoken, within this assembly...
There was a bodhisattva named Abhijñā-vibhu-rāja.
He adjusted his physical deportment upon a lotus seat and placed his right knee upon the pedestal of the lotus.
With palms joined in reverence, he addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One, I am able to do as the Buddha has commanded and remain at this site of enlightenment."
He made offerings to Maitreya and all the Tathāgatas, Arhats, Samyaksaṃbuddhas of the Bhadrakalpa.
At that time, there was a magical being (*māra*) with supernormal powers named Sunirmita,
