who resided over the four great continents.
Having heard these words, he immediately addressed the Bodhisattva Sovereign King of Supernatural Powers, saying:
"Noble One, by what kind of vessel are these various jewel necklaces placed as they adorn this site of enlightenment?"
After that period of time had passed, so that [the scripture] was not damaged,
the Bodhisattva Sovereign King of Supernatural Powers addressed that Māra,
saying: "O Benevolent One, you should know this."
All physical vessels are quickly destroyed and subject to many obstacles;
space as a vessel cannot be damaged and is without obstacles.
Among all vessels, this is the most supreme.
"Do not blink; gaze intently at my body, and you shall naturally behold my vast vessel.
Māra followed these instructions and gazed intently at the Bodhisattva.
Within the navel-wheel of the Bodhisattva’s body, he saw a world-system named Water-Light King (*Jalaprakāśarāja*).
This world was so filled with vast waters that it resembled the great ocean; for this reason, it was given that name.
In this world-system, there is a Tathāgata named Śrīratnapadma,
a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidhyācaraṇasaṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Puruṣadamyasārathi, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, Buddha, Bhagavān.
There was only a pure assembly of great bodhisattvas;
within that water, various precious lotus flowers grew and spread everywhere,
and the Tathāgata Śrī sat upon the king of these precious flowers.
The assembly of bodhisattvas sat together upon jeweled flowers, respectfully surrounding him.
At that time, within that great assembly, the Tathāgata taught the profound and wondrous Dharma,
instructing, exhorting, benefiting, and gladdening them.
At that time, the Mara of Supernatural Powers, having witnessed this event, immediately rose, joined his palms in reverence, and paid homage to the Bodhisattva King of Sovereign Supernatural Powers.
Then the Bodhisattva addressed him, saying:
"O Benevolent One, do you see such a vast vessel as this Bodhisattva?
Māra replied, "I have seen it.
How marvelous! Great Being, you are capable of accomplishing such a task."
Such a great vessel cannot be destroyed even in hundreds of thousands of koṭis of nayutas of kalpas;
therefore, this Great Jewel Adorned Bodhimanda maintains its integrity without deficiency, being stainless and pure.
"How could it not be possible for there to be no change?
Having spoken these words, the Māra of Supernatural Powers prostrated at the Buddha's feet and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One, as I reflect upon the past,
I have never before seen such miraculous feats of the Bodhisattva Sovereign King of Spiritual Powers,
nor have I ever heard this Dharma-gate.”
They diligently practice with vigor within the Śrāvaka Vehicle,
desiring to transcend the triple world and seek their own nirvāṇa;
having seen and heard this today, I [reflect upon it].
He then gave rise to a firm and most profound resolve toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*. "World-Honored One,
even if I were to remain for as many eons as there are grains of sand in the Ganges River..."
I shall undergo various sufferings while dwelling in the great hells;
only after that will I attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
I am willing to endure this suffering and will never abandon the mind of enlightenment (*bodhicitta*).
At that time, the World-Honored One praised Māra, saying:
"Excellent, excellent! You, Great Being, are able [to aspire] toward Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi."
Donning the great armor,
before long you shall likewise become like the Bodhisattva Sovereign King of Supernatural Powers,
fully perfecting all meritorious virtues.

Chapter Six: The Ornamentation of the Bodhisattva’s Necklaces. *The Dhāraṇī Sūtra of the Sovereign Who Protects the Realm*, Chapter Six: The Ornamentation of the Bodhisattva’s Necklaces, Part One. At that time, there were bodhisattvas who had come from various Buddha-fields throughout the ten directions.
And to this great assembly of devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, humans, and non-humans;
and to the bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, and upāsikās.
Their hearts gave rise to a longing thirst to hear the sublime Dharma.
At that time, the World-Honored One, knowing the thoughts in the minds of this assembly—
that they delighted in hearing the profound Dharma and were capable of upholding the treasury of the Dharma— was filled with joy and serenity.
Furthermore, wishing to again provide an exposition and a clear explanation of the *Dhāraṇī-sūtra of the Protector of the Realm*,
he emitted the light from the invisible crown of his head,
which is one of the marks of a Great Man; this light is named "Undespairing Diligence."
After the light had circled this great assembly of bodhisattvas seven times,
it further circled the youth Mañjuśrī a hundred thousand million times.
Having performed these deeds, it entered the crown of Mañjuśrī’s head.

Once that light had entered, it caused the body of Mañjuśrī and the lion throne upon which he sat to possess a majestic radiance exceeding that of the great assembly by hundreds of thousands of millions of times.
Just as the full moon eclipses all the stars,
at that time the youth Mañjuśrī,
empowered by the Buddha’s majestic spiritual authority, rose from his seat.
Baring his right shoulder, kneeling with palms joined, he praised the Buddha’s merits and spoke these verses:
“The Buddha emits from his body the great radiance of wisdom; The Universal Eye perceives all meanings without exception.”
Naturally endowed with all innate skillful means, All inconceivable virtues are perfectly complete.
The Bull among Men emits a great light, Universally illuminating the three karmas throughout the pervasive purity.
He circles me a hundred thousand times; Having circled, he enters my body and mind through the crown of my head.
My former wisdom and eloquence, as well as my dhāraṇīs and the light of my radiance, were all faint and inferior.
As soon as the Light of the Lord of Men touched me, I surpassed my former state by more than a thousandfold.
My body became cool and my mind pure; I leaped for joy with equanimity in all things.
The Buddha’s wisdom and sublime eloquence are boundless; They all flow entirely into my body.
The Tathāgata’s majestic power is difficult to fathom; Those of little strength cannot maintain this in mind.
Relying now on the power of the Buddha’s wisdom, I inquire, Desiring to bring benefit and happiness to all sentient beings.

In order to enter the gateways of all bodhisattva practices, and to further attain the supernormal powers, the emission of light, and the wisdom of empowerment through which the Buddhas appear in the world—may I accomplish these virtues. I ask the Tathāgata:
this assembly is vast and boundless; they have already trained and entered into the Supreme Vehicle.
May those who have not yet attained it incline their hearts toward mindfulness; for the sake of the benefit and happiness of others, may you question the Tathāgata.
May your peerless wisdom accord with the needs of the times, opening the treasury of the sublime Dharma to benefit all sentient beings.
May the retinues of Māra be utterly destroyed, and may you practice well within the teachings of the Tathāgata.
The Great Hero’s wisdom is boundless; His skillful means are inexhaustible and limitless.

My own wisdom cannot comprehend it; Therefore, I inquire of the Tathāgata, Whose wisdom knows reality as it is, And who has turned the wheel for immeasurable eons throughout the long duration of time.
Having diligently practiced through vast eons, you now possess mastery; I pray that you open the Buddha-wisdom to show it to all sentient beings.
At that time, after the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī had spoken these verses, he addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One..."
The realm of the Tathāgata is inconceivable;
it is not a realm that can be measured by Bodhisattvas.
Yet, the Buddha’s wisdom expounds the Dharma without weariness.
Out of great compassion and pity, not abandoning sentient beings, I now rely on the Buddha's power to venture to ask:
World-Honored One, what is called the "bodhisattva’s necklace" (ratnāvalī)?
How does a bodhisattva adorn themselves with this necklace?
How does a bodhisattva attain superior conduct?
How does a bodhisattva attain the inconceivable light of the sublime Dharma,
thereby remaining far removed from ignorance, darkness, and all doubts?
"How does a bodhisattva obtain the great dharma-lamp gate of the Tathāgata and become able to purify it entirely?
How excellent, World-Honored One! We pray that you will explain this for us."
This is the definitive teaching on the Dharma-gate for the birth of the assembly of bodhisattvas.
If bodhisattvas hear this, they will be able to destroy the hosts of Māras and the enemies that are their afflictions.
Entering into all phenomena without any doubt,
they directly realize the realm of the Tathāgatas and gradually penetrate deeper into the spheres of the bodhisattvas.
Furthermore, they are able to gradually enter the realm of all-knowledge;
they know the minds of sentient beings and purify the conduct of sentient beings;
they travel through all Buddha-fields and subdue the armies of Māra.
One will swiftly be able to embrace all the Buddha-teachings and exercise sovereign mastery over all phenomena.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī, saying:
Excellent, excellent, son of good family!
You have been able to give rise to a heart of great courage and let out a lion’s roar,
questioning the Tathāgata regarding such a sublime meaning.
"You have already been able to clearly understand and penetrate the immeasurable realms of all Tathāgatas, such that you can inquire about this meaning.
Good son, listen attentively, listen attentively, and reflect upon it well."
I shall now analyze and explain for you these realms and other immeasurable qualities of merit,
so that you may all swiftly attain their full perfection.
He exercises sovereign mastery over all phenomena.
Mañjuśrī replied, “So be it,” and received the instruction.
The Buddha then said to Mañjuśrī:
"Good son, all bodhisattvas are fully endowed with four kinds of necklaces.
What are these four?"
That which is called the adornment of ethical discipline, the adornment of meditative concentration,
the adornment of wisdom, and the adornment of the gateways of dhāraṇī—
these are known as the four.
"Good son, what is meant by 'precepts as an ornament'?
Good son, a bodhisattva possesses one pure precept-ornament:
namely, giving rise to a mind free from anger and free from obstruction toward all sentient beings."
It causes all sentient beings who see it to rejoice, never wearying of it.
Furthermore, son of good family, there are two kinds of pure precept-garlands for bodhisattvas:
namely, closing the gates to the evil realms and opening the path to humans and devas.
Furthermore, son of good family, there are three ornaments of pure precepts for a bodhisattva, namely:
the body, speech, and mind are all entirely pure.
Furthermore, son of good family, there are four ornaments of pure precepts for a bodhisattva.
This means that all desires are fulfilled, all aspirations are accomplished,
and all that is wished for is attained from beginning to end.
Furthermore, son of good family, there are five kinds of pure precept-garlands for a bodhisattva.
This refers to being fully endowed with samādhi, fully endowed with wisdom, fully endowed with liberation,
fully endowed with the knowledge and vision of liberation, and fully endowed with great parinirvāṇa.
Furthermore, son of good family, a bodhisattva has six kinds of pure precept-garlands.
This means that because one does not break the precepts, there is ultimately no regret;
because the precepts are not pierced or leaking,
there are no further faults.
The unadulterated precepts are so called because they lack admixture;
the pure precepts because they increase wholesome dharmas;
and the sovereign precepts because their essence is fully endowed, allowing one to proceed wherever one intends.
The morality of sovereign transformation is due to the sovereignty of wisdom at all times.
Furthermore, son of good family, a bodhisattva has seven ornaments of pure morality:
namely, purity through giving and purity through patience.
Through diligence one attains purity; through meditative concentration one attains purity;
through wisdom one attains purity; through skillful means one attains purity; and through heedfulness one attains purity.
Furthermore, son of good family, there are eight garlands of pure precepts for a bodhisattva, each of which is individually perfected.
That is to say: the perfection of the ten stages, the perfection of non-regret,
the perfection of non-laziness, the perfection of non-resentment,
the perfection of making offerings to the Buddha, and the perfection of being free from the eight difficulties.
By perfecting the practice of generosity, one attains the perfection of spiritual friends.
Furthermore, son of good family, a bodhisattva has nine ornaments of pure ethical discipline.
What are these nine?
That is to say: attaining fearlessness; attaining freedom from alarm and dread;
attaining a mind of certainty; attaining proximity to tranquility;
attaining a tamed mind; attaining a mind free from greed; attaining a courageous mind; attaining knowledge of the mental activities of all sentient beings; and attaining the ground of tranquility.
These are called the nine.
Furthermore, son of good family,
a bodhisattva has ten garlands of pure precepts.
What are the ten? They are as follows:
the body-garland, for the purpose of adorning it with the perfection of the marks and signs.
The necklace of speech,
because it is said that cultivation serves as an adornment;
the necklace of mind.
Because they are adorned with the absence of afflictions,
the buddha-fields are like jeweled necklaces;
because they are adorned with the fulfillment of vows, [the fields are so adorned].
The necklace of benefiting others,
because it serves as an adornment that purifies the mind;
the necklace of the place of birth.
The bodhisattva’s practice is an ornament because refraining from all evils serves as its adornment;
it is an ornament because following and learning the conduct of the Buddha serves as its adornment.
The wisdom-garland,
because it understands that all phenomena are entirely illusory transformations serving as adornments;
the bodhimanda-garland.
All roots of goodness are dedicated for the sake of adornment.
The powers, fearlessnesses, and unique qualities of a Buddha serve as his necklace.
Not abandoning the fundamental nature of pure precepts serves as adornment; these are called the ten.
"Good son, how does a bodhisattva cultivate the adornment of the various samādhi-garlands?
Good son, there is one kind of adornment of the samādhi-garland for a bodhisattva."
What is this one?
It is the arousal of a mind of loving-kindness toward all realms of sentient beings.
Son of good family, there are further two kinds of samādhi-garland adornments for a bodhisattva.
This refers to a straightforward mind and a supple mind.
Furthermore, there are three kinds of samādhi-garland ornaments for a bodhisattva, namely:
that which is not illusory, not deceitful, and not artificial.
Furthermore, there are four kinds of samādhi-garland adornments for a bodhisattva:
namely, not conforming to desire, not conforming to hatred,
not conforming to delusion, and not conforming to fear.
Furthermore, there are five kinds of samādhi-garland ornaments for a bodhisattva, which consist of severing five kinds of hindrances:
first, sensual desire; second, malice; third, torpor and drowsiness; fourth, restlessness and regret; and fifth, doubt.
The severing of these five hindrances serves as their adornment.
Furthermore, bodhisattvas possess six kinds of samādhi-garland adornments, namely:
mindfulness of the Buddha, mindfulness of the Dharma, and mindfulness of the Saṅgha.
They maintain mindfulness of the precepts, mindfulness of renunciation, and mindfulness of the devas.

Furthermore, the bodhisattva possesses seven kinds of samādhi-garlands as adornments, namely: never forgetting the mind of enlightenment and practicing in accordance with the seven factors of awakening.
That is to say: the awakening factor of mindfulness, the awakening factor of investigation of phenomena,
the awakening factor of energy, the awakening factor of joy,
the awakening factor of tranquility, the awakening factor of equanimity, and the awakening factor of concentration.
Furthermore, there are eight kinds of samādhi-garland ornaments for a bodhisattva,
namely the Eightfold Noble Path:
right view, right intention, right speech, and right action.
Right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness, and right concentration.
Furthermore, a bodhisattva has nine kinds of samādhi-garland adornments. What are these nine?
Good son, this bodhisattva’s mind is free from forgetfulness;
through the power of great compassion, he does not abandon sentient beings,
and he cultivates and establishes the nine successive meditative attainments.
That is to say, being detached from sensual desires and unwholesome states,
with directed thought and sustained thought, and with the joy and happiness born of seclusion,
he enters and dwells in the perfection of the first dhyāna.
With the subsiding of applied and sustained thought, and with internal clarity and one-pointedness of mind,
free from applied and sustained thought, he enters and dwells in the second dhyāna, which is born of concentration and characterized by joy and bliss.

Detached from joy, he dwells in equanimity, mindful and clearly aware, experiencing happiness with the body; that which the noble ones describe as "dwelling in equanimity, being mindful, and experiencing happiness," he enters and abides in the perfection of the third dhyāna.
With the abandoning of pleasure and the prior removal of pain, and with the disappearance of joy and sorrow,
he enters and dwells in the fourth dhyāna, which is neither painful nor pleasant and possesses purity of equanimity and mindfulness.
Transcending all perceptions of form and extinguishing perceptions of sensory resistance,
and no longer attending to perceptions of diversity, one enters and dwells in the fulfillment of the sphere of infinite space, having attained the sphere of infinite space.
Transcending the sphere of infinite space,
one enters the sphere of infinite consciousness and, having attained it, dwells in its fulfillment.
Transcending the sphere of infinite consciousness,
one enters and dwells in the perfection of the sphere of nothingness, wherein there is nothing whatsoever.
Transcending the sphere of nothingness,
he enters the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception and dwells in its full attainment.
Transcending the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception,
he enters the attainment of the cessation of perception and feeling,
and dwells in the perfection of that attainment of the cessation of perception and feeling.
Thus, by the power of skillful means (*upāyakauśalya*), the reality-limit (*bhūtakoṭi*) manifests before one;
through the power of prior cessation, one abides therein,
and subsequently brings benefit and happiness to all sentient beings.
By means of various Dharma-gates, they bring beings to maturity;
this is called the bodhisattva’s ninth kind of adornment of the samādhi-garland.
Son of good family, bodhisattvas further possess ten kinds of adornment of the samādhi-garland.
What are these ten? They are:
because the nature of phenomena (dharmatā) is undisturbed;
and because sublime concentration (samādhi) is perfected.
Because they do not abandon diligence;
because they always delight in tranquility;
and because they do not sever their roots of goodness.
Because the mind is not distracted;
because the body attains peace and happiness;
and because one observes all phenomena.
Because they have attained mastery over the mind and because they have attained the lineage of the noble ones,
son of good family, these are the ten kinds of samādhi-garland ornaments of a bodhisattva.
“Good son, what is called the bodhisattva’s adornment of the wisdom-garland?
Good son, a bodhisattva mahāsattva possesses one adornment of the wisdom-garland.”
What is this one? It is the severing of doubt and confusion regarding all phenomena.
Furthermore, son of good family, there are two further kinds of wisdom-garland adornments for a bodhisattva.
This refers to remaining far removed from remorse and the manifest afflictions.
Furthermore, there are three kinds of wisdom-garlands with which a bodhisattva adorns themselves:
namely, severing ignorance, breaking open the storehouse of nescience, and dispelling darkness.
Furthermore, there are four kinds of wisdom-garland adornments for bodhisattvas:
namely, the wisdom that knows suffering, the wisdom that abandons the origin [of suffering],
the wisdom that realizes cessation, and the wisdom that cultivates the path.
Furthermore, there are five kinds of wisdom-garland adornments for a bodhisattva.
These are: first, the purity of the aggregate of ethical discipline (*śīlaskandha*), because the essence of ethical discipline is like space and cannot be apprehended.
The aggregate of concentration is purified because it gives rise to superior wisdom and activates mindfulness.
The aggregate of liberation is purified.
Because the essence of all phenomena is non-dual,
the aggregate of liberation-knowledge-and-vision is pure;
because one thoroughly understands that the essence of the three periods of time is equal.
The aggregate of dharmas is pure,
because the intrinsic nature of all phenomena is free from defilement and attachment.
Furthermore, a bodhisattva possesses six kinds of wisdom-garlands as adornments.
This refers to the purity of the three spheres of the perfection of generosity (dānapāramitā).
That is to say, it is the purity of the sphere of the self,
because one knows that the self is equal in essence to an illusion.
The wheel of sentient beings is pure,
for one realizes that all beings to be transformed are like dreams.
The wheel of the bodhicitta is pure.
Because one does not seek the ripened fruits of the mundane world,
the perfection of ethical discipline (*śīlapāramitā*) is characterized by the purity of the three spheres (*trimaṇḍalapariśuddhi*);
that is to say, the purity of the sphere of the body (*kāyamaṇḍala*).
The wheel of speech is pure because its essence is equal to that of a reflection in a mirror;
it is like an echo because its essence is equal to that of a valley resonance.
The wheel of mind is purified because one realizes that the nature of the mind is equal to an illusion;
this is the threefold purity of the perfection of patience (*kṣānti-pāramitā*).
This refers to purity through the abandonment of hatred,
because one endures coarse abuse and insults;
and purity through the abandonment of attachment.
Because of severing praise, veneration, offerings, and the like,
one severs the limbs and joints for the sake of purity;
because of observing that the dharma-body is non-dual, it is pure.
The perfection of diligence is the purity of the three spheres;
that is, it is the purity of effortlessness,
because one contemplates saṃsāra as being like a dream.
It is firm and pure,
for the mind is indestructible like a vajra;
it is pure in its taking up and discarding.
Because it transcends all signs and is free from grasping or rejecting,
the perfection of meditative concentration (*dhyānapāramitā*) is characterized by the purity of the three spheres;
that is, because it is naturally pure and possesses non-conceptualizing wisdom (*avikalpajñāna*).
Sublime contemplation is pure because it is free from attachment;
its causal conditions are pure.
Because they give rise to supernormal powers,
the perfection of skillful means is characterized by the purity of the three spheres; that is,
the purity of gathering [beings] through material gifts.
Because they bring all realms of sentient beings to maturity,
their dhāraṇīs are pure;
because they receive and uphold all sublime dharma-gates.
Their great vows are pure,
for they adorn various pure Buddha-fields.
Furthermore, Bodhisattvas possess seven kinds of wisdom-garlands as adornments.
What is called the wisdom of non-conceptualization is so called because it abides in the four foundations of mindfulness that are free from conceptualization;
it is the wisdom of non-arising and non-ceasing because it abides in the right efforts.
Because they abide in the bases of psychic power through the tranquility of body and mind;
because they abide in the faculties through the wisdom of the faculty of final knowledge;
and because they abide in the powers by crushing and destroying the four māras.
Because they know the fundamental nature of phenomena through abiding in the seven factors of enlightenment;
because they know the wisdom of the past and future through abiding in the eightfold noble path.
Furthermore, bodhisattvas possess eight kinds of wisdom-garlands as adornments.
This means: knowing through the entry into tranquility by means of sublime and correct wisdom;
knowing through the wisdom of profound contemplation being free from obscuration;
and knowing through the wisdom of the aggregates by awakening to the aggregate of dharmas.
The wisdom that knows the various elements (dhātus) is because it realizes their emptiness and equality;
the wisdom that knows the various bases (āyatanas) is because it understands them as a collection of emptiness;
the wisdom that knows causes and conditions is because it abides in non-self.
Because the mind is undisturbed by the knowledge of the true truths,
and because one observes the reality of phenomena as they truly are through the knowledge of wearying detachment,
the bodhisattva further possesses nine kinds of wisdom-garlands as adornments.
What are the nine? They are:
knowledge of the past, because it is pure regarding the prior limit;
and knowledge of the future, because it is pure regarding the subsequent limit.
Knowledge of the present is because the middle limit is pure;
knowledge of those with right determination is because their causes are non-extinguished;
knowledge of those without fixed determination is because conditions are in harmony.
Because the wisdom that knows false concentration realizes the accomplishment of false karma;
because the Buddha’s wisdom of equality is the virtue of the Dharma-body;
and because the wisdom of the equality of phenomena is the non-defilement of phenomena.
Because of the merit of the unconditioned and the equal wisdom of the Saṃgha,
these are called the nine.
Furthermore, there are ten kinds of wisdom-garland ornaments by which Bodhisattvas adorn themselves.
What are the ten? They are:
the wisdom that knows [all things] are like illusions because of the accumulation of their characteristics;
and the wisdom that knows [all things] are like dreams because of the differentiation of their characteristics.
One knows through the wisdom that [all things] are like a flame because they manifest as a revolving wheel;
one knows through the wisdom that they are like a reflection because they neither come nor go;
one knows through the wisdom that they are like a shadow because they arise from the conjunction of causes and conditions.
The wisdom that knows [reality] as an echo, because it perceives the characteristics of dependent origination;
the wisdom that knows the dharma-realm, because it is indestructible;
and the wisdom that knows true suchness, because it has no abiding characteristic.
Because the wisdom that knows the limit of reality is profoundly still and pure;
because the wisdom that knows conditioned phenomena is the nature of the unconditioned—
these are called the ten.
"Noble son, these are called the ten kinds of wisdom-garland ornaments of a bodhisattva.
Noble son, what is meant by the 'garland ornament of all bodhisattva dharani-gates'?"
Good son, there is one dhāraṇī-gateway for Bodhisattvas known as the Adornment of Necklaces.
What is this one? It is so-called because it is right mindfulness without forgetfulness.
Furthermore, son of good family, there are two dharani-gates for the bodhisattva’s adornment with garlands:
namely, the retention of words and the retention of meaning.
There are three dharani-gates for the bodhisattva’s adornment with garlands.
That is to say: skill in meaning, skill in phrasing, and skill in analysis.
A bodhisattva possesses four dharani-gates as ornaments of adornment.
That is to say, speech that is unattached, speech that is not stammering or halting,
speech that is clear and distinct, and speech that is free from confusion.
These are the five dharani-gateways that serve as the jeweled ornaments of the Bodhisattva.
That is to say: practicing in accordance with the meaning of what has been heard;
practicing in accordance with the various collections of syllables (*vyañjana-kāya*);
and practicing in accordance with the sūtras of definitive meaning (*nītārtha*).
Because they know how to practice in accordance with the knowledge of the sounds and dharmas of all individuals (pudgala),
and because they know how to practice in accordance with all mundane and supramundane dharmas.
Bodhisattvas possess six dharani-gates as ornaments of adornment. These are:
practicing according to the principles as they have been taught;
and realizing the truth to give rise to speech, expounding it in accordance with what is appropriate.
Their speech is truthful because it is free from flattery and deception;
their words are always majestic because they never abandon great compassion while preaching the True Dharma;
and they skillfully expound the teachings according to the capacities of beings, without exaggeration or omission.
Because they have attained worldly wisdom, they speak at the proper time and not at an improper time.
Thus, a bodhisattva possesses seven dharani-gates as ornaments and adornments:
namely, swift eloquence and sharp, incisive eloquence.
The eloquence that accords with one's intent, the unimpeded eloquence,
the eloquence of majestic power, the eloquence free from error,
and the most supreme and wondrous eloquence in all the world.
Bodhisattvas possess eight dharani-gates as ornaments of adornment,
namely: skillfully knowing the languages of devas, nagas, yakshas, and gandharvas.
The language of asuras, the language of garuḍas,
the language of kinnaras, mahoragas, humans, non-humans, and so forth—
the languages of all sentient beings.
Bodhisattvas possess nine dharani-gates as ornaments for their adornment.
What are these nine? They are:
being fearless when amidst the assembly; [and so forth].
He subdues all heterodox teachers,
preaches the Dharma with fearlessness,
and skillfully answers difficult questions.
He knows the extensive teaching;
he knows the teaching according to one's inclination;
he practices the straight and upright path, manifesting adamantine power.
Manifesting the conflagration at the end of an eon to destroy attachment to the notion of permanence,
and preaching the various vehicles of the Dharma to bring sentient beings to maturity—
this is called the ninth.
Bodhisattvas possess ten dharani-gates that serve as ornaments for adornment.
What are these ten? They are:
being well able to eliminate and sever all doubts and difficulties.
They skillfully know all vast dharma-gates;
they have skillfully attained teacherless, spontaneous wisdom;
and they skillfully expound dharma-gates of inexhaustible words and phrases.
He skillfully explains all the profound meanings of perfection;
he is adept at revealing the boundless qualities of the Buddha-dharma;
and he skillfully describes the faults and afflictions of limitless defilements.
He skillfully expounds immeasurable gates of profound liberation;
he is adept at penetrating the faculties and natures of sentient beings;
and he skillfully enters the Tathāgata’s unattached and unimpeded eloquence and wisdom.
These are called the ten.
Good son, this is called the Bodhisattva’s Adornment of the Garland of Dharani-Gates.
*The Dhāraṇī Sūtra of the Sovereign Who Protects the Realm*, Scroll Seven.
The Dhāraṇī Sūtra of the Lord Who Protects the Realm of the Nation, Scroll Eight.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Śramaṇa Prajña of Kaśmīra together with Munisri.
Part Two of Chapter Six: The Ornamentation of the Bodhisattva’s Necklace.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate the meaning of these four necklaces, spoke in verse:
"The one of great wisdom adorns the four necklaces, The most supreme and foremost of vehicles."
The gate of pure precepts, samādhi, and wisdom, The supreme and wondrous mantra definitively proclaimed;
Sentient beings free from anger all find joy in it, It closes the gates to all evil destinies,
Causing the wise to dwell among humans and devas— This perfection of precepts serves as an ornament.
The actions of body, speech, and mind are all pure; All vows and desires are entirely fulfilled.

With firm progress in right exertion, one seeks to achieve this body adorned with the garland of precepts, as well as concentration, wisdom, and liberation, and likewise the knowledge and vision of liberation.
And realizing the unsurpassed Great Nirvāṇa—this body adorned with the garland of precepts does not break the pure morality of the *śīla*; it is pure, unadulterated, and cool.
Attaining mastery over the body, the Dharma is likewise so; this is the body adorned with the garland of precepts.
If one attains the purity of complete generosity, as well as the purity of patience, diligence,
and likewise all meditative concentrations, wisdom, and the gateway of skillful means; and if one possesses the purity of non-negligence,
immovable wisdom, firmness, and sublime establishment, then there shall be no retreat from the mind that realizes the profound teaching.
Staying far from indolence and practicing contentment—this is the body adorned by pure ethical discipline (*śīla*).

The Noble Ones praise ethical discipline, diligence, and vigor; for such a person, sorrow and affliction never arise, and there is no regret for the manifold virtues performed. This, indeed, is the body adorned by pure ethical discipline.
Fearless and untroubled when amidst the multitude, Having attained an utterly certain and tranquil mind,
one cannot be bound by the prison of the three realms of existence. Having attained great renown and the power of endurance,
being self-subdued and knowing the minds of others— This is the adornment of pure ethical discipline.
Adorning the body with the various marks and signs is the very embodiment of the adornment of pure precepts;
acting according to what one has taught purifies speech, which is the fulfillment of the adornment of wise speech;
and attaining a mind free from afflictions is the necklace of pure precepts.
Adorning the Buddha-field with supreme great vows, Bringing sentient beings to accomplishment through the foremost vehicle;
Refraining from all causes of unwholesome karma, Causing every place of rebirth to be adorned;
Training in the Bodhisattva practices that can adorn the Buddha-way, Dedicating roots of goodness to adorn the site of enlightenment.
Adorned with the powers, fearlessnesses, and dharmas, Furthermore adorned with the necklaces of transformative wisdom,
compassion, and meditative concentration, which can universally cover all; With gentle, upright, and perfect wisdom,
having already severed the mind of illusion, falsehood, flattery, and deception, He does not follow after attachment, hatred, delusion, or fear.
Severing the five hindrances serves as one’s adornment; One is graced by the diligent cultivation of the six recollections.
The seven factors of enlightenment, the eightfold path, and samādhi, The nine successive attainments, are constantly practiced;
Diligently cultivating śamatha and vipaśyanā in accordance with their true nature, One delights in dwelling in tranquility and reflects with discerning wisdom.
With right mindfulness, they do not sever the roots of goodness; having attained the lineage of the noble ones, their minds possess sovereign wisdom.
Regarding all phenomena, they are free from doubt; never again will unwholesome deeds arise.
The darkness of ignorance and delusion is entirely removed, and the light of knowledge regarding the Truths shines everywhere.
The knowledge of suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path is purified; because it is ungraspable, ethical discipline is pure.
It transcends mindfulness and wisdom, and through the purity of meditative concentration, both dualistic marks are forgotten.
Pure liberation and the vision of knowledge do not cling to the three periods of time; the aggregates of phenomena are pure and accomplished without defilement.
There is also no one who can conceive of their pure mind; they are fully endowed with the adornment of wisdom.
By taking wisdom as their necklace, they are able to purify the three spheres of giving, morality, and so forth.
By bestowing gifts upon sentient beings without abiding in signs, they attain the purity of the three spheres of generosity.
Knowing that sentient beings, awakening, and oneself are like dreams and illusions and thus nothing to be sought,
one adorns oneself with the precepts through wisdom; thereby, one attains the purity of the three spheres of the precepts,
wherein body, speech, and mind are like reflections in a mirror, like echoes, and like illusions— pure and without flaw.
Through wisdom, they are adorned with patience; that patience is purified in its three spheres.
With knowledge that reaches the absence of high or low, they constantly contemplate the pure and wondrous true Dharma-body.
Through wisdom, they are adorned with diligence; diligence is likewise purified in its three spheres.
The mind spontaneously becomes firm and stable; Without grasping or rejecting, all marks are empty.
Adorned with concentration through wisdom, One attains the purity of the three spheres through meditative absorption.
By deeply contemplating the nature of dependent origination, One becomes unmoving and unattached, giving rise to supernormal powers.
Adorned with skillful means through wisdom, they attain the complete purity of the three wheels;
well-gathering the mantras and vows with diligence, they manifest the adornment of the wondrous Dharma-realm.
Constantly abiding in the foundations of mindfulness with a mind free from conceptual thought, their minds are non-dual within the right abandonments.
Desire, diligence, mind, and contemplation are the bases of supernormal power;
Knowing the diverse faculties and natures of all beings, one abides in the powers and subdues the hosts of Māra. With right mindfulness, one awakens to the nature of all phenomena;
The Path is likewise without coming or going— This is called the adornment of the wisdom-garland.
Deeply entering the tranquility of *śamatha*, they possess the wisdom that fully illuminates and understands all aggregates of phenomena through *vipaśyanā*.

They know the equality of the elements (*dhātu*) to be like space, and they well understand that the sense bases (*āyatana*) are empty villages. They know that phenomena are fundamentally selfless and arise through dependent origination.
Knowing the Four Noble Truths without distraction, they contemplate the reality of phenomena and grow weary of the three periods of time.

With pure wisdom and an unattached mind, they bring peace to sentient beings by understanding the three groups and knowing that the essence of the Three Jewels is of one and the same mark— all adorned with the garland of wisdom.
The accumulation of wisdom is like an illusion; the root of conceptualization is entirely like a dream.
Wandering through cyclic existence is without reality, like a mirage;
there is no going and no coming, for the mirror-like body arises from the conjunction of causes and conditions, like a shadow. It originates solely from conditions, just like an echo.
The true and eternal nature of the dharma-realm is indestructible; Only by not dwelling upon the ultimate truth can one know the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*).
Profoundly still and unshakable, conditioned and unconditioned are non-dual in essence;
This deep and vast wisdom serves as an ornament, Adorning the bodhisattvas as they realize enlightenment.
They attain the dhāraṇī-door of non-forgetfulness, retaining the meaning of all heard words without loss;

they clearly comprehend the subtle meanings of all syllables. Their skillful analytical wisdom is ever-pervasive, and all speech characterized by attachment or stammering has vanished; their expression and reasoning are distinct and free from confusion.
Constantly seeking the meaning of whatever Dharma they hear, Possessing complete knowledge of the texts and excelling in relying on sūtras of definitive meaning;
Knowing that within the essence of phenomena there is no mark of self,
And skillfully understanding both mundane and supramundane dharmas— All these are adorned by the power of dhāraṇī.
Turning according to the ultimate truth and practicing as taught, The teacher who knows the time and speaks the Dharma is respectfully received;

For one who speaks this Dharma, no effort is in vain. In accordance with the timing, without deficiency or regret, One attains swift and wondrous eloquence— Agile, as desired, and free from attachment.
Possessing virtue and free from error, you analyze with exquisite discernment; like a garland skillfully adorned, you are wonderfully embellished.
You thoroughly know the various languages of devas and nāgas, as well as those of yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, and all other sentient beings.
Fearless among the assembly like a bull king, you crush all non-Buddhists like a fragrant elephant;
preaching the Dharma without fear like a lion, you answer every difficult question as if from a spring.
You expound the vast and great Dharma, destroying the mountains of pride; according to their inclinations, your joyful speech fulfills all wishes.
Manifesting as a Vajra-form for the sake of the fierce, he burns away the minds of the five desires with the fire of the kalpa;
according to the inclinations of beings, he teaches the three vehicles.
He clearly discerns and reveals both what is meaningful and what is not, manifesting the vast Dharma of awakening. Spontaneous wisdom appears without reliance on a teacher.
He expounds the inexhaustible syllables of wisdom without remainder; He explains subtle meanings with complete perfection.
He proclaims the boundless teachings of all Buddhas; He knows the faults of afflictions are likewise boundless.
The merit of his liberation is difficult to measure; He knows the faculties of sentient beings without exception.
Having attained the four fearlessnesses spoken by the Buddha, they are adorned with the secret *muktāhāra* (necklace).
With those necklaces adorning their bodies, whether the merits have already been proclaimed or are yet to be proclaimed,
even if one were to expound them with diligent effort for an eon, all such merits could never be exhausted.
At that time, having heard this Dharma, the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī rose from his seat,
joined his palms in reverence, and prostrated at the Buddha’s feet.
He addressed the Buddha, saying: "It is rare, World-Honored One!
The Buddha has appeared in the world and preached the supreme and wondrous Dharma, bringing great benefit and happiness to all sentient beings."
They all accord with their faculties and natures to bring them joy;
in future ages, they will be able to generate all roots of goodness in Bodhisattvas and cause all those who have first resolved their minds to give rise to a pure mind.
They proceed toward enlightenment by practicing the path of the One Vehicle;
they attain non-retrogression and receive the Buddha’s consecration,
thereby attaining the factors of enlightenment in this very life.
In one lifetime, they shall realize unsurpassed bodhi.
This demonstrates that the cause and effect of these bodhisattvas are not extinguished;
for those beings fixed in the right determination, he explains their cause.
For sentient beings fixed in wrong views, he manifests great compassion to lead them toward entry [into the path] over a long period.
For those of indeterminate nature, he establishes each according to the distinctions of their own minds.
For those who delight in the three vehicles, he causes each to fulfill their aspirations according to their respective faculties.
Even unto the devas, humans, asuras, and so forth—this entire world is made completely adorned. Why is this?
Because when a Buddha appears in the world...
Then, various such rare and extraordinary phenomena all appeared,
as did the precious thrones and precious canopies for the assembly of great bodhisattvas.
Various jewel trees, exquisitely adorned,
all appeared throughout the great assembly at the site of enlightenment;
so too did all the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas.
It could not be measured even in hundreds of thousands of kalpas, much less fully revealed.
World-Honored One, as I reflect upon this,
ignorant sentient beings are truly to be pitied.
When the Buddha has thus spoken this profound Mahāyāna and revealed such a marvelous place of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa),
those who are unable to give rise to the mind of great awakening (mahābodhicitta) [are truly lost].
On the contrary, it is pitiable that they instead long for the nirvana of the two vehicles and the bliss of humans and devas.
Why is this? Because all the merits of a bodhisattva who has first resolved upon bodhicitta are immeasurable and boundless.
Because it cannot be attained by any of those of the two vehicles.
World-Honored One, it is as if there were a person who cast away a priceless lapis lazuli gem.
They then take up counterfeit glass beads.
All sentient beings are likewise;
they abandon the Mahāyāna and instead seek the enlightenment of śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, as well as the bliss of humans and devas.
Blessed One, if sons or daughters of good family hear this Dharma-gate,
whether they have already generated the mind of great enlightenment or shall generate it in the future,
they will all before long attain unsurpassed bodhi.
Furthermore, when this *Mālā-dharmaparyāya*, which is endowed with the supreme qualities previously described, was being taught,
there were thirty *koṭi-nayuta-śata-sahasra* of sentient beings in this assembly.
All of them resolved their minds upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.

Chapter Seven: The Universal Radiance Adornment. *The Dhāraṇī Sūtra of the Protector of the Realm*, Chapter Seven: The Universal Radiance Adornment. At that time, the World-Honored One surveyed the great assembly of bodhisattvas, humans, and devas.
Knowing that his deep yearning for the Dharma was not yet satisfied,
he addressed the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī, saying:
"O son of good family, bodhisattva mahāsattva..."
There is the Dharma-gate of the Universal Illumination and Adornment of the Eightfold Great Light.
Because of that light’s illumination, the mind opens and becomes clear, remaining far removed from the darkness of ignorance.
One adorns one's body with the adornments of a mahāsattva bodhisattva, cultivates the bodhisattva practices, and brings peace to sentient beings.
Within this practice, what are the eight? They are:

the light of mindfulness universally illuminating, the light of intention universally illuminating, the light of liberation universally illuminating, the light of phenomena universally illuminating, and the light of wisdom universally illuminating.
The light of truth shines universally;
the light of supernormal powers shines universally; the light of spiritual practice shines universally.
These are the eight kinds of radiant adornments.
"Good son, what is meant by 'the light of mindfulness universally illuminating'?
Good son, there are eight adornments of the bodhisattva’s light of mindfulness that universally illuminate.
What are these eight?"
That which is called the first is to maintain mindfulness of all that is wholesome and never forget it.
The second is to cause the roots of goodness already cultivated to increase.
The third is to retain and not forget whatever Dharma one has heard.
Fourth, they possess subtle and profound understanding of the deep meaning.
Fifth, their minds do not turn toward the objects of the six sense-fields.
Sixth, they constantly guard the doors of the sensory faculties with right mindfulness.
Seventh, they constantly mindfully recollect all Buddhas in order to sever all unwholesome dharmas and to bring wholesome dharmas to full perfection.
Eighth, they do so because they desire to protect the Dharma-city of all Buddhas.
With mindfulness as the forerunner, one attains great radiance.
Good son, these are called the eight kinds of radiant light of mindfulness that universally illumine and adorn the Bodhisattva.
Good son, the Bodhisattva possesses eight kinds of radiant light of intention that universally illumine and adorn.
What are these eight? They are:
relying on the meaning rather than the letter;
relying on wisdom rather than consciousness.
Rely on the intention of the Dharma and not the intention of afflictions;
rely on the intention of principle and not the intention of what is contrary to principle;
rely on the intention of the bodhicitta and not the intention of the two vehicles.
Rely on a vast intention and not a narrow or inferior one;
rely on the intention of the Buddha and not the intention of the māras;
rely on the intention of great compassion and not an intention to harm sentient beings.
This is called the Bodhisattva’s eightfold adornment of the universally illuminating light of the mind.
Good son, the Bodhisattva has an eightfold adornment of the universally illuminating light of liberation.
He is able to know all phenomena; what are these eight?
That is to say: knowing all phenomena; knowing the conduct of sentient beings;
knowing the minds of sentient beings; knowing the four analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*);
and knowing that the essential nature of phenomena is originally luminous.
They know the dharmas of vast adornment;
they know the definitive and non-definitive dharmas;
and they know all the profound, extensive, and wondrous dharmas of the Buddhas.
This is called the Bodhisattva’s eightfold adornment of the universal illumination of the light of liberation.
Son of good family, there are eight dharmas that constitute the Bodhisattva’s adornment of the universal illumination of light. What are these eight?
This refers to the adornment of the illumination of worldly dharmas,
because it explains the karmic actions performed by all sentient beings;
and the adornment of the illumination of supramundane dharmas.
Because he teaches the Prajñāpāramitā for the sake of all sentient beings seeking liberation,
he is adorned by the illumination of the stainless Dharma;
this is because he cultivates sublime wisdom and the Noble Path.
It is adorned by the illumination of the dharma of the absence of afflictions,
because it does not give rise to the views of ignorance regarding desire or existence;
it is adorned by the illumination of unconditioned dharmas.
Because the liberation of non-action is constantly manifest;
because it is adorned by the light of the noble ones' afflictive dharmas,
as they observe that afflictions are merely adventitious dust.
It is adorned by the light of the dharma of the absence of afflictions,
because it knows that the intrinsic nature of the mind is pure luminosity;
it is adorned by the light of the dharma of great nirvāṇa.
Because they know that all phenomena are fundamentally quiescent.
These are the eight kinds of light of the Dharma that universally illumine and adorn the bodhisattva.
Son of good family, the bodhisattva possesses eight kinds of light of wisdom that universally illumine and adorn.
What are these eight? They are:
the adornment of the illumination of wisdom of the person on the eighth stage;
and the adornment of the illumination of wisdom of the stream-enterer (srotāpanna).
The adornment of the illumination of the wisdom of the Sakṛdāgāmin;
the adornment of the illumination of the wisdom of the Anāgāmin;
and the adornment of the illumination of the wisdom of the Arhat.
The adornment of the illumination of the wisdom of pratyekabuddhas;
the adornment of the illumination of the wisdom of all bodhisattvas;
the adornment of the illumination of the wisdom of the Buddha’s bodhi.
This is called the Bodhisattva’s eightfold adornment of the universally illuminating light of wisdom.
Son of good family, the Bodhisattva has an eightfold adornment of the universally illuminating light of the truths.
What are these eight?
This means that by practicing the True Truth (*satya*), one attains liberation through the manifestation of direct awakening.
This constitutes the Bodhisattva’s first adornment of universal illumination through the light of the Truth.
By practicing the True Truth, one attains the stage of *srotāpanna*.
This is the second adornment of light-radiance.
By practicing the True Truths, one attains the stage of Sakṛdāgāmin;
this is the third adornment of light-radiance.
By practicing the true reality, one attains the stage of Anāgāmin;
this is the fourth adornment of radiant illumination.
By practicing the true reality, one attains the stage of Arhat.
This is the fifth adornment of radiant light.
By practicing the true reality, one attains the state of a pratyekabuddha;
this is the sixth adornment of radiant light.
By practicing the ultimate truth, one attains the bodhisattva's patience;
this is the seventh adornment of radiant light.
By practicing the ultimate truth, one awakens to the bodhi of the Buddha.
This is the eighth adornment of radiant illumination.
These are called the eight kinds of adornments of the universal illumination of the light of truth of a bodhisattva.
Noble son, a bodhisattva possesses the eight great lights of supernormal powers that universally illuminate as adornments.
What are the eight? They are:
the adornment of the universal illumination of great light, because the divine eye perceives all various forms.
The adornment of the illumination of subtle wisdom,
because the divine ear hears various teachings from afar;
the adornment of the illumination of conforming to right mindfulness.
Because he recollects the events of his past lives throughout immeasurable eons;
because his innate wisdom is adorned with the illumination of light;
and because he minutely and skillfully observes the minds of sentient beings.
One knows that the nature of space is unobstructed and adorned with the illumination of light,
because of the sovereign practice within infinite classes of buddha-fields;
it is adorned with the illumination of pure wisdom.
Because the wisdom free from afflictions has attained perfection,
he is adorned by the radiance of a great mass of merit;
because he nurtures all sentient beings with thoughts of loving-kindness.
The adornment of the illumination of the mass of great wisdom is so called because it severs the various doubts of all sentient beings;
this is known as the Bodhisattva’s eighth adornment of the illumination of supernormal powers.
Good son, there are nine causes of cultivation through which a bodhisattva attains the adornment of radiant illumination. What are these nine?
They are as follows: namely, from the cause of cultivation, one attains the radiance of wisdom as an adornment.
From the cause of practice, one attains the adornment of the illumination of prajñā;
from the cause of practice, one attains the adornment of the illumination of awakening;
from the cause of practice, one attains the adornment of the illumination of right view.
From the cause of cultivation, one attains the adornment of the illumination of śamatha;
from the cause of cultivation, one attains the adornment of the illumination of profound and wondrous light;
from the cause of cultivation, one attains the adornment of the illumination of knowledge of others' minds.
From the cause of practice, one attains non-retrogression and the adornment of the illumination of right liberation;
from the cause of practice, one attains the ultimate culmination and the adornment of illumination.
These are called the nine causes of a bodhisattva’s practice,
through which they attain universal illumination as their adornment.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:
Pure karma from past lives, The thought to benefit sentient beings never forgotten,
Accumulating roots of goodness through concentration and wisdom, Dedicating all for the sake of beings,
Correctly recollecting whatever is heard, And knowing the profound meaning in its subtle details.
Guarding the sense-doors with right mindfulness, The realm of sensory objects naturally becomes still.
One should not engage in unwholesome dharmas; One must cultivate wholesome dharmas to perfection.
Adorned with perfect mindfulness, One shall spontaneously receive the Buddha’s protection.
The city of Dharma is well-guarded; the supreme Dharma benefits sentient beings.
With wisdom free from darkness and a perfect light, it can benefit the multitudes of humans and devas.
By attaining this illumination of mindfulness, all doubts and delusions are entirely eliminated.
Within the wisdom of natural mindfulness, one swiftly realizes the fruit of Bodhi;
Adorning the mind with meaning, one does not follow sounds or letters,
But practices according to the purity of wisdom, without relying on discriminative consciousness.
Adorning the mind with the knowledge of the Dharma, The wisdom of the Prajñāpāramitā teachings destroys delusions and abandons ignorance.
Seeking supreme enlightenment with an undisturbed intent for Bodhi, One remains unmixed with the two vehicles.
Vast and without inferiority of mind, Following the Buddha’s teachings and opposing those of Māra;
Adorned with the intention of great compassion, Never momentarily troubling sentient beings;
Having no doubt regarding the dharmas known, And skillful in the provisional meaning.
Knowing that sentient beings are fearless, With unimpeded wisdom,
the infinite creator is primordially empty; Skillfully and extensively teaching the dependent origination of phenomena, This is the supreme, essential, and profound gateway.
The dharmas of all Buddhas are boundless; Through complete understanding, they are all fully exhausted.
By the illumination of worldly dharmas, They know the karma of sentient beings entirely.
The light of supramundane dharmas Is the mark of emptiness of prajñā.
Whether there is fault or no fault, the sovereign wisdom knows them all;
Wisdom accords with the cultivation of the noble path. Benefiting sentient beings brings forth all fruits, Whether they be tainted or untainted;
In the light of the Dharma, there is nothing that is not known.
Forever severing the source of afflictions, Able to bring benefit to humans and devas;
Regarding conditioned and unconditioned phenomena, Wisdom always conforms to them,
knowing that defilements are entirely absent, And all formations attain certainty.
Far removed from the phenomena of birth and death, With unimpeded wisdom,
one constantly knows the root source of afflictions; The nature is pure, luminous,
and its essence is liberation— the dharma of nirvana— Its arising is originally such as it is.
The light of the infinite Dharma adorns the essence of the Mahāyāna;
the wisdom of the eighth stage, as well as that of the *srotāpanna*,
the *sakṛdāgāmin*, and likewise the *anāgāmin*— all are thus.
The wisdom of the Arhats, Pratyekabuddhas, Bodhisattvas, and Tathāgatas—
within this Dharma, each and every one of them turns in accordance with the truth;
they are fully endowed with the illumination of the light and possess courageous and sublime practice.
Riding upon causes, one attains the perfection of the fruit;
By cultivating the true and supreme meanings and the various noble truths, One enters the gateway to the fruit of liberation;
The four fruits are successively accomplished, And the patience of the pratyekabuddhas and bodhisattvas is attained.
Able to crush all heterodox paths, like the lion king;
awakening to the Buddha’s Bodhi, all through the light of the Truths;
seeing with the supernormal power of the divine eye, leaving no subtle form unseen.
With the divine ear, clearly hearing, they universally comprehend the sounds of the ten directions;
remembering the *nayuta* eons of the past, they well know the minds of all sentient beings throughout the Dharma-realm, as the light of their spontaneous wisdom shines forth.
Sovereignly roaming through all lands, The light of wisdom shines without exception;
Your physical form is like space, Adorned with the body of untainted radiance and fully endowed with boundless merit, Universally nurturing all sentient beings.
Adorned with non-attached wisdom, you sever the web of doubt for sentient beings;
through cultivation, you have attained wisdom, awakened to boundless eloquence,
and possess a mind of right view characterized by śamatha and vipaśyanā, reaching the ultimate limit of the infinite.
Knowing that the teachings and practices are complete, The mind contemplates the Dharma, wisdom is perfected,
and the light of truth and supernormal powers shine forth; The illumination adorns the Dharma,
and these eight aspects are all pure— This is the light of great majestic power.
"Though they have not yet attained bodhi, they are able to perform the works of all Buddhas.
At that time, when the World-Honored One had finished preaching this Dharma of the Great Radiance Universally Illuminating Adornment of Supernatural Powers,
the bodhisattvas who had come from the various Buddha-fields of the ten directions—
And various humans, devas, bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas,
and upāsikās made manifold offerings, paid homage, and prostrated before him;
so too did immeasurable, incalculable, and boundless sentient beings.
All of them resolved their minds upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
Immeasurable bodhisattvas attained the patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).

Chapter Eight: The Adornment of the Fundamental Activity of Prajñā. *The Dhāraṇī Sūtra of the Protector of the Realm*, Chapter Eight: The Adornment of the Fundamental Activity of Prajñā. At that time, there was a bodhisattva in the assembly named Prajñākūṭa (Peak of Wisdom).
Empowered by the Buddha’s spiritual authority, he immediately rose from his seat,
bared his right shoulder, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet,
knelt with his right knee on the ground, and joined his palms in reverent salutation.
Then he addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, as the Buddha has taught,
the dhāraṇī-gate of dedication for adornment is the great compassionate activity of all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas."
Regarding the Bodhisattva’s Ornament of Great Radiance Universally Illuminating Adornment Dharma Gate:
how does one cultivate and attain all those dharmas?
What dharma serves as their fundamental basis?
"How does one, having attained it, never forget it, and how does one cherish and nurture all sentient beings with compassion?
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Prajñākūṭa, saying: "Good son, when a bodhisattva..."
If one can abide immovably in the root of profound *prajñā* and perform the activities of *prajñā*,
then one will attain the merits previously described, such as the *dhāraṇī* of dedication up to the adornment of radiant illumination.
"Having attained it, not losing it is precisely the place where all sentient beings are nurtured, grown, and sustained.
Then, the Bodhisattva Prajñākūṭa again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Excellent, World-Honored One! I pray that you will explain this to me."
"What is called the root of prajñā?
What is called the activity of prajñā?
The Buddha said, "Good son,"
Listen attentively, listen attentively, and reflect upon this well.
I shall analyze and explain it for you.
Good son, the root of Prajñā is that which can give birth to Prajñā; it is the mother of Prajñā.
The activity of prajñā is that which gives birth.
Son of good family, when bodhisattvas hear all the dharma-gates they have never heard before,
this is the mother of the root of prajñā.
To extensively explain to others what one has heard is the work performed by prajñā;
to reflect with careful discernment upon the teachings as they have been heard is likewise its function.
This is the very mother of the root of prajñā; if,
having contemplated it, one reveals it to others,
this is the activity performed by prajñā.
Observing with right mindfulness is the mother of prajñā.
Establishing sentient beings in right mindfulness is the activity of prajñā.
Diligence in what is to be done is the mother of prajñā.
Engaging in correct practice is the activity of *prajñā*.
Clarity within one's own mind is the mother of *prajñā*.
Revealing it to others is the activity of *prajñā*.
Delighting in dwelling in tranquility is the mother of prajñā;
knowing that which is fundamentally tranquil is the activity of prajñā.
Delighting in solitary seclusion is the mother of prajñā.
A single path of purity is the activity of prajñā.
Cultivating sublime contemplation is the mother of prajñā.
Attaining liberation through wisdom is the activity of prajñā.
Cultivating the three gates of liberation is the mother of prajñā;
the manifestation of the three knowledges is the activity of prajñā.
Cultivating the foundations of mindfulness is the mother of prajñā.
Freedom from conceptualization and purity is the activity of prajñā;
the cultivation of the right efforts is the mother of prajñā;
knowing the severance of the nature of phenomena is the activity of prajñā.
The cultivation of the bases of psychic power is the mother of prajñā;
effortless practice is the activity of prajñā;
being able to believe in causes and conditions is the mother of prajñā.
Transcending all attachments is the activity of prajñā;
being pure and unadulterated is the mother of prajñā;
physical and mental peace and happiness are the activity of prajñā.
Constantly recollecting wholesome dharmas is the mother of prajñā.
Not dwelling upon the characteristics of mindfulness is the activity of prajñā.
Knowing the sequence of meditative concentrations is the mother of prajñā.
Attaining meditative equipoise of the nature of equality is the activity of prajñā.
Cultivating the faculty of wisdom (prajñendriya) is the mother of prajñā.
Skillfully knowing the successive nature of the faculties regarding the past is the activity of prajñā.
Firmly abiding in the five powers is the mother of prajñā;
being able to crush all māras is the activity of prajñā.
Accordance with patience and the seven factors of enlightenment are the mother of prajñā.
To know the nature of all phenomena and to awaken accordingly is the activity of *prajñā*.
To gather the factors of the noble path is the mother of *prajñā*.
To know that it is like the simile of the raft is once one has awakened to the essence of the Dharma.
Not abiding in either dharmas or non-dharmas is the activity of prajñā.
Skillfully practicing the truths of suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path is the mother of prajñā.
The manifestation of the truth of cessation is the activity of prajñā.
Thoroughly examining the sūtras of provisional meaning (*neyārtha*) is the mother of *prajñā*.
Practicing in accordance with the sūtras of definitive meaning (*nītārtha*) is the activity of *prajñā*.
Retaining all teachings as they are heard without forgetting them is the mother of *prajñā*.
Practicing in accordance with the meaning is the activity of prajñā;
investigating by relying on wisdom is the mother of prajñā;
acting in conformity with wisdom is the activity of prajñā.
Not grasping at a self or a person is the mother of prajñā;
practicing in accordance with the Dharma is the activity of prajñā.
Contemplating that all phenomena are entirely impermanent is the mother of prajñā.
To know that all phenomena are fundamentally neither arising nor ceasing is the activity of prajñā.
To observe that all conditioned formations are entirely suffering is the mother of prajñā.
To realize that all phenomena are fundamentally without conditioned formation is the activity of prajñā.
The subtle observation that all phenomena are without self is the mother of prajñā.
Knowing the primordial purity of all sentient beings is the activity of prajñā.
The subtle observation of the tranquility of nirvāṇa is the mother of prajñā.
To know that all phenomena are fundamentally and originally in nirvāṇa is the activity of prajñā.
To hear profound meanings without fear or alarm is the mother of prajñā.
To attain unimpeded mastery over meaning is the activity of prajñā.
Not being terrified when hearing the ultimate truth (paramārthasatya) is the mother of prajñā.
Attaining unimpeded mastery over phenomena (dharmapratisaṃvid) is the activity of prajñā.
Not being terrified when hearing sublime expressions and analyzing the meaning of phrases is the mother of prajñā.
Attaining unimpededness in terminology is the activity of prajñā.
Hearing the Buddha’s eloquence without being startled or terrified is the mother of prajñā.
Attaining unimpededness in discernment is the activity of prajñā.
Compassion based on sentient beings and phenomena is the mother of prajñā;
unconditioned compassion is the activity of prajñā.
Compassion for oneself and others is the mother of prajñā.
To remain far removed from both self and other is the activity of prajñā;
to contemplate the joy of the Dharma is the mother of prajñā;
to be without grasping and without abandoning is the activity of prajñā.
Equanimity free from desire and hatred is the mother of prajñā;
non-dual equanimity is the activity of prajñā;
and constant mindfulness of all Buddhas is the mother of prajñā.
To understand the Dharma-body is the activity of prajñā;
to constantly mind the Dharma is the mother of prajñā, and to be unstained by the Dharma is the activity of prajñā.
To single-mindedly mind the Saṃgha is the mother of prajñā.
Contemplating the nature of the unconditioned is the activity of prajñā;
constant mindfulness of relinquishment is the mother of prajñā;
abandoning all afflictions is the activity of prajñā.
Constantly recollecting the pure precepts is the mother of prajñā;
knowing that there is no practice of the precepts is the activity of prajñā.
Constantly recollecting the devas is the mother of prajñā.
The purity of the essence of phenomena is the activity of prajñā;
being fully endowed with extensive learning is the mother of prajñā;
and being fearless when amidst the assembly is the activity of prajñā.
Cultivating superior wholesome karma is the mother of prajñā.
Knowing that there is no karmic retribution is the activity of prajñā.
Knowing the transformations of the Buddha is the mother of prajñā.
Attaining great wisdom is the activity of prajñā;
acting for one's own benefit is the mother of prajñā;
benefiting both oneself and others is the activity of prajñā.
To be able to equally receive and uphold the eighty-four thousand aggregates of Dharma is the mother of this Prajñā;
to attain the eighty-four thousand wisdoms of the Dharma is the activity of this Prajñā.
Knowing how to teach the Dharma is the mother of prajñā;
knowing how to teach that which is not empty is the activity of prajñā.
Instructing sentient beings to resolve upon bodhicitta is the mother of prajñā.
To establish sentient beings upon the stage of non-retrogression through skillful means in the *prajñāpāramitā* is the activity of *prajñā*.
To cause those who fear rebirth within the three realms of existence to transcend it is the mother of *prajñā*.
Not abandoning birth and death while assuming bodies at will is the activity of prajñā.
Enduring sounds and voices is the mother of prajñā.
Cultivating the patience of nature is the activity of prajñā.
If one attains the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*), this is the mother of prajñā;
if one attains the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*), this is the activity of prajñā;
if one attains the patient acceptance that accords with reality (*anulomikī kṣānti*), this is the mother of prajñā.
Attaining the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*) is the activity of prajñā;
abiding on the stage of non-retrogression (*avaivartika-bhūmi*) is the mother of prajñā;
attaining the stage of consecration (*abhiṣeka-bhūmi*) is the activity of prajñā.
Sitting beneath the Bodhi tree is the mother of Prajñā.
Knowing that there is nothing not exhausted, one universally awakens to subtle thoughts and realizes the suchness (*tathatā*) through direct manifestation.
When the mind ceases in a single instant (*kṣaṇa*), it accords with wisdom and attains *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
This is the ultimate adornment of the bodhisattva’s activity of prajñā.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:
Hearing the Dharma without negligence, Purely upholding the Mother Prajñā.
To speak of it for others with the power of compassion, diligently cultivating the practice of Prajñā,
maintaining right mindfulness, and reflecting well— this is the mother of Prajñā.
To reflect upon it for oneself and then speak of it for others is the very activity of Prajñā.
If one cultivates with right mindfulness, this is the mother of Prajñā;
establishing oneself and others therein is the activity of Prajñā.
If one cultivates with correct diligence, this is the mother of Prajñā.
If one has cultivated it and then expounded it, that is the activity of Prajñā;
if the mind and wisdom are conjoined, this is the Mother of Prajñā.
If one can explain the mind and wisdom, that is the activity of Prajñā.
If one practices in solitary stillness, this is the mother of prajñā;
If there is neither body nor mind, this is the activity of prajñā;
If one remains far removed from clamor and bustle, this is the mother of prajñā.
If one dwells alone in right mindfulness, that is the activity of prajñā;
If one delights in profound contemplation, this is the mother of prajñā;
If one attains wisdom and liberation, that is the activity of prajñā.
If one cultivates the three liberations, this is the mother of prajñā;
when the three knowledges manifest before one, this is the activity of prajñā.
If one cultivates the foundations of mindfulness, this is the mother of prajñā.
When non-conceptualization manifests before one, that is the activity of prajñā;
abandoning evil and cultivating virtuous deeds—this is the mother of prajñā.
This dharma is pure by its very nature; this is the activity of prajñā.
Cultivating the four bases of psychic power—this is the mother of Prajñā;
The bases of psychic power are effortless—this is the activity of Prajñā;
Deep faith and liberation are the gateways—this is the mother of Prajñā.
To be far removed from the mind and free from attachment is the activity of prajñā;
to always exert oneself without diminishing in this activity is the mother of prajñā.
If body and mind are at peace and blissful, that too is the activity of prajñā.
Virtuous mindfulness and heedfulness—this is the mother of prajñā.
Not abiding in any place—this is the activity of prajñā.
Sublime concentration that accords with awakening—this is the mother of prajñā.
The practice of natural meditative equipoise is the activity of prajñā;
if one abides in the faculty of sublime wisdom, this is the mother of prajñā.
Knowing the various faculties of sentient beings is the activity of prajñā.
If one cultivates the five powers, this is the mother of prajñā;
one attains the wisdom that cannot be overcome. This is the activity of prajñā, the patient acceptance in accordance with reality, and the seven factors of enlightenment—this is the mother of prajñā.
To realize the nature of all phenomena is the activity of prajñā;
to cultivate the branches of the noble path is the activity of prajñā.
This mother of prajñā is able to relinquish both dharma and non-dharma; this is the activity of prajñā.
Knowing suffering and the origin of evil—this is the mother of Prajñā;
when cessation is present before one, this is the activity of Prajñā.
Examining that which is not of definitive meaning—this is the mother of Prajñā.
Relying upon sūtras of definitive meaning, one listens to the Dharma and maintains it without forgetfulness; this is the activity of Prajñāpāramitā.
Following the teachings and being able to practice them accordingly is the mother of Prajñāpāramitā; this is the activity of Prajñāpāramitā.
Not relying on consciousness to cultivate dhyāna—this is the mother of Prajñā.
Practicing in reliance upon wisdom—this is the activity of Prajñā.
Being free from even the slightest attachment to self or person—this is the mother of Prajñā.
Practicing in accordance with the Dharma is the activity of Prajñā;
Knowing that all conditioned phenomena are impermanent is the mother of Prajñā;
Knowing that phenomena are fundamentally unborn is the activity of Prajñā.
To have faith that all conditioned phenomena are suffering—this is the mother of prajñā.
If one knows that there are no conditioned phenomena, this is the activity of prajñā.
To contemplate the meaning of emptiness—this is the mother of prajñā.
In accordance with the meaning, there are no two extremes;
this is the activity of Prajñā, the meaning of non-self that severs doubt. This is the Mother of Prajñā;
this Dharma is fundamentally pure; this is the activity of Prajñā.
Faith in the tranquility of nirvāṇa—this is the mother of prajñā.
The inherent nature of sentient beings is tranquil—this is the activity of prajñā.
Contemplating in accordance with the profound meaning—this is the mother of prajñā.
To realize the meaning of non-obstruction is the activity of Prajñā;
If one has deep faith in the nature of phenomena (dharmatā), this is the mother of Prajñā;
To attain unimpeded analytical knowledge of phenomena (dharmanirukti-pratisaṃvid) is the activity of Prajñā.
Hearing all sounds without fear—this is the mother of Prajñā;
Analyzing words without impediment—this is the activity of Prajñā;
A mind that does not fear eloquence—this is the mother of Prajñā.
Attaining unimpeded eloquence is the cause for the arising of the activity of *prajñā*;
from this, compassion arises—this is the mother of *prajñā*.
If one attains objectless compassion (*anālambana-maitrī*), that is itself the activity of *prajñā*.
To give rise to compassion for oneself and others is the mother of Prajñā;
To give rise to compassion for the non-dual benefit [of self and others] is the activity of Prajñā.
To feel joy in delighting in the Dharma is the mother of Prajñā.
Without sorrow, without craving, and without joy—this is the activity of Prajñā.
If one can be without craving and without aversion, this is the mother of Prajñā.
Liberation from these two is the activity of Prajñā.
To be fully endowed with mindfulness of all Buddhas—this is the mother of Prajñā.
If one accords with the Dharmakāya—this is the activity of Prajñā.
To be able to constantly maintain mindfulness of the Dharma at all times—this is the mother of Prajñā.
If one knows that phenomena are without attachment, this is the fulfillment of the activity of prajñā;
mindfulness of the Saṅgha is the mother of prajñā.
To awaken accordingly to the unconditioned is the activity of prajñā.
The wise person always contemplates renunciation; this is the mother of Prajñā.
If one abandons all afflictions, that is the activity of Prajñā.
If one contemplates pure ethical discipline, this is the mother of Prajñā.
