Abiding in the precept free from afflictions,
one contemplates the deity of great majesty as the activity of Prajñā;
this is the Mother of Prajñā who constantly dwells in tranquility— this is the activity of Prajñā.
Whosoever seeks and hears the Dharma, this is the Mother Prajñā;
there is no other dharma to be sought. She who can perform sublime virtuous deeds through the activity of Prajñā—this is the Mother Prajñā.
There is no further karma to be performed;
this is the manifestation of nirvāṇa through the activity of Prajñā.
This is the Mother of Prajñā who attains the majestic power of great wisdom; this is the activity of Prajñā.
Attaining the perfection of self-benefit—this is the Mother Prajñā;
Able to greatly benefit sentient beings—this is the activity of Prajñā;
Upholding the sublime aggregate of Dharma—this is the Mother Prajñā.
Knowing oneself and awakening sentient beings is the activity of Prajñā;
If one knows the minds of others, this is the Mother of Prajñā.
Abiding in the three vehicles and attaining liberation is the activity of Prajñā.
Causing the arousal of conduct for the benefit of others—this is the Mother of Prajñā.
If one can benefit others with equanimity—this is the activity of Prajñā.
Terrifying all states of existence and incinerating them—this is the Mother of Prajñā.
Not abandoning saṃsāra is the activity of prajñā;
the patience that accords with sounds is the mother of this prajñā.
Practicing the patience of the nature is itself the activity of prajñā.
If one attains the knowledge of exhaustion, this is the mother of prajñā;
If one attains the knowledge of non-arising, this is the activity of prajñā;
If one cultivates the conforming patience, this is the mother of prajñā.
If one attains the patience of non-arising, that is the activity of Prajñā;
If one reaches the stage of non-retrogression, this is the mother of Prajñā;
If one attains the stage of consecration, that is the activity of Prajñā.
If one sits beneath the Bodhi tree, this is the mother of Prajñā;
if one attains omniscience, that is the activity of Prajñā.
All these activities of Prajñā arise from the generation of the bodhicitta.
If one attains liberation of mind, One accomplishes all activities of prajñā.
If one always dwells unmoving within the bodhicitta,
Then it becomes the mother of prajñā, Constantly performing all enlightened deeds.
Such various virtuous deeds, as well as the Buddha’s supreme ultimate powers and unimpeded eloquence— all these merits arise from the sublime bodhicitta;
if one praises the bodhicitta, all such qualities are attained.
Even after many billions of eons, one could not exhaustively praise it;
Because it gives birth to all the merits of the Buddhas of the three periods of time,
The Bodhicitta is said to be the Mother of all Buddhas in the ten directions.
If there are those who wish to make offerings to the immeasurable, tranquil Honored One,

The immeasurable and innumerable Buddha-fields of the ten directions shook in six ways;

While dwelling in the void, there were also six earth-tremblings.

The Buddhas of the past have already spoken it;

If bodhisattvas attain this prajñā,

I now proclaim this Dharma-gate for you and for this great assembly.

In the distant past, there appeared a Buddha named Śrīrakṣa Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidhyācaraṇasaṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Puruṣadamyasārathi, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, Buddha, Bhagavān. His world was named Subhavyūha, and his eon was named Vimala.
The sentient beings in that realm experience various forms of happiness;
their lifespan lasts for half an eon, and none suffer an untimely death.
All the humans and devas within that world—
Their physical forms, food and drink, palaces, towers,
and all articles of enjoyment are equal and without distinction;
they differ only in that humans dwell upon the earth while devas reside in the void of space.
In that world, there is only the Buddha, the King of Dharma; there are no other kings, nor do they serve other devas,
nor do they pay homage to or serve any other deities.
They perform no other deeds and give rise to no other thoughts;
they strive only to make offerings to the Buddhas and listen to the sublime Dharma,
and rather than dwelling in a womb, they are all born through transformation.
There will be no name for women, nor any name for offenses, nor any name for transgressions of the precepts.
The sentient beings therein will constantly and diligently cultivate this Mother Prajñā, the Dharma-gate of the adornment of the activities of Prajñā.
That Tathāgata Śrīrakṣa had a community of forty-two thousand bodhisattvas and eighty-four thousand śrāvaka disciples.
Good son, those bodhisattvas...
All of them possessed vast, immeasurable, and boundless eloquence and wisdom.
At that time, that Buddha compiled one hundred koṭis of difficult questions and addressed the entire assembly of bodhisattvas, saying:
"Who among you in this great assembly is capable of being courageous and generating the supramundane mind of a Great Man,
[to withstand] my hundred koṭis of accumulated hardships?"
Regarding how long it would take to explain each of these difficult points individually by means of hundreds of thousands of koṭis of Dharma gates, at that time,
a certain bodhisattva in this assembly came forward and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"I shall be able to explain it in a single day," some bodhisattvas said;
others said, "I shall be able to explain it in seven days and nights";
some said a fortnight, and others said a month.
Regarding those who say it is six months or one year,
at that time there was a bodhisattva in the assembly named Smṛtimatī.
He stepped forward and addressed the Buddha Śrīrakṣita, saying:
"Blessed One, without rising from my seat and without changing my posture,
I shall be able to resolve all such difficulties before the Tathāgata and the great assembly."
Having spoken these words, at that very moment he let out a lion’s roar and manifested his sovereign power,
causing the trichiliocosm to quake in six ways.
He emitted a great radiance that illuminated the world universally, causing all beings to awaken. At that time,
the great assembly and the gods of the Four Great Kings, the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven,
the Suyāma Heaven, the Tuṣita Heaven, the Nirmāṇarati Heaven, and the Paranirmita-vaśavartin Heaven were present.
Even unto the gods of the Śuddhāvāsa heavens,
all were awakened by the light and assembled together;
as did the nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, humans, and non-humans.
Householders and renunciants of immeasurable varieties,
having been awakened by the light, all came to the assembly and sat down;
thus it was accomplished in the span of a single kṣaṇa, before even a brief moment had passed.
He caused this site of enlightenment to be ten thousand yojanas in length and breadth,
perfectly equal on all sides. At that time,
the Bodhisattva Cintamati saw that this great assembly had already gathered like clouds.
By the power of merit and the power of wisdom;
by the power of mindfulness, the power of the Dharma, and the power of dhāraṇī;
by the power of sublime eloquence, the power of great fearlessness, and the majestic power of the Buddha.
By this power, having heard the hundred koṭis of difficult [teachings] gathered therein,
they shall receive and uphold them before those Tathāgatas and the great assembly.
Within each of the aforementioned difficulties, he provides explanations through hundreds of thousands of koṭis of Dharma gates;
these are complete and flawless, incapable of being refuted or destroyed,
and accord with the various categories of beings according to their respective faculties.
He expounded it in an uninterrupted succession,
analyzing the words, phrases, and meanings with subtle precision;
as he taught this Dharma, his voice pervaded the entire trichiliocosm.
From the Heaven of the Four Great Kings up to all the gods of the Pure Abodes,
they all heard his voice and understood its meaning.
These hosts of devas spoke these words:
"How extraordinary and rare it is that the Bodhisattva Smṛtimatī is able to act in such a way!
Son of good family, while the Bodhisattva Smṛtimatī was expounding this Dharma,
there were sixty thousand koṭis of nayutas of sentient beings in the assembly."
They resolved their minds upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
Forty thousand *koṭi-nayuta* bodhisattvas attained the patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).
At that time, the Tathāgata Śrī-rakṣita—
He praised the Bodhisattva Smṛtimat, saying, "Excellent, excellent! You are a true mahāsattva.
Then Śākyamuni Buddha addressed the Bodhisattva Abhayapratibhāna, saying:
"Good son, what do you think?
Was the Bodhisattva Mindfulness at that time someone else?
It was none other than the present Bodhisattva Prajñākūṭa."
Good son, because this bodhisattva possesses such immeasurable eloquence and supremely exalted wisdom,
he is named Prajñāśikhara (Peak of Wisdom).
Therefore, through the eloquence and wisdom of the Bodhisattvas,
this Mother Prajñāpāramitā— the Dharma-gate of the adornment of the activities of Prajñā— has appeared in the world.
When the Buddha had finished speaking these words,
at that time there were immeasurable, innumerable, incalculable, ineffable,
and unfathomable great bodhisattva-mahāsattvas of various buddha-fields throughout the ten directions, all possessing great majestic virtue.
And there were immeasurable devas of great majesty and power,
as well as nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, humans, and non-humans.
The entire great assembly— monks, nuns, laymen, and laywomen—
heard the Buddha teach this Dharma gate of the adornment of the activity of Prajñā, the Mother Prajñāpāramitā.
They leaped for joy with great delight,
offering various kinds of flowers, perfumes, ointments, and powdered incense,
as well as necklaces, garlands, sashes, garments, banners, pennants, and parasols.
And with various kinds of music— namely, the *konghou*, the *pipa*,
drums, flutes, songs, and wind instruments—
with these exquisite musical sounds they made offerings to the Buddha and the great assembly.
Immeasurable sentient beings resolved their minds upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
Thirty-six *koṭi-nayuta* of bodhisattvas all attained the patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).

Chapter Nine: The Ritual Procedures for the Merits of the Dhāraṇī.
At that time, there was a bodhisattva-mahāsattva within the assembly.
The one named Guhyapati Vajrapāṇi rose from his seat, bared his right shoulder,
knelt with his right knee on the ground, and prostrated at the feet of the Buddha.
With palms joined in reverence, he addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One, regarding the gateways of dhāraṇī as spoken by the Buddha,
it is thus with all such gateways of dhāraṇī."
What is called the gateway of dhāraṇīs?
Which dhāraṇī can serve as the mother of all dhāraṇīs?
Which dhāraṇī is universally able to bring benefit and happiness to all sentient beings?
"What dhāraṇī can cause sentient beings to swiftly attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi?
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Guhyapati Vajrapāṇi, saying:
Excellent, excellent, son of good family!
You are able to ask the Tathāgata about such a profound meaning.
I shall now analyze and explain it for you.
"Good son, there is a dhāraṇī that is the mother of all dhāraṇīs;
it is named 'The Sovereign Who Protects the Realm.'"
If there is a bodhisattva who receives, maintains, and realizes this dhāraṇī,
their body will become identical to a wish-fulfilling jewel;
all sentient beings who see them will have their aspirations fulfilled.
One will also be able to swiftly attain unsurpassed bodhi.
At that time, having heard these words, Vajrapāṇi addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Excellent, World-Honored One! I pray that you will explain this dhāraṇī for me."
Having heard even a small portion of its powers, procedures, and rules,
we shall diligently practice them and will thereby be able to realize this dhāraṇī.
The Buddha addressed the Lord of Secrets, saying:
"Good son, the World-Honored One Vairocana has already extensively proclaimed this for Śakra, the Lord of Devas, and the assembly of devas in the Akaniṣṭha Heaven."
Now, beneath this Bodhi tree at the Vajra-maṇḍala,
for the sake of all kings and for you,
I shall briefly explain this gateway of dhāraṇī; you should listen attentively.
Noble son, the mother of dhāraṇīs is the syllable Oṃ. Why is this?
Because the combination of three syllables constitutes the syllable Oṃ.
That is to say: A, U, and Maṃ. Regarding the syllable A:
it signifies the bodhicitta, it signifies the meaning of all dharma-gates, it signifies the meaning of non-duality, and it also signifies the fruit of all dharmas.
It also carries the meaning of "nature" and the meaning of "sovereignty," just as a king has sovereign control over black and white, good and evil, according to his will.
Furthermore, it carries the meaning of "Dharmakāya."
The second, the syllable *u*, signifies the Reward Body (*saṃbhogakāya*).
The third, the syllable *maṅ*, signifies the Emanation Body (*nirmāṇakāya*).
By combining these three syllables together, they form the syllable *oṃ*.
Because it encompasses boundless meanings, it serves as the foremost of all dhāraṇīs;
it acts as the precursor to the meanings of all syllables,
and is the very source from which all phenomena arise.
All Buddhas of the three periods of time have attained bodhi by contemplating this syllable;
therefore, it is the mother of all dhāraṇīs,
and all bodhisattvas are born from it.
All Buddhas appear from this; it is the place where all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas assemble for the gathering of dhāraṇīs,
just as a king dwells within his royal city.
Attended by ministers and aides and surrounded by palace women,
whether he goes out on tours of inspection or returns to the imperial residence,
he is invariably escorted by the four divisions of the army in a procession of tens of millions.
It is like when one speaks only of the king’s dwelling, his coming, and his going;
although other matters are not mentioned, nothing is excluded.
This dhāraṇī is also just like this.
Although it is said that not a single syllable is left uncomprised,
at that time the Lord of Secrets, Vajrapāṇi,
again addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One..."
As the Buddha has taught, all Buddhas abide eternally in the samādhi of equality and regard all sentient beings as their only child.
Why then do you now speak only of being the protector of the realm?
There are those who are impoverished, orphaned, destitute, and suffering;
they have no support, no refuge, no protector, and no guardian.
Why do you not take pity on them and protect them?
At that time, the Tathāgata, the unsurpassed tamer, addressed the Lord of Secrets, Vajrapāṇi, saying:
"Son of good family, listen attentively, listen attentively; I shall speak for you."
The Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, do not fail to abide in the samādhi of equanimity.
By virtue of this equanimity, they protect kings.
Good son, it is like a skilled physician who sees a small infant.
His body was afflicted by illness such that he could not withstand medical treatment;
he therefore took excellent medicine and had his mother consume it,
whereby the power of the medicine she ingested reached her milk.
Just as the child’s drinking of the milk removes all illnesses,
so too it is with the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas;
out of compassion for all beings, they protect the kings of nations.
If one protects the king, one obtains seven kinds of supreme benefits. What are these seven?
Namely, if one is able to protect the king, it is equivalent to protecting the crown prince of the kingdom.
If one protects the crown prince, one protects the great ministers;
if one protects the great ministers, one protects the common people;
if one protects the common people, one protects the treasury.
If one protects the treasury, one protects the fourfold army;
if one protects the fourfold army, one protects neighboring states.
If one can do all this, everything will be at peace.
Good son, for this reason, the king serves all sentient beings as the sun,
as the moon, as a lamp, as eyes, and as father and mother.
If sentient beings were without eyes, without lamps, without the sun, without the moon, and without father and mother, their lives could not be sustained.
If there were no king, it would be impossible to establish stability.
Furthermore, son of good family, it is like a great dragon pond:
as long as the dragon dwells therein, the water is always full.
The turtles, crocodiles, fish, and turtles—all aquatic creatures—are at peace.
Yet, when the dragon departs, the water immediately dries up;
all those belonging to the watery realm perish without exception.
It is the same for kings: if various kings uphold this dharani-gate,
they can cause immeasurable and innumerable sentient beings [to attain liberation].
Now, you enjoy peace and happiness, long preserving your noble status;
when the body perishes and life ends, you shall be reborn in a happy realm.
Thus it is known that the sovereign is well able to close the gates to the evil destinies.
He reveals the correct path to nirvāṇa for humans and devas;
therefore, I have specifically taught the protection of kings.
At that time, the Blessed One again addressed the Lord of Secrets, Vajrapāṇi, saying:
"Noble son, as to the rules and procedures you have asked about,

The ritual rules for the procedure of the Great Maṇḍala of the Vajra City are now explained.
Noble son, when one wishes to establish a maṇḍala,
the Vajrācārya first selects the site, whether it be a mountain or a wilderness.
If that land possesses various fruit-bearing trees,
soft grasses, and fragrant flowers, and is level and delightful;
or if it contains pure ponds, clear pools, and flowing springs filled to the brim.
The Buddhas have praised that one may establish a maṇḍala site by the side of a great river or near a dragon pond adorned with lotuses—
namely, blue utpala flowers, kumuda flowers, padma flowers, and puṇḍarīka flowers.
Furthermore, there were ducks, geese, mandarin ducks, white cranes, peacocks,
parrots, śārikas, kokilas, and other such wondrous bird kings,
all soaring and gathering together in majestic adornment.
Or it may be a place where Buddhas, bodhisattvas, pratyekabuddhas,
and śrāvakas have formerly dwelt— a quiet and praiseworthy location protected by devas, nāgas, and others.
And in other cities, towns, and villages; in monasteries, houses, halls, and pavilions;
at stupas, shrines, and cow-pens;
and within secluded gardens and empty dwellings.
One may also establish this maṇḍala; however,
if there is no location that accords with the prescribed dharma,
one need not further discriminate, but may install it wherever is convenient.
One should simply construct the maṇḍala according to the mind.
Furthermore, son of good family, when the ācārya selects the ground,
if that ground contains sand, stones, tiles, rubble, tree roots, stumps, hair, body hair, nails, teeth, husks, flour, ashes, charcoal, bones, graves, snake dens, or ant holes;
Such sites as these are unfit for establishing a maṇḍala ground.
Once the site has been selected, the ācārya should choose an auspicious day and lunar mansion (tithi-nakṣatra).
At the time of early dawn, during an auspicious moment, [he should proceed].
Prostrating with the five limbs touching the ground, they paid homage at the feet of the Tathāgata.
According to their respective capacities and the breadth or narrowness of their resolve, they established the ritual mandalas;
those of the greatest extent measured one thousand yojanas.
Or again, measuring nine hundred, seven hundred, five hundred,
three hundred, one hundred, or one yojana;
or measuring seven cubits, five cubits, or three cubits.
Whether it be the measure of one cubit, or one palm, or even the measure of a single fingernail,
I shall now explain the ritual procedure for constructing the supreme maṇḍala of the Vajra City.
It should be constructed as a square with one gate opened on each face;
above, a decorative archway (toraṇa) should be installed for adornment.
Each side shall measure thirty-two *vitasti* in length.
The surrounding railings are painted in three tiers with twelve corners,
adorned with flower garlands fashioned from various jewels.
In the center of the maṇḍala, one should paint an image of the Tathāgata Vairocana.
Also depict the four Pāramitā Bodhisattvas; in each of the four directions,
depict one of the four Buddhas, each accompanied by four Bodhisattvas,
or alternatively, place their seed-syllables.
Each and every bodhisattva has one koṭi-nayuta of bodhisattvas as their retinue;
next, twelve offering bodhisattvas are established.
In the outermost enclosure are stationed the ten deities of the directions.
Each of these deities has its own mantra.
The mantras of the five Buddhas have already been explained above.

Having completed the arrangement of all [elements] according to this sequence of ritual procedures,

First, one should bestow the samaya precepts as a preliminary guide.
Then, after the consecration has been performed,
one should subsequently instruct them in the recitation of the mantra.
With lips and teeth joined and the tongue moving slightly, do not allow sounds to escape.
According to one's capacity, keep count and establish a regular limit for the duration of time.
One must resolutely set the goal of attaining the supreme state.
If one does not achieve results, one shall not depart from the maṇḍala.
Thus, one should strive with such diligence to seek siddhi.
I shall now explain the distinctions regarding the use of the *maṇi* (beads).
And he spoke in verse:
"For the Buddha Family, which perpetuates the lineage of the Buddhas, One should use bodhi seeds;
for the Vajra Family, One may also use vajra seeds."
Within the Ratna family, use gold and other precious gems as beads, with pearls for the rosary; this is praised by all Buddhas.
Within the Padma family, use lotus seeds as the primary [beads].
The Beads within the Karma Family: The Method for Counting Beads of the Five Families through Various Combined Practices.
For the Buddha Family, use the thumb and the index finger; for the Vajra Family, use the middle finger.
For the Ratna family, use the ring finger; for the Padma family, join the three [fingers] and support with the fourth [finger] of Karma. All should be used at the first joint.
A golden bead yields double the merit, while a pearl obtains ten million.
The *vajra* and the lotus-seed bead (*bodhi-ja*)— if one holds these, they bring hundreds of thousands of koṭis of merit; likewise,
the combined beads bring immeasurable merit and adornment, as taught by all the Buddhas.
There are one hundred and eight beads; they restrain the distracted mind from wandering.
This is the seal of Vairocana. One should fix one’s mindfulness upon the tip of the nose to eliminate afflictions and the like, thereby increasing samādhi.
One should contemplate the deity, diligently performing homa and recitation;
first visualizing the pure lunar disc, one imagines oneself seated within that wheel,
emitting blazing, radiant light, with a celestial glow adorning one's own body.
The Buddhas of the present in the ten directions, adorned with five-colored blue and white pearls,
are most worthy of veneration; constantly contemplating them as they abide before me,
as numerous as the atoms of three thousandfold worlds, they all enter into my body.
My body is equal to space; through the *śāntika* offering, one visualizes the Bodhisattva’s joy.
This increasing *homa* causes the wrathful deity to enter my body, whereby all internal and external enemies are extinguished.
The Bodhisattva Rūpavati enters the yoga of the internal homa of the visualization of the signs of loving-kindness and affection. Thus spoke the Buddhas of the past.

"Noble son, listen attentively, listen attentively!
This single-syllable dhāraṇī gateway is the mother of all dhāraṇīs."
It has infinite koṭis of dharanī-doors as its retinue.
If one contemplates this dhāraṇī,
infinite koṭis of samādhis will manifest before them.
All Buddhas of the past and present have attained anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi by means of contemplating this dhāraṇī.
"Good son, I now briefly explain a single syllable for the sake of all kings, so that they may receive and uphold it.

In a single instant, five kinds of samādhis will manifest before you,
and all afflictions will no longer arise.
Son of good family, this is the Great Vajra City Maṇḍala.
All its functions are inconceivable.
If there are good men or good women who are able to enter this maṇḍala, [they shall attain these benefits].
This constitutes having already seen all Buddhas and all Bodhisattvas.
Why is this? Because this maṇḍala is the place where all Buddhas and holy sages assemble to discuss the profound Dharma.
If one is able to enter [this state],
then one will be certified and protected by all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas,
becoming a true child of the Dharma-kings, the Tathāgatas.
He is able to act as the father of all sentient beings;
he continues the lineage of the Triple Gem, severs the three evil destinies,
opens the gates for humans and devas, and abides on the stage of non-retrogression.
Having distanced himself from all transgressions, he attains the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment, the ten powers, and the fearlessnesses;
with these as his ornaments, he adorns himself.
Good son, wherever that city or town may be—
Wherever this maṇḍala is upheld and practiced,
it shall be protected by the Four Great Heavenly Kings, Śakra, the various devas, and the eight classes of beings;
in such lands, there will always be no famine, nor will there be enemies or adversaries.
All people and livestock were free from calamities and epidemics;
the minor kings of various states admired his virtue and submitted to him,
so that among all kings he was preeminent and foremost.
They will remain far removed from all sorrow, affliction, and distress;

they will delight in practicing generosity and be able to cultivate patience.
Endowed with wisdom and delighting in wholesome dharmas,

There is not even the slightest dharma that can be diminished,

it is also not for the sake of the arising of even the slightest dharma.

nor is it for the sake of the exhaustion of even a slight dharma;
nor is it for the sake of even a slight tranquility.

nor is it for the sake of the quiescent nature of all sentient beings;
nor is it for the sake of being free from fear.
Nor is it for the sake of the extinction of the body;
nor is it for the sake of the extinction of speech;
nor is it for the sake of the extinction of mind.
He does not practice patience toward such phenomena as these.

One observes with mastery that the nature of speech is empty and cannot be grasped;
its essence is quiescent and has no place of abiding.

The stage of wisdom is unshakable; this dharma of the dhāraṇī is taught.
Countless bodhisattvas who seek unsurpassed enlightenment obtain this dhāraṇī, and for them, enlightenment is not difficult to attain.
All Buddhas of the ten directions, Teaching the Dharma to benefit sentient beings,
Attain this most supreme illumination, And their eloquence is never interrupted;
Having attained this true dharma of illumination, Their preaching of the Dharma is never in vain.
Knowing the distinctions of the body-faculty’s bliss,
immeasurable sentient beings joyfully abide in this Dharma of true illumination; turning the most supreme wheel,
they liberate sentient beings from the source of suffering and dwell securely in the most supreme vehicle.
Even if one were to praise this efficacy and these boundless merits for *nayuta* billions of kalpas,

At that time, the Lord of Secrets, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Vajrapāṇi...
Having heard this, he was filled with joy and exultation; he immediately rose, joined his palms,
and circumambulated the World-Honored One to the right one hundred thousand times.
They returned to their original seats and gazed upon the Buddha with reverence.
When the Buddha spoke this chapter on the merits of the dhāraṇī,

Immeasurable and innumerable sentient beings resolved their minds upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.

10. Chapter Ten: The Prophecy of King Ajātaśatru. Chapter Ten: The Prophecy of King Ajātaśatru.
At that time, within the assembly, Ajātaśatru, the King of Magadha, rose from his seat,
bared his right shoulder, knelt with his right knee on the ground,
and joined his palms in reverent salutation.
Prostrating at the Buddha’s feet, he addressed the Buddha,
saying: “World-Honored One, Tathāgata, you are now beneath the Bodhi tree in my land,
preaching dhāraṇīs and maṇḍalas.”
Since there are already such immeasurable merits [in this land],
why is it that in the kingdom of Magadha the wind and rain are not timely, and drought and flooding are not regulated?
Famines follow one after another, and hostile enemies invade and harass us;
epidemics and calamities are beyond measure, numbering in the hundreds of thousands.
We only pray that the World-Honored One will sever the net of our doubts.
At that time, the World-Honored One praised Ajātaśatru, saying:
"Great King, excellent, excellent! It is well that you have asked about this meaning;
it will bring great benefit to all sentient beings in future ages."
"Great King, listen attentively, listen attentively, and reflect upon it well.
I shall analyze and explain it for you.
Great King, it is as the King has said."
If there should ever be famine, hostile enemies, and the like within my kingdom,
this Dhāraṇī of the Sovereign Who Guards the Realm has sixteen koṭi-nayuta dhāraṇīs as its retinue.
This Great Vajra City Maṇḍala has three thousand five hundred maṇḍalas as its retinue;
yet all of them take faith as their fundamental basis.
With profound prajñā as its precursor,
adorned with the great bodhicitta and great compassion—
O Great King, all wholesome dharmas arise from this dhāraṇī.
All evil deeds have a lack of faith in cause and effect as their root.
Great King, you now do not believe in cause and effect;
you are addicted to the pleasures of the five desires like a violent gale.
The wind of their faith and bodhicitta blows away all their great compassion and dhāraṇīs, so that they vanish entirely.
Great King, although you now possess eyes and ears, you are like one who is deaf and blind.
One does not hear thunderclaps, nor does one see the sun and moon.
Why is this? You do not even hear the name of your own king, let alone any other sound.
What is meant by the name "King" (Rāja)?
The term "King" carries the meaning of *rāja*.
As for the sound of the syllable *ra*, it is said to be the sound of suffering and affliction.
Wailing, grieving, and lamenting with cries for one who has no master, no refuge, and no protector,
the king should comfort them by speaking thus:
"Do not distress yourselves."
"I am your master; I shall protect and guard you.
Wiping away his tears, he nurtured him with compassion.
He said that the sound of the syllable *ja* signifies the supreme meaning.
This is the meaning of wealth and nobility; this is the meaning of sovereignty.
This is the meaning of excellence; this is the meaning of valor.
This is the meaning of physical perfection; this is the meaning of wisdom.
This is that which can destroy all the pride, self-exaltation, and contempt for others held by sentient beings.
Great King, you now do not believe in cause and effect,
and you have drawn near to the evil friend Devadatta.
He killed his biological father, imprisoned him, and subjected him to hunger and thirst;
though he did not die from these deprivations, the father’s feet were severed.
Furthermore, he caused Devadatta to draw blood from the Buddha’s body.
"You have caused a schism in the Saṃgha and further released the intoxicated,
wicked elephant Dhanapāla to trample the Tathāgata.
Great King, you now possess yet another most grievous sin."
This refers to plucking out and destroying the pure Dharma-eye of all sentient beings;
severing the gate of the Buddhas' true and correct Dharma;
and closing the door to nirvana for humans and devas.
He revealed the three miserable realms and the evil destinies of birth and death.
Why was this? Because you were a king who went out to stroll in the gardens, having prepared ten thousand or twenty thousand elephant carriages.
He appointed two to three hundred thousand charioteers and cavalrymen as his retinue.
Furthermore, he used the fat and blood of the common people to coat his elephants and horses.
When King Ajātaśatru heard these words, he...
He addressed the Buddha, saying, "World-Honored One,
as I reflect upon this now, I do not recall ever having used the blood and fat of the common people to anoint elephants and horses.
World-Honored One, why do you speak in such a manner?"
The Buddha said, "Great King, regarding the elephants and horses of the king,
each one is smeared with fragrant paste made by blending saffron,
dragon’s brain (agarwood), sandalwood, aloeswood, and musk."
Such fragrances as these all originate from the common people;
yet the taxation of the commoners is like pressing sesame seeds for oil,
such that the wealth of a thousand households is exhausted by their poverty and suffering.
It cannot even suffice to cover the cost of a single elephant;
therefore, one should know that the blood and fat of the common people are very easy to obtain,
whereas such things as this incense are extremely difficult to acquire.
"Great King, if you have doubts, you should personally inspect all the prisons yourself.
The common people suffer there as if in the great hells.
Your Majesty has forcibly seized all the wealth and property of the people to bestow upon the wealthy and noble."
Consequently, the wealthy became increasingly extravagant,
while those who were destitute grew ever more impoverished.
Causing all the poor, the orphaned, the widowed,
and those suffering in misery— who have no place to set foot—
to seek ordination; such persons shall have neither preceptors nor ācāryas.
Having donned the *kāṣāya* robe yet not receiving the prohibitive precepts, you dwell without the Dharma;
this causes all sentient beings to feel contempt and have no desire to see or hear you.
You are truly, O Great King, plucking out the Eye of the Dharma and severing the extinction of the Buddha-dharma.
It closes the path for humans and devas and opens the gates to the evil realms;
therefore, I say that since Your Majesty has not even heard your own name,
by what cause and condition could you possibly obtain the empowerment and protection of this dhāraṇī’s spiritual power?
"Great King, I shall now relate an ancient causal account.
You, O King, should contemplate it with care and understand its meaning.
Great King, in a time long past, there appeared a Buddha in the world."
He was named Kāśyapa, the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidyācaraṇasaṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Puruṣadamyasārathi, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, Buddha, Bhagavān.
That Buddha taught the Dharma that is excellent in the beginning, excellent in the middle,
and excellent in the end, revealing the holy life (*brahmacarya*). At that time,
there was a king named Kṛkin who conceived deep and pure faith in that Tathāgata.
In the middle of the night, the king had two dreams.
In the first, he saw ten monkeys;
nine of these monkeys seized and disordered all the people—wives, concubines, men, and women—within the city.
They plundered food and drink,
destroyed household goods,
and defiled them with impurities.
Only one monkey was content in mind;
he sat peacefully upon a tree, undisturbing the inhabitants of the village.
At that time, nine monkeys conspired together to harass and disturb this contented one.
They created various obstacles and drove him out from the assembly of monkeys.
As for the second dream, he saw a white elephant.
It is like a great mountain standing at the gate of a sovereign;
it has mouths at both its head and tail, all of which consume water and grass.
Although it constantly drinks and eats, its body is perpetually emaciated.
When the king awoke, he was seized with great terror.
He summoned diviners and physiognomists to interpret his dream.
The diviners said to the king, "The nine monkeys are none other than the nine kings."
The one who was content is none other than the Great King.
These nine kings were of one mind in usurping the Great King’s precious throne.
As for the elephant with two mouths, it represents these nine kings who consume both their own cities and districts as well as the kingdom of the Great King.
Upon hearing these words, the king was struck with such terror that his hair stood on end, yet his mind remained undecided.
Desiring to see the Buddha in order to sever his doubts,
he immediately commanded his attendants to prepare various kinds of offerings.
With single-minded devotion, he proceeded to the abode of Kāśyapa Buddha. Upon arrival, he prostrated himself,
presented various offerings to the Tathāgata,
and with body bowed and palms joined, addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Blessed One, last night I had an inauspicious dream; I only pray that the Blessed One will explain it for me so as to sever the net of my doubts.
Then the king related his dream in detail to the Buddha.
The Buddha said, "Great King, that which you have dreamed does not concern you;
do not give rise to anxiety or fear.
Listen attentively, O King, and I shall explain it for you."
This is the future world of the five turbidities and evil ages.
A Buddha will appear there named Śākyamuni;
these are the characteristics of the remaining Dharma after his parinirvāṇa.
"Great King, those ten monkeys were the ten kinds of disciples of that Buddha.
The king addressed the Buddha, saying, "World-Honored One, what are the names of those ten kinds of disciples of that Buddha?"
Kāśyapa Buddha said: "First, there is the poor man who becomes a śramaṇa out of fear of being unable to survive;
second, there is the slave who becomes a śramaṇa out of fear;
third, there is one who becomes a śramaṇa out of fear of debt."
Fourth, they become śramaṇas seeking out faults in the Buddha-dharma.
Fifth, they become śramaṇas for the sake of overcoming others.
Sixth, they become śramaṇas for the sake of fame.
Seventh, one becomes a śramaṇa for the sake of being reborn in heaven.
Eighth, one becomes a śramaṇa for the sake of gain and honor.
Ninth, one becomes a śramaṇa out of a desire to seek royal power in the future.
One becomes a śramaṇa through ten kinds of genuine mind.
At that time, the great king addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One, what are the characteristics of these ten types of śramaṇas?"
That Buddha replied, "Great King, those who become śramaṇas out of poverty or fear of being unable to survive are many among the sentient beings who do not believe in cause and effect,
and who greedily seek wealth and treasures while mutually encroaching upon and seizing one another."
Consequently, they moved Heaven and Earth so that the rains did not fall at their proper times;
the five grains failed to ripen and were insufficient to meet official taxes.
Pressed by hunger and poverty, people sold their sons and daughters.
Having no one to rely upon, he donned a discarded *kāṣāya* robe hanging from a tree;
he shaved his own beard and hair to assume the appearance of a śramaṇa,
having neither an *ācārya* nor an *upādhyāya*.
Lacking precepts and lacking the Dharma, these pseudo-śramaṇas practice all manner of evil dharmas for a long time;
yet upon entering a monastery, they claim of themselves: "I am a master of discipline," "a master of meditation," "a master of the Dharma," or "a venerable one (bhadanta)."
Sitting at the head of the assembly, he said to the other monks,
"All of you are my disciples; [you have been received] into the households of lay devotees, noble clansmen, and brahmins."
Moving about and following others, they frequently commit transgressions.
This is called the first type of poor person who becomes a śramaṇa out of fear of being unable to support themselves.
Great King, what is meant by one who becomes a śramaṇa out of fear of servitude?
That is to say, lowly slaves and servants think to themselves:
"How can I endure being driven and commanded by others for the duration of this life?
To flee and leave the household life is the second [cause]."
"Great King, what is meant by becoming a śramaṇa out of fear of debt?
It refers to sentient beings who have public or private debts and liabilities;
because the interest has grown so great, they are unable to repay them."
Having been thus coerced, he fled and went forth into homelessness; this is the third.
Great King, what is meant by becoming a śramaṇa while seeking faults in the Buddha-dharma?
It is said that the various non-Buddhists, having conceived feelings of jealousy, gathered together to deliberate:
"Who among us possesses intelligence, keen faculties,
and eloquent wisdom such that they may enter the Buddha's Dharma and study all its mundane and supramundane teachings?"
Having scrutinized their right and wrong, they shall return to our assembly and,
before the king, ministers, and elders,
raise the banner of debate to expose their faults.
To destroy, ruin, and annihilate the true Dharma of that Buddha—
this is called the fourth.
Great King, what is meant by becoming a śramaṇa for the sake of seeking victory over others?
That is to say, there may be sentient beings who, upon hearing that a certain person has donned the robes and shaved his head,
possesses great skill and mastery of the Tripitaka,
feel a burning distress in their hearts and immediately leave the household life to study the sutras, vinaya, and abhidharma.
To cultivate all wholesome dharmas with the desire to surpass others—
this is called the fifth.
Great King, what is meant by becoming a śramaṇa for the sake of reputation?
That is to say, there may be someone who reflects to themselves:
"If I remain at home, I shall have no reputation;
I ought to shave my hair, don the robes, and go forth into homelessness."
To diligently study and gain extensive learning, to receive and uphold the prohibitive precepts,
and to sit in meditation and enter samādhi amidst the great assembly so that others may know one's name— this is the sixth.
Great King, what is meant by becoming a śramaṇa for the sake of seeking rebirth in heaven?
It refers to someone who hears that among the various devas there is long life and happiness,
yet thinks, "I lack the means to attain birth there."
He then shaved his hair, donned the dyed robes, and left the household life.
He cultivated wholesome dharmas with the sole wish to be reborn in heaven;
this is the seventh [cause].
"Great King, what is meant by becoming a śramaṇa for the sake of gain and offerings?
It refers to someone who, having already possessed wealth and treasures, seeks an even superior station,
obtaining a fine vihāra with courtyards and exquisite floral decorations."
One may dwell at ease and enjoy all the wealth and property belonging to oneself and others;
this is called the eighth.
Great King, why is it that one becomes a śramaṇa out of a desire to seek the position of a future sovereign?
It refers to those sentient beings who, seeing that kings are sovereign,
honored, wealthy, noble, and at ease,
conceive a longing for such status and consequently seek to leave the household life.
"May I, through these roots of goodness I have cultivated, be born to occupy the royal throne.
This is called the ninth.
Great King, what is meant by becoming a śramaṇa out of a sincere heart?
That is to say, there are sentient beings who, though born into the clans of kṣatriyas, great ministers, or brahmins,
or into the wealthy and noble families of elders, householders, or merchant lords, are in the prime of their youth and possess beautiful appearances.
Observing that all wealth, beauty, nobility,
and glory are like floating clouds, bubbles, illusions, or flashes of lightning— arising and ceasing without remaining—
they consequently give rise to weary detachment and resolve to attain bodhicitta.
He renounced all kinsmen, friends, and precious wealth;
leaving the household life to seek the Way, he upheld the moral precepts,
studied the Dharma, and practiced dhyāna with unremitting diligence.
Whatever one does is solely for the sake of sentient beings,
seeking only the fruit of unsurpassed bodhi;
this is called the tenth true mind with which one becomes a śramaṇa.
"Great King, you should know that this corresponds to what you saw in your dream:
the monkey who was modest in desire and contented,
dwelling alone upon a tree without disturbing others."
These are the true śramaṇas within the legacy dharma of Śākyamuni Tathāgata.
As for those nine monkeys who disturbed the multitude and conspired together to expel one monkey: [they represent those who reject the true teaching].
These are the first nine types of śramaṇas within the legacy of the Tathāgata Śākyamuni;
because they lack the true qualities of a śramaṇa, they are collectively termed "semblance śramaṇas.
Practicing evil deeds together, they collectively ostracize a single authentic śramaṇa from their midst.
"Great King, this wicked śramaṇa has violated the precepts and committed evil deeds;
he has defiled all noble families and now addresses himself to the king,
the ministers, and the high officials."
The treatise states that they slander true śramaṇas, speaking recklessly of right and wrong, claiming: "This is an evil person who has broken the precepts and performs wicked deeds;
he should not dwell together with me, a bhikṣu who upholds the precepts, nor should he participate in the poṣadha or the recitation of the precepts."
Furthermore, they shall not dwell together in the same monastery or reside within the same kingdom or town.
They shall attribute all evil deeds to those who are true śramaṇas,
thereby deceiving kings, ministers, and officials.
Consequently, he ordered that all authentic śramaṇas be driven out of the kingdom's borders,
while those who had broken the precepts were allowed to roam at will and became intimate with the king, ministers, and high officials.
Great King, all the teachings of that Tathāgata Śākyamuni cannot be undermined even in the slightest degree by any celestial Māras, non-Buddhists, evil persons,
or seers possessing the five supernatural powers.
And these evil śramaṇas, along with their names and appearances,
shall all be utterly destroyed until not a single one remains.
It would be as if Mount Sumeru were used as fuel, having exhausted all the grasses and trees within the three thousandfold world system.
Though burned for a long duration, it remains entirely unharmed;
yet if the fires of the kalpa were to arise from within it,
they would further burn it away until not even a trace of ash remained.
At that time, Kāśyapa Buddha spoke these verses again for King Kṛkī:
"Out of fear of not being able to survive, one shaves their head; claiming to have attained honor and sustenance, one seeks to escape poverty."
Distracted, arrogant, and preoccupied with great wealth, their inner nature is hollow and unsubstantial like a reed;
deluded and intoxicated by the retinue of afflictions, such people remain far removed from Great Bodhi—
like one who carries pure gold yet casts it away to joyfully shoulder a burden of firewood.
Entangled by fame and profit, laziness increases; as laziness increases, pure faith is extinguished.
Once pure faith is extinguished, there is no pure precept; without precepts, one cuts off the fruits of humans and devas.
Though one dwells in peace within a secluded forest, it was originally sought for the sake of fame, profit, and acquaintances.
Far removed from the mind of ethical discipline, meditative concentration, and wisdom, They rely solely on the wealthy, the noble, and their kinsmen;
Seeking for themselves the three evil realms and the eight difficult conditions, Born into poverty, lowliness, or remote borderlands—
It is like one born blind arriving at an island of jewels, Who takes up stones and casts away the wish-fulfilling gem.
Through heedlessness and dissipation, they increase their competitiveness; having abandoned ethical conduct and right mindfulness, they fall into the most terrifying Avīci hell.
Even after passing through koṭis of kalpas, they find it difficult to be liberated;
yet their minds constantly seek fame and reputation, while their bodies and speech outwardly profess the pursuit of bodhi.
Like a bird flying through the sky that encounters a fierce wind, They are cast down into the great ocean of suffering of birth and death.
Those of meager merit who indulge in and become attached to celestial maidens, And who break their precepts, abandoning the causes of wholesome karma—
The Buddha’s teachings show that they are all consumed by the fire of desire, Just as Mount Sumeru meets the fires at the end of an eon.
Lacking the flavor of enlightenment, they seek only profit; constantly preaching to others that they seek the bodhicitta, they do not abide in liberation themselves.
Like a monkey that has found a hard coconut, the Tathāgata, for the sake of seeking the jewel of the True Dharma, threw himself down from a precipice into a pit of great fire.
Having heard the Dharma, they practice in accordance with it; They treat enemies and kin with equality, providing compassionate relief to all.
How can one hear of the Buddha’s manifold virtues And yet not give rise to even a single thought of joy?
Clinging only to what is non-Dharma and distancing oneself from Bodhi— It is like a person born blind showing the way to others.
After Kāśyapa Tathāgata had spoken these verses,
he further addressed King Kṛkin, saying:
"Great King, as for the two white elephants you saw at the gate of the royal palace in your dream— "
Those who constantly eat water and grass and whose bodies are emaciated and thin are likewise not engaged in the affairs of kings; rather,
they are the ministers, officials, and magistrates within the degenerate world of the five turbidities during the bequeathed Dharma of Śākyamuni Tathāgata, who do not believe in cause and effect.
Above, they receive the imperial favor, glory, and emoluments of kings and emperors;
below, they unreasonably pursue the wealth of the common people.
Although they greedily seek these things, they remain largely impoverished.
Taxation was without measure, and the myriad people were impoverished.
They traded away their descendants and their family estates until all were exhausted;
they then fled to temples to shave their heads and become monks, yet even the temples fell into ruin and desolation.
Many wicked bhikṣus lacked the ground for generating the resolve [for awakening].
Consequently, they abandoned the path and went forth as heterodox practitioners under teachers such as Roga and Gayā, who held various views of eternalism and nihilism.
Due to these causes and conditions of false views, both teacher and disciples fell and entered hell.
Furthermore, they open the gates of hell for many people,
leading them on by mutual enticement to rush toward the three evil realms;
they close off the paths of humans and devas, leaving no means for liberation.
"Great King, you should know that these two dreams are both signs of the bequeathed Dharma of Śākyamuni Tathāgata;
they have no concern with your royal affairs.
When King Kṛkin heard this, he [understood].
Having forever severed the net of doubt, he rejoiced and leaped for joy;
he then further honored and made offerings to the Tathāgata Kāśyapa with various kinds of supreme and exquisite requisites.
They prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, circumambulated him to the right,
and withdrew. At that time, after the Tathāgata Śākyamuni had spoken these words,
Ajātaśatru, the King of Magadha, again addressed the Buddha, saying:
World-Honored One,
as the Buddha has said,
all evil sentient beings enter into hell.
How is it known who has previously seen [this]?
Furthermore, how is it known that one will fall into the realms of hungry ghosts or animals?
And who is it that sees one being born among humans or devas?
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Ajātaśatru,
saying: "Great King, you should listen with single-minded attention as I speak for your sake,
O King, so that you may directly perceive and understand it."
Great King, you should know that if a person’s life comes to an end, there are fifteen signs indicating they will fall into hell;
eight signs indicating they will be born among the hungry ghosts;
and five signs indicating they will be born among the animals.
When one is about to be born among humans or devas, there are ten signs for each.
Great King, what are the fifteen signs of being about to be born in hell?
First, one looks upon one's own spouse, children, and kinsmen with an evil eye.
Second, raising both hands to feel and trace the empty space;
third, not following the instructions of a spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*);
fourth, wailing and weeping with sobbing and streaming tears.
Fifth, they are unaware and unconscious of their excrement and urine.
Sixth, they keep their eyes closed and do not open them.
Seventh, they constantly cover their heads and faces.
Eighth, he sleeps on his side while eating and drinking.
Ninth, his body and mouth become foul-smelling and filthy.
Tenth, his feet and knees tremble and shake.
Eleventh, the bridge of the nose is tilted to one side.
Twelfth, the left eye twitches.
Thirteenth, both eyes turn bloodshot red.
Fourteenth, they lie face down.
Fifteenth, they lie curled up on their left side with their body touching the ground.
Great King, you should know that if there are sentient beings who possess these fifteen signs at the time of death, [they will fall into the lower realms].
They will certainly be reborn in the Avīci Hell.
Great King, you should know that if there is another person who,
at the time of their death, exhibits eight signs:
You should know that such a person will certainly fall into the realm of Yama within the preta destiny. What are the eight?
First, they are fond of licking their lips.
Second, their bodies are hot like fire.
Third, they are constantly afflicted by hunger and thirst and have a craving for food and drink.
Fourth, their mouths remain agape and cannot be closed.
Fifth, both eyes become parched and withered like those of a hawk or a peacock.
Sixth, there is no loss of urine or feces through leakage.
Seventh, the right knee becomes cold first.
Eighth, his right hand is always clenched in a fist.
Why is this? Because he harbors a mind of stinginess, even refusing to give water to others.
Great King, if one possesses these eight characteristics...
Upon the end of life, one will certainly be reborn among the hungry ghosts.
Great King, you should know that if there is another person who manifests five signs at the time of death:
Such a person will certainly fall into the realm of animals.
What are the five? First, they are stained by attachment to their wife and children, gazing at them with greed and unable to let go.
Second, the fingers of the hands and feet are curled;
third, sweat flows over the entire body;
fourth, coarse and raspy sounds are emitted.
Fifth, they chew foam with their mouths.
Great King, if one possesses these five traits,
at the end of life they will certainly fall into the realm of animals.
Great King, you should know that if there is a person who,
at the time of their death, experiences the manifestation of ten signs,
that person will certainly be reborn in the human realm.
What are the ten? First, at the time of death, one gives rise to wholesome thoughts;
that is to say, one generates a mind of gentleness, a mind of merit, a subtle and wondrous mind, a joyful mind, an initiating mind, and a mind free from sorrow.
Second, his body is free from pain.
Third, he is able to speak a few words and single-mindedly recollect his parents who gave him birth.
Fourth, he conceives a heart of compassion toward his wife, children, and grandchildren.
One gazes as usual, without attachment or aversion;
one desires to hear with the ear the names of brothers, sisters, and close acquaintances;
and fifth, one’s mind is not confused regarding what is wholesome or unwholesome.
Sixth, his mind is upright and free from flattery or deception.
Seventh, he knows that his parents, friends, and kinsmen protect and care for him well.
Eighth, he feels admiration in his heart when seeing them manage their affairs.
Ninth, he entrusted his household affairs to him, showing him where the treasures were stored and instructing him to bring them forth.
Tenth, he gave rise to pure faith and invited the Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha, personally taking refuge in and paying homage to them.
"I say: Homage to the Buddha, homage to the Dharma, homage to the Saṅgha; I now take refuge.
If there is no Buddha in the world, one takes refuge in the seers possessing the five supernatural powers.
Great King, if you are at the point of death, you shall possess these ten signs."
One will certainly be reborn among the human realm.
